অনেকেই জিজ্ঞাসা করেন, “ধর্মনিরপেক্ষ সংগীত শোনা কি পাপ? CCM (সমকালীন খ্রিস্টীয় সংগীত)-এ কি কোনো সমস্যা আছে? খ্রিস্টানদের র‍্যাপ, রক, কান্ট্রি, পপ বা রিদম অ্যান্ড ব্লুজ শোনা কি ঠিক?” এই প্রবন্ধের জন্য, উপরে উল্লিখিত সব সংগীতকে আমি “ধর্মনিরপেক্ষ” সংগীত বলব।

খ্রিস্টানদের কি শুধু “আ ক্যাপেলা” সংগীতই শোনা উচিত? সংগীত আকর্ষণীয়, এবং আমরা কীভাবে জীবন যাপন করি তার ওপর এর উল্লেখযোগ্য প্রভাব থাকতে পারে। সংগীত আমাদের নেতিবাচক বা ইতিবাচকভাবে প্রভাবিত করে। আমাদের জিজ্ঞাসা করা উচিত, “আমি যে সংগীত শুনি তা কি আমাকে ঈশ্বরের আরও কাছে টানে, নাকি তাঁর কাছ থেকে দূরে সরিয়ে শয়তানের আরও কাছে নিয়ে যায়?”

সংগীতের প্রধান উদ্দেশ্য হলো উপাসনা করা (কোনো কিছুর বা কারও প্রতি শ্রদ্ধা ও আরাধনা প্রকাশ করা)। তবু কখনো কখনো বিশ্বাসী হিসেবে আমরাও ভালো, নির্মল সংগীত শুনতে ব্যর্থ হই। এটি একটি সমস্যা, কারণ অধিকাংশ ধর্মনিরপেক্ষ সংগীত মন্দ এবং ঈশ্বর যা ঘৃণা করেন তা প্রচার করে।

ধর্মনিরপেক্ষ সংগীত খুব আকর্ষণীয় এবং আসক্তিকর। আমাদের দৈহিক স্বভাব ঈশ্বরভক্তিমূলক সংগীতের চেয়ে ধর্মনিরপেক্ষ সংগীত শুনতেই বেশি পছন্দ করে। এই ধরনের সংগীত মনকে নেতিবাচকভাবে প্রভাবিত করে এবং কোনো উপকারে আসে না। গানটি যদি মন্দ কাজ করতে উৎসাহ দেয়, জাগতিকতাকে প্রচার করে, আপনার মনে খারাপ চিন্তা আনে, আপনার কাজকর্মকে ভুল পথে বদলে দেয় এবং আপনার কথাবার্তাকে ভুল পথে প্রভাবিত করে, তাহলে আমাদের তা শোনা উচিত নয়। সংগীতের ব্যাপারে আমরা সহজেই নিজেদের কাছে মিথ্যা বলতে পারি। আপনি কি নিজেকে মিথ্যা বলেছেন? আপনি কি বলেছেন, “এই ধরনের সংগীত ঈশ্বরের কাছে গ্রহণযোগ্য,” অথচ অন্তরের গভীরে জানেন যে তিনি আপনাকে এ বিষয়ে দোষী সাব্যস্ত করছেন, এবং তিনি এটি মোটেই গ্রহণযোগ্য মনে করেন না?

ধর্মনিরপেক্ষ সংগীত প্রায়ই ইন্দ্রিয়সুখপরায়ণ হয়। ইন্দ্রিয়সুখপরায়ণতার অর্থ হলো “ইন্দ্রিয় ও শারীরিক তৃপ্তি জাগিয়ে তোলে এমন।” আমরা যে সংগীত শুনি তা কি ইন্দ্রিয়সুখপরায়ণ? তা কি আমাদের মনকে শুধু ছন্দের তালে চলার অবস্থায় নিয়ে যায়? এমন সংগীত শুনলে আমাদের শরীর কীভাবে সাড়া দিতে চায়? সংগীতের ছন্দে যদি আমাদের শরীর দোলে, তবে তা প্রভুকে সম্মান করে না; তা তাঁর নামের মহিমা প্রকাশ করে না; তা আমাদের মন ও শরীরকে প্রভুর উপাসনার উপযুক্ত অবস্থায় রাখে না।

সংগীত শুনলে আমরা সব সময়ই কোনো কিছুর উপাসনা করি। আমরা যদি ঈশ্বরের নয় এমন সংগীতে মনোযোগ দিই, তাহলে আমরা আমাদের দৈহিক স্বভাবের, জগতের, এমনকি শয়তানেরও উপাসনা করছি। সাধারণত, CCM-এর মতো সংগীত আমাদের দৃষ্টি ঈশ্বরের দিকে নয়, নিজেদের দিকে টানে। এই ধরনের সংগীত খুব ইন্দ্রিয়সুখপরায়ণ। এ ধরনের সংগীত শুনে কি আমরা সত্যিই ঈশ্বরের উপাসনা করতে পারি?

CCM হলো আধুনিক জনপ্রিয় সংগীতের একটি ধারা, যার গানের কথা খ্রিস্টীয় বিশ্বাস-সংশ্লিষ্ট বিষয়গুলোর ওপর কেন্দ্রীভূত। ১৯৬০-এর দশকের “যিশু আন্দোলন”-এর পুনর্জাগরণে প্রভাবিত ব্যক্তিরা যখন আরও সমকালীন সংগীতশৈলীতে নিজেদের প্রকাশ করতে শুরু করেন, তখন এই ধারার উদ্ভব হয়। তার আগে, সেই সময়ে গির্জায় স্তোত্র ও অন্যান্য গসপেল সংগীতই প্রচলিত ছিল। আমরা জানি বা না জানি, CCM-এর অনেক সংগীতে এমন স্থানে স্পন্দিত ছন্দ (সিঙ্কোপেশন) যোগ করা হয়, যেখানে তা স্বাভাবিকভাবে থাকার কথা নয়। CCM-এ প্রচলিত এই স্পন্দিত ছন্দ উপাসনায় মানুষের আত্মাকে আকৃষ্ট করে না; বরং তা দৈহিক স্বভাবকে আকৃষ্ট করে। যে সংগীত দৈহিক স্বভাবকে আকৃষ্ট করে তা ঈশ্বরের নয়, শয়তানের। আজ CCM শব্দটি পপ, রক বা প্রশংসা ও উপাসনার এমন ছন্দ ও তালের শৈলী বোঝাতে ব্যবহৃত হয়, যদি তার গানের কথা CCM-এর সংজ্ঞার মধ্যে পড়ে।

ফিলিপীয় পত্রে বলা হয়েছে, … যা কিছু সত্য, যা কিছু সম্মানজনক, যা কিছু ন্যায়সঙ্গত, যা কিছু পবিত্র, যা কিছু মনোহর, যা কিছু সুখ্যাতির যোগ্য; যদি কোনো সদ্‌গুণ থাকে এবং যদি কোনো প্রশংসার বিষয় থাকে, তবে সেই সব বিষয় চিন্তা করো –ফিলিপীয় ৪:৮।

ধর্মনিরপেক্ষ সংগীত ফিলিপীয় ৪:৮-এর পরীক্ষায় উত্তীর্ণ হয় না। অধিকাংশ ধর্মনিরপেক্ষ সংগীতে অপবিত্র গানের কথা থাকে, আর সেগুলোর সবকটিতেই এমন ছন্দ বা তাল রয়েছে যা ঈশ্বরের ব্যবস্থার বিরোধী। শয়তান এগুলো সবই ব্যবহার করে মানুষকে পাপ করতে বা পাপের কথা ভাবতে প্রভাবিত করে। কোনো না কোনোভাবে এটি আপনাকে প্রভাবিত করবে। আমরা যে সংগীত শুনি তার প্রভাব ভালো, না মন্দ? উদাহরণস্বরূপ, আমরা যদি এমন সংগীতে মনোযোগ দিই যা আমাদের চিন্তাভাবনা বা জীবনধারাকে ভুল পথে প্রভাবিত করে, তবে তা নেতিবাচক প্রভাব, যা আমাদের জীবন থেকে দূর করতে হবে।

দ্বিতীয় মন্দিরের পতনের পর, ৭০ খ্রিস্টাব্দে, ইহুদিরা বাদ্যযন্ত্র ছাড়া সংগীত ব্যবহারের প্রথা শুরু করে; পতনের পর শোকের সময় বাদ্যযন্ত্র ব্যবহারের অনুমতি ছিল না। ইতিহাসের ধারায় রেনেসাঁ যুগ পর্যন্ত বাদ্যযন্ত্রের সংগীতের সঙ্গে মূলত নাচ ও আমোদ-প্রমোদের সম্পর্ক ছিল। উপাসনার স্থানে খুব বেশি আনন্দ-ফুর্তি করা যেত না বলে, এই ধরনের আমোদমূলক সংগীত ধর্মীয় নেতাদের কাছে জনপ্রিয় ছিল না।

আ ক্যাপেলা একটি ইতালীয় শব্দবন্ধ, যার অর্থ “উপাসনালয়ের শৈলীতে”। প্রথমে এটি এমন সংগীত বোঝাতে ব্যবহৃত হতো, যা কোনো চ্যাপেল বা ছোট উপাসনাস্থলে বাদ্যযন্ত্রের সঙ্গত ছাড়া গাওয়া হতো; এর বিপরীতে, বড় গির্জায় সাধারণত কণ্ঠসংগীতের সঙ্গে অর্গান বাজানো হতো। সেই থেকে এই শব্দটির অর্থ হয়েছে সঙ্গত ছাড়া গাওয়া যেকোনো সংগীত—তা পবিত্র (ধর্মীয়) হোক বা ধর্মনিরপেক্ষ (অধর্মীয়)। আ ক্যাপেলা সংগীত বড় গায়কদল, ছোট দল অথবা এককভাবে গাওয়া যেতে পারে।

অর্থোডক্স ও রক্ষণশীল ইহুদি মণ্ডলীগুলোতে এখনো মূলত আ ক্যাপেলা গান গাওয়ার প্রথা রয়েছে। এসব সিনাগগে, একজন ক্যান্টর শাস্ত্রগ্রন্থ থেকে কোনো প্রামাণিক পাঠ আবৃত্তি বা গান করে শোনান, আর মণ্ডলী একইভাবে সাড়া দেয়—এটাই রীতি। ব্যবহৃত একমাত্র বাদ্যযন্ত্র হতে পারে সবার জন্য শুরুর স্বর নির্ধারণের একটি পিচ পাইপ, অথবা বিশেষ উপলক্ষ কিংবা ছুটির দিনে একটি ভেড়ার শিং।

প্রাথমিক মণ্ডলী ইহুদিদের ঐতিহ্য থেকে আ ক্যাপেলা গান গাওয়ার প্রথা গড়ে তোলে—গীতসংহিতা বা অন্যান্য শাস্ত্রাংশ আবৃত্তি করে এবং একজন ক্যান্টরকে নেতা হিসেবে ব্যবহার করে। প্রায় ৫৯০ খ্রিস্টাব্দ থেকে গ্রেগরীয় স্তোত্র ছিল গির্জার সংগীতের প্রধান ধরন। এটি একটি একক, সরল, সুরেলা ধারা, যা মুক্ত ছন্দে অর্ধেক কথার মতো, অর্ধেক গানের মতো করে গাওয়া হয়। প্রাথমিক মণ্ডলীতে বাদ্যযন্ত্রের সংগীতকে পাপপূর্ণ বহির্জগতের সঙ্গে যুক্ত করা হতো এবং নেতিবাচক প্রভাব বলে মনে করা হতো।

রেনেসাঁ যুগেও বাদ্যযন্ত্রের সঙ্গতবিহীন পবিত্র কণ্ঠসংগীতের প্রথা অব্যাহত ছিল। যদিও কখনো কখনো বাদ্যযন্ত্র কণ্ঠের কোনো সুরের সঙ্গে মিলিয়ে বাজানো হতো বা তার বদলে ব্যবহৃত হতো, তবু কণ্ঠসংগীত বেশির ভাগ সময় নিজস্বভাবেই পরিবেশিত হতো। চমৎকার ধ্বনিতত্ত্বসম্পন্ন কোনো চ্যাপেলে কণ্ঠশিল্পীদের গায়কদলের সুরের এক বিশেষ অতীন্দ্রিয় প্রভাব ছিল।

জিওভান্নি পিয়েরলুইজি দা প্যালেস্ত্রিনা ছিলেন ইতালির রেনেসাঁ যুগের অন্যতম গুরুত্বপূর্ণ সুরকার; তিনি গির্জার জন্য শত শত মাস ও মোটেট রচনা করেছিলেন। ‘প্যালেস্ত্রিনা শৈলী’ নামে পরিচিত এই শৈলী ছিল একটি পরিশীলিত আ ক্যাপেলা রীতি, যেখানে অনেক কণ্ঠশিল্পী ভিন্ন ভিন্ন সুর ও কথা গাইতেন, এবং সেগুলো বিভিন্ন সময়ে শুরু হতো। একে বলা হতো বহুস্বরিক; এর বিপরীতে, সমস্বরিক বলতে বোঝায় একটি সুরের ধারা, যা একসঙ্গে বা একই ছন্দে গাওয়া হয়।

প্রেরিত পৌল লেখেন, গীতসংহিতা, স্তোত্র ও আত্মিক গানের মাধ্যমে পরস্পরের সঙ্গে কথা বলো; তোমাদের হৃদয়ে প্রভুর উদ্দেশে গান করো এবং সুর তোলো; –ইফিষীয় ৫:১৯। এটি কি বাদ্যযন্ত্র দিয়ে সংগীত তৈরির মতো শোনায়? নাকি বরং হৃদয় থেকে ঈশ্বরের প্রশংসা গাওয়ার মতো মনে হয়?

আর মধ্যরাত্রে পৌল ও সীল প্রার্থনা করছিলেন এবং ঈশ্বরের প্রশংসা গাইছিলেন; আর বন্দিরা তা শুনছিল –প্রেরিত ১৬:২৫। পৌল ও সীল যখন কারাগারে ছিলেন, বেড়িতে বাঁধা অবস্থায় মধ্যরাতে গান গাইছিলেন, তখন আমার মনে হয় না যে তাঁরা নিজেদের মহিমা বাড়ানোর জন্য গাইছিলেন। তাঁরা ঈশ্বর পিতার মহিমা প্রকাশ করার জন্য গাইছিলেন। ঈশ্বরকে মহিমা দেওয়ার ফল ছিল অত্যন্ত বিস্ময়কর। ভূমিকম্প হলো, কারাগারের ভিত্তি কেঁপে উঠল, দরজাগুলো খুলে গেল, আর সবার শিকল খুলে গেল। এই ঘটনা ঘটার পর কারারক্ষক কাঁপতে কাঁপতে পৌল ও সীলের সামনে এসে জিজ্ঞাসা করলেন: “পরিত্রাণ পেতে হলে আমাকে কী করতে হবে?”

কলসীয় পত্রেও বলা হয়েছে, আমাদের উচিত খ্রিস্টের বাক্যকে সমস্ত প্রজ্ঞাসহ তোমাদের মধ্যে প্রচুর পরিমাণে বাস করতে দেওয়া; গীতসংহিতা, স্তোত্র ও আত্মিক গানের মাধ্যমে পরস্পরকে শিক্ষা ও উপদেশ দেওয়া, এবং তোমাদের হৃদয়ে অনুগ্রহসহকারে প্রভুর উদ্দেশে গান করা –কলসীয় ৩:১৬। আমরা কি গীতসংহিতা, স্তোত্র ও আত্মিক গানকে আমাদের শিক্ষা দিতে, উপদেশ দিতে এবং উৎসাহিত করতে দিই?

অলিভ পর্বতে যাওয়ার আগে শেষ ভোজে যিশু তাঁর শিষ্যদের সঙ্গে কোন স্তোত্র গেয়েছিলেন, তা ভাবি। আমার সন্দেহ, তাঁরা নিজেদের উদ্দেশে গাইছিলেন না। আমার বিশ্বাস, তাঁরা তাঁদের স্বর্গীয় পিতার উদ্দেশে গাইছিলেন।

বিশুদ্ধ ও পবিত্র সংগীত প্রভুর কাছ থেকে এক আশীর্বাদ। এটি এমন সুন্দর ও শক্তিশালী বিষয় যে একে হেলাফেলা করা উচিত নয়। কখনো কখনো ঈশ্বর এর মাধ্যমে আমাদের সঙ্গে কথা বলেন। আমি দৃঢ়ভাবে বিশ্বাস করি, সব খ্রিস্টানেরই সপ্তাহজুড়ে ঈশ্বরভক্তিমূলক সংগীত শোনা দরকার, শুধু রবিবারে নয়। এটি আমাকে শান্ত থাকতে, উৎসাহ পেতে এবং প্রভুর প্রতি মনোযোগ ধরে রাখতে সাহায্য করে। আমার মন যখন প্রভুর প্রতি নিবদ্ধ থাকে, তখন আমি আশীর্বাদপ্রাপ্ত হয়ে দিন কাটাতে পারি।

ঈশ্বরের বিষয়গুলো নিয়ে আমাদের নিজেদের শৃঙ্খলাবদ্ধ করতে হবে। আমাদের জীবন থেকে এমন বিষয়ও দূর করতে হবে, যেগুলোতে ঈশ্বর সন্তুষ্ট নন—তা আমরা জানি। ঈশ্বরভক্তিমূলক সংগীত (যে সংগীত আমাদের আত্মা ও মনকে ঈশ্বরের কাছ থেকে আসা বিষয়গুলোর দিকে টানে) হলো সেই ধরনের সংগীত, যা বিশ্বাসীদের শোনা উচিত। শেষ পর্যন্ত বিষয়টি উপাসনার—আমরা কি ঈশ্বরের উপাসনা করি, নাকি অন্য কিছুর?

যিশু বলেন, কিন্তু সেই সময় আসছে, আর এখনই তা উপস্থিত, যখন সত্য উপাসকেরা আত্মায় ও সত্যে পিতার উপাসনা করবে; কারণ পিতা এমন উপাসকদেরই খোঁজেন –যোহন ৪:২৩।

তাই, এসো আমরা আমাদের সৃষ্টিকর্তার উদ্দেশে আন্তরিক উপাসনায় গান করি; তিনি আমাদের যে কণ্ঠ দিয়েছেন, তার জন্য ঈশ্বরকে মহিমা দিই; আর আমাদের ঈশ্বরের উদ্দেশে ঈশ্বরভক্তিমূলক, নির্মল গান গাই ও শুনি।

Ramona* was a little girl who was very busy and active. Like other four-year-old’s, there were a lot of things Ramona could do. She could ride a bike, climb a tree, wash dishes, write her name, and ride her pony all by herself. One of Ramona’s favorite things to do was to ride horses. Her family had two horses and a pony. How fun those evenings were when they would hitch their pony, Tony, to the cart, and the whole family would take turns riding. Or when Ramona and three of her sisters would pack onto Tony’s back and go for a ride.

There were lots of things Ramona could do, but sometimes she thought she could do more than she really could. And sometimes she thought she was bigger than she really was.

One beautiful Summer evening, some guests came to Ramona’s house. When guests came, that usually meant a fun time.

On this particular evening, after supper, Ramona’s older siblings were riding horses with the guests. It looked like so much fun as they trotted around the pond and through the lawn. Ramona wanted to ride too, but she had to wait her turn. While she waited, she played on the lawn with Clifford, the dog. She soon tired of that and went for a spin on her bike. Then an idea popped into her mind. She ran off to the pasture entrance and climbed up the gate. She liked to pretend she was a monkey, swinging on the bars and climbing up and down. Then she tried balancing on a bar and taking her hands off the gate. Her siblings and their guests were riding nearby. Ramona threw her arms into the air, and while balancing on the gate, yelled to the riders, “Look at me! Look at me!” She felt very big to be balancing on the gate. Suddenly, her foot slipped and, down she went, into the dust. She blinked with surprise and quickly jumped up, brushing off her dress. She looked around, embarrassed, but no one seemed to notice. She climbed back up the side of the gate and began playing again. Ramona grew impatient, waiting for her ride. No one seemed to remember that she wanted to ride the horses. She thought it would be fun to see how high she could balance on the gate, so she climbed as high as she dared. She wanted others to see how brave she was, so waving her arms, she shouted, “Hey everyone! Look at me!” But again, her foot slipped off the gate. This time, however, she narrowly escaped falling to the ground. Ramona’s dad saw her and walked over to her. “Ramona,” he said, “I want you to stay off the gate.”

Ramona got down and tried to find something else to do. After playing for a while, her father’s command to stay off the gate seemed to slip from her mind, and she started climbing on the gate again. Then Ramona’s older sister, Elise, walked over, and quietly told her, “Ramona, you shouldn’t be showing off to our guests.” Ramona didn’t like that advice. Into one ear and out the other it went. She assured herself that she wasn’t showing off! She was just… well, just playing.

She climbed up just as high as she could, and once again, she waved her arms in the air, crying, “Look at me, everyone!” Suddenly, before she knew what was happening, she had landed on the ground with a thud and began to cry at the top of her lungs. Sure, she felt some pain, but mostly she was shocked and ashamed.

Ramona’s father came over to her and picked her up, making sure she wasn’t badly hurt, and carried her to the house. It was yet light outside, and still early in the evening, but he took her upstairs to her bed.

Before putting her to bed, he talked with her. Ramona was still crying, and Papa attempted to dry her tears. “Ramona, listen, can you be quiet for a bit? Why do you think you fell?” She sniffled and shrugged her shoulders. Papa continued, “If you would have obeyed me, and stayed off the gate like I told you to, you would not have fallen. Elise also told you to stop showing off, but you didn’t listen. Do you know that showing off is really pride? The Bible says, Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall –Proverbs 16:18.

Ramona nodded her head. “Are you sorry for disobeying me, Ramona?” Papa asked. “Yes, Papa, I am sorry” she replied tearfully. Papa decided to let her fall and going to bed early be her punishment this time. Ramona would have preferred a spanking instead of needing to go to bed early, which was a great grief to her little heart. But it was good for her because it caused her to repent.

Ramona never forgot this lesson, partly because of her fall, and partly because she was sent to bed early and missed the fun of riding horses. Not only had she been proud in showing off, she had also been willfully disobedient to Papa.

Elise had written a tune to the verse that Papa had mentioned to Ramona. From then on, whenever Ramona sang that song, she remembered how true that verse proved to be for her.

Ramona* era una bambina molto indaffarata e vivace. Come gli altri bambini di quattro anni, Ramona sapeva fare tante cose. Sapeva andare in bicicletta, arrampicarsi su un albero, lavare i piatti, scrivere il suo nome e cavalcare da sola il suo pony. Una delle cose che preferiva fare era andare a cavallo. La sua famiglia aveva due cavalli e un pony. Che belle serate erano quelle in cui attaccavano il pony, Tony, al calesse e tutta la famiglia faceva a turno per salirci. Oppure quando Ramona e tre delle sue sorelle si stringevano sulla schiena di Tony e facevano un giro.

C’erano tante cose che Ramona sapeva fare, ma a volte pensava di saper fare più di quanto fosse realmente capace. E a volte pensava di essere più grande di quanto fosse davvero.

Una bella sera d’estate, alcuni ospiti vennero a casa di Ramona. Quando arrivavano degli ospiti, di solito ci si divertiva.

Quella sera, dopo cena, i fratelli e le sorelle maggiori di Ramona cavalcavano con gli ospiti. Sembrava così divertente vederli trottare intorno allo stagno e attraversare il prato. Anche Ramona voleva cavalcare, ma doveva aspettare il suo turno. Mentre aspettava, giocò sul prato con Clifford, il cane. Ben presto si stancò e fece un giro in bicicletta. Poi le venne un’idea. Corse all’ingresso del pascolo e si arrampicò sul cancello. Le piaceva fingere di essere una scimmia, dondolandosi sulle sbarre e arrampicandosi su e giù. Poi provò a stare in equilibrio su una sbarra e a staccare le mani dal cancello. I suoi fratelli e le sue sorelle e i loro ospiti cavalcavano lì vicino. Ramona alzò le braccia in aria e, mentre stava in equilibrio sul cancello, gridò ai cavalieri: «Guardatemi! Guardatemi!» Si sentiva molto grande, mentre stava in equilibrio sul cancello. All’improvviso, il piede le scivolò e cadde a terra, nella polvere. Sgranò gli occhi per la sorpresa e si rialzò in fretta, spolverandosi il vestito. Si guardò intorno, imbarazzata, ma nessuno sembrava essersi accorto di nulla. Si arrampicò di nuovo sul lato del cancello e ricominciò a giocare. Ramona diventava impaziente mentre aspettava di poter cavalcare. Nessuno sembrava ricordarsi che anche lei voleva andare a cavallo. Pensò che sarebbe stato divertente vedere quanto in alto riuscisse a stare in equilibrio sul cancello, così si arrampicò più in alto che osava. Voleva che gli altri vedessero quanto fosse coraggiosa, così, agitando le braccia, gridò: «Ehi, tutti! Guardatemi!» Ma il piede le scivolò di nuovo dal cancello. Questa volta, però, per poco non cadde a terra. Il papà di Ramona la vide e le si avvicinò. «Ramona», disse, «voglio che tu stia lontana dal cancello».

Ramona scese e cercò qualcos’altro da fare. Dopo aver giocato per un po’, l’ordine di suo padre di stare lontana dal cancello sembrò svanirle dalla mente e ricominciò ad arrampicarsi sul cancello. Allora sua sorella maggiore Elise si avvicinò e le disse piano: «Ramona, non dovresti metterti in mostra davanti ai nostri ospiti». A Ramona quel consiglio non piacque. Le entrò da un orecchio e le uscì dall’altro. Si ripeté che non si stava mettendo in mostra! Stava solo… beh, stava solo giocando.

Si arrampicò più in alto che poteva e, ancora una volta, agitò le braccia in aria, gridando: «Guardatemi tutti!» All’improvviso, prima ancora di rendersi conto di cosa stesse succedendo, era atterrata a terra con un tonfo e cominciò a piangere a squarciagola. Certo, sentiva un po’ di dolore, ma soprattutto era sconvolta e mortificata.

Il papà di Ramona le si avvicinò e la sollevò, assicurandosi che non si fosse fatta male seriamente, poi la portò in casa. Fuori c’era ancora luce ed era ancora presto, ma lui la portò di sopra, a letto.

Prima di metterla a letto, parlò con lei. Ramona piangeva ancora e papà cercò di asciugarle le lacrime. «Ramona, ascolta, puoi stare zitta un momento? Perché pensi di essere caduta?» Lei tirò su col naso e alzò le spalle. Papà continuò: «Se mi avessi obbedito e fossi stata lontana dal cancello, come ti avevo detto, non saresti caduta. Anche Elise ti aveva detto di smettere di metterti in mostra, ma tu non l’hai ascoltata. Sai che mettersi in mostra è in realtà orgoglio? La Bibbia dice: La superbia precede la rovina, e lo spirito altero precede la caduta – Proverbi 16:18.

Ramona annuì. «Ti dispiace di avermi disobbedito, Ramona?» chiese papà. «Sì, papà, mi dispiace», rispose lei tra le lacrime. Papà decise che, quella volta, la punizione sarebbe stata la caduta e l’andare a letto presto. Ramona avrebbe preferito una sculacciata piuttosto che dover andare a letto presto, cosa che le causava un grande dispiacere nel suo piccolo cuore. Ma le fece bene, perché la portò a pentirsi.

Ramona non dimenticò mai questa lezione, in parte per via della caduta e in parte perché era stata mandata a letto presto e si era persa il divertimento di andare a cavallo. Non solo era stata orgogliosa nel mettersi in mostra, ma aveva anche disobbedito deliberatamente a papà.

Elise aveva composto una melodia per il versetto che papà aveva citato a Ramona. Da allora, ogni volta che cantava quella canzone, Ramona ricordava quanto quel versetto si fosse dimostrato vero per lei.

We asked the Lord for him, our third child, third son. He came with the springtime, the crowning creation of new life, bewailing his shuffled surroundings. Folks commented on his wail: they thought it was adorable. We thought so, too. We loved him, we snuggled him, and we called him Judson.

Sterling and I had committed, prior to Judson’s birth, to take our youth group on a mission trip to Mexico. The date to leave for this trip fell five weeks after Judson came. As the leader’s wife, I was responsible to take food along to feed our group for the entire time. Making lists and shopping for it consumed me with preparation.

Judson did his own preparing. He developed bowel trouble. He went seven days without a messy pamper. I asked my midwife about it, but she was unruffled by the occurrence. When it went another seven days until the next full diaper, I asked his pediatrician. She, too, was unconcerned. So, we headed for Mexico: Sterling and I, our five-week-old baby, and two vanloads of youth.

Although the preparation had been taxing for me, the time in Mexico was like vacation. My only requirements while there were to take care of my baby and oversee mealtimes. But Judson didn’t like the trip at all. I cuddled him for hours, sitting under a tarp on a dramatic hillside, overlooking the construction site where our group was laboring. Judson acted restless and uncomfortable with me. He cried if anyone else held him. I felt something was amiss, but I had no definite signs of what, except that day after day passed without a dirty diaper.

On our sixth night in Mexico, I laid Judson on his cot. But the Lord drew me back, prompting me to pull him into bed beside me. I felt this nudge distinctly and obeyed, although I had let Judson sleep in the cot the other nights. We slept. Somewhere in the night, Judson awoke, refusing to be pacified. I tried this and that, half asleep myself. Suddenly he screamed out, only to choke mid-scream and then go limp.

“Sterling!” I yelped. “Turn on the flashlight! He’s not breathing!” I sat up in bed, examining my baby in the flashlight’s beam. His little face worked desperately, but no breath or sound came forth. Within seconds, his breath returned, and he screamed again. Then he choked. As surely as an invisible hand clutching his fragile neck, his breath ceased, and his eyes bulged in terror. I swiped my finger through his mouth, checking for something lodged in his airway, finding nothing. Shuddering, Judson gasped and cried. Tears forced themselves out of his eyes. “Oh, pray,” I begged. Sterling prayed, jumbling pleas together in a heavenward heap as our baby ceased breathing again. The episode repeated itself several more times: seconds of terrified screaming, then seconds of tortured silence. Sweat popped out on Judson’s face. It was agonizing to watch. Thoughts flew through my head: Our baby’s going to die. Just like that. No warning. Out here with no medical aid. Oh God! Help us, help us, help us! How does one just watch their baby die?

“I’m getting the missionary’s wife,” Sterling decided. I stammered dangling prayers while supporting Judson. When the missionary’s wife appeared, I handed him to her, grateful for the presence of a woman older than I. We prayed together, begging God to intervene. Judson began to cry and breath normally while she examined him. She handed him back to me as he calmed down.

“I don’t know what it is,” she said, after we told her the story. We thanked her for rousing in the night, then returned to our room. I cried while Judson peacefully slept in my arms.

“I sense it was a demoniac display,” Sterling stated. “If the devil can get us scared over what could happen to our baby while we are out in the boondocks, then he can get us to pack up our whole group and leave. The devil knows there are good things happening here, spiritually; this is not the time to flee. We can’t let him fill us with fear.”

I agreed. The unusual way Judson’s breath came and went looked as if an evil hand was gripping his neck. There seemed to be no natural explanation otherwise for the horrifying event. Sterling laid his hand on Judson and prayed, specifically rebuking the devil, and seeking the protection of God. We laid us down in peace and safety and slept.

In the morning, Judson seemed untroubled by the episode, although his restlessness increased. Eight, nine, and then ten days passed with no bowel movement. He cried, his soft, adorable cry agitating my heart. As we traveled back to the States, I fretted over the way he drew back from nursing, squirming and fussing until he fell asleep instead.

Then he began spitting up. When he finally spit up bright yellow liquid, I was alarmed. On the eleventh day, we visited a nurse practitioner in a Mennonite colony in Mexico. She examined Judson, listened to my report, and calmly replied, “And this is your first child?”

“No,” I responded, matching calm with calm. “This is my third.” She met my eyes then, silently, and reexamined Judson. She gave him a suppository, suggesting all babies are different. And so, they are. This one certainly was! With the topical relief of the suppository, Judson seemed to feel better.

He was seven weeks old when we came home. From the time he was three weeks until he was seven months, he struggled with his bowels.

On Sundays, people fingered his tiny face, commenting on his sweet little cry. Other days, I huddled in the rocker, hearing but not hearing his sweet little cry. Some days it seemed it never stopped. I held him except while he napped. I became familiar with his cycle: a span of days with no mess in which he gradually grew grumpier, a slacking off nursing, and finally, outright crying until I gave him the temporary relief of a suppository. Contrary to regular suspicion, he was not constipated. It appeared to my mother-sense that something within him did not naturally trigger his bowels to move.

“Grain free,” prompted one book. “It could be Hirschsprung’s, which can be naturally treated by going grain-free.” So, I ate grain-free. Five weeks dragged by on my altered diet. Judson didn’t seem to notice my efforts.

His pediatrician listened to my recital of his routine, then ordered a test for Hirschsprung’s.

The test came back clear. I gratefully resumed eating grains, only to meet with new advice the next Sunday. An experienced mother sought me out in the nursery where I took refuge from the noisy fellowship hall, rocking my sonny, rocking, rocking, rocking. “Have you considered dairy-free?”

Well, no, I hadn’t.

“I think you should try dairy-free,” she decided. Like a well-thumbed medical manual, she recounted the reasons for this route.

His pediatrician didn’t approve of the dairy-free idea. I visited her office after three weeks of it. “You need the fats in dairy to keep up your milk supply,” she scolded. “Besides, the first sign of a milk intolerance is blood in the stool, not lack of stool.”

I didn’t mind stopping the dairy-free diet. We tried other things. Judson held enemas in stubbornly. A prescribed dosage of laxative didn’t produce results. At one point, the doctor instructed me to just wait it out with Judson, convinced his bowels would move on their own. Judson outwaited me. By 17 days along, I resorted to suppositories to give my miserable baby relief.

But it wasn’t only the digestive mystery that gave us heartache over my baby. Even on a freshly emptied system, he was cantankerous. Mealtimes became misery. Judson fought when I sat down at the table to join the family for a meal. I became used to pinning him over my shoulder while I quickly ate, one-handed. Except I didn’t become used to it. I never became accustomed to his fussing. I learned to do the housework while he napped, as anything other than tending him was impossible when he was awake.

Church was also a sore spot. Judson acted worse in any place of activity, but he became unreasonable at church. I wrestled with him until he fell asleep, usually in time for me to hear the last part of the sermon.

Fellowship meals were a disaster. Judson screamed. He would let no one touch him other than me, and even then, I couldn’t calm him down. By the time we had fixed plates and fed our little family, I was exhausted and ready to go home. It seemed like he was afraid of something. What it was, I couldn’t figure out.

Gradually I became aware he even acted afraid of Sterling. Whereas our other boys by this age had learned to recognize Sterling as “more fun than Mommy”, Judson didn’t. He pulled away from his daddy. He resisted Sterling’s efforts to make up, clinging to me fiercely.

And my mother-instinct, grounded deep beneath the waves of weariness, responded. In an oxymoron of emotions, I no sooner handed Judson to someone else than his obvious desperation for me tugged at my heart; and I would take him back, nestling him close, calming him down. It seemed even as he ruled and berated and emptied me, his intense need fulfilled me. I didn’t understand it.

“I think you need to get him on a quality probiotic,” my mother-in-law suggested. That sounded good, at least on Sunday evening. Somehow the weeks passed, and I didn’t find time to locate a quality probiotic.

“Try a good multivitamin,” another friend advised after observing us during prayer meeting. “It really could be worms. I knew this little girl who was totally unreasonable; she just screamed and screamed, and once they treated her for worms, it totally cleared up…”

That sounded good, too. It also sounded huge. I didn’t know where to begin research on “worms”, nor did I have the mental space.

When he was about six months old, we had the worst stint with him: almost a week wherein he cried and cried, refusing to nurse or be comforted. We requested an anointing by our ministry. We waited expectantly after the anointing. Within hours Judson was back to his restless fussing. We waited a couple more days before updating his pediatrician. Per her advice, Sterling & I took him to the hospital, where a specialist in pediatric gastroenterology could help us. It frightened us to take our puzzling, vulnerable baby to the hospital. “Pray for us,” we requested as we told our families and brotherhood about it.

By the time we checked in to the hospital, Judson had perked up. The nurse showed us to a room. She laid Judson in the cold, caged hospital bed and dressed him in a coarse gown. While we waited for the doctor to come in, Sterling and I marveled at the change in our son. He lay in the bed quietly, fingering the rails and looking around. Not for three minutes, not for 30, but for an hour, finally drifting off to sleep. This was unheard-of behavior for Judson. We looked at each other sheepishly.

“I feel pretty foolish,” I confessed to Sterling. “What are the doctors going to think when they find this healthy little fellow? What about the huge hospital bill?” I covered my face with my hands.

Sterling shrugged, as puzzled as I. “I think people must have been praying.”

That was the turning point in Judson’s physical wellbeing. The hospital released us the next day, signing a bill of good health in Judson’s report. They couldn’t find anything wrong with our child. Soon thereafter, his bowel trouble cleared up. He became regular as the sunrise, all too regular for the lady who hitherto had needed no extra diapers, wipes, or clothes. We praised the Lord for answered prayer.

But he still cried. Months passed while we looked ahead to each accomplishment: maybe when this tooth comes in, maybe when he starts crawling, maybe when he starts walking. Judson crawled at six months, walked at ten months, ate—or more accurately didn’t eat—table food, and still he fussed. I walked around with a little “leech” on my skirt some days. Other days I didn’t walk. Sterling attempted to hold him while I ate supper, but Judson hated that worse than he hated sitting with me for meals, and I would soon relent to his pleading cries. About the only time he was content was while he slept. Most puzzling was his apparent fear of Sterling and his irrational behavior at church.

“Are we just spoiling him?” I asked Sterling. “Maybe he just doesn’t want to sit still in church like any other baby.”

Sterling thought. “If that was so, then why would he resist fellowship meals so fiercely? That should be a fun time. Or if you were spoiling him, why wouldn’t he want to do fun things like come outside with me, or eat snacks?”

I didn’t know. I didn’t think I was spoiling him, but I couldn’t tell. I thought even a spoiled baby should enjoy being away from its mother occasionally. Not Judson. He rode around with me continually, one hand clutching my neckline, the other hand pushing himself away to see where we were headed. If he didn’t like our direction, he often attempted to steer me by surprisingly strong lunging. His anxious, overly alert actions puzzled me. Perhaps something more was wrong, something relating to his nervous system.

“You know, when we took in my niece, she had bonding issues,” one sister told me over fellowship meal. Judson had his open mouth turned away from her, so we were actually visiting over the hubbub in the hall. “She had never bonded with anyone due to her poor home situation. I took to carrying her around with me everywhere I went until she bonded with me. The way Judson acts insecure, even when he is with you, makes me think he hasn’t bonded. Perhaps that’s why he panics whenever you put him down.” Maybe. But where and when would he have gotten bonding issues?

“Did he have a traumatic birth?” the lady inquired.

I thought it over. “Well, no…” I glanced back at the scary episode in Mexico. Perhaps that had undone the natural bonding process. Or maybe the time in the hospital. Maybe his stint with whooping cough as an eight-month-old. As these moments scrolled through my mind, I realized Judson’s babyhood really had been difficult. Maybe there was good reason his emotional balance was off kilter. He did seem insecure now. Frightened. On “survival mode” all the time, me being his dubious source of momentary safety. If he did have bonding issues, then I would have been doing the wrong thing his entire baby life. I repeatedly tried to let other people, like his grandmothers, hold him, hoping he would realize he was fine with them. It didn’t work. Talking with this lady caused me to look doubtfully at my tactics, worried I had hurt Judson worse by doing this. At least carrying him around all the time would be free.

I procured a baby carrier and took to wearing him as I worked. He loved it, but my back did not. I soon gave that practice up, too, after no hopeful signs of bonding occurred. If my spirit was going to be worn down by caring for this child, at least my back didn’t need to be.

We tried discipline. After all, we were working on raising two other boys, and discipline was not a new thing in our home. It didn’t seem we had done anything different with Judson than we did with the other boys, but the results were certainly different. Judson responded with uncontrollable terror. The soft infant cry was long gone. We were unsure how to teach him to be happy in Sterling’s care, for discipline only seemed to heighten his distress. And how does one teach a child to play away from his mother? After a few exhausting sessions at church, wherein he refused to respond, we began to feel a spanking wasn’t the tool to get through to him. Indeed, it felt we never got through to him. But if a spanking didn’t work, how else could we teach him? I recalled seeing other mothers clamp their hands over their toddler’s mouth to teach them that wailing didn’t bring the desired result. Perhaps he needed to be taught how to stop crying. I tried it for a while.

Shortly after Judson turned one, his behavior reached a terrible climax. He was big enough to refuse direction or pacification. Discipline seemed to make him go crazy. Finally, I reached for a book about child development. One description on a condition called retained fear reflex described our child exactly. With simple therapeutic practice, the book promised, we could correct this. However, we would need an expert in this field to work with us, teaching us the therapy.

“What do you think?” I asked Sterling after sharing the book’s information with him.

His face looked unsure. “I don’t know,” he pondered aloud. “This isn’t what I would have been taught about raising a child. I always thought love, prayer, and consistent discipline were the keys to normal childcare. We have no proof other than fussiness that something is wrong with Judson. I hesitate to label him.”

I did, too. While we both acknowledged the special needs of some children, and the gift of specially trained caregivers, we didn’t want to hastily tack an excusing name on Judson’s behavior.

But the exhaustion of caring for him rolled back in like a fog the next day. We talked about the retained fear reflex again. We’d tried the love, definitely. We’d tried prayer, at least in a measure. The consistent discipline was another matter. Unlike our other boys, it didn’t seem to work with Judson. According to the text on retained fear reflexes, discipline could be accomplishing the opposite of its intention.

“You may call and get an appointment with the therapist,” Sterling decided. “It’s worth a try. She’s a Christian, too, and isn’t suggesting anything beyond physical exercises to retrain the brain.”

So I did. The therapist lived eight hours away, which was nothing to brush aside. But the promise of help seemed worth the drive to us. In the meantime, I shared with a few people what we were thinking. A few of them promised to pray for us. My mother-in-law offered a children’s supplement for calming and focus. I also made it to the health food store and procured a probiotic and multivitamin. The time for the therapist appointment drew close.

“I don’t see how we can go,” Sterling said a few days before. “Our weeks have been super busy, and we are all tired. I can’t see how we can fit in a two-day road trip just for one short appointment. But I guess we’ll have to. If it helps Judson, that will be worth it.”

Tension tugged at my neck, too, just thinking about the trip. That week we made a concentrated effort on Judson’s training. We worked with him firmly, attempting to bring his will into line with ours. He despised it. Any time Sterling took him, he reacted violently. I set aside times each day to sit with him on the sofa, holding his hands and requiring silence, with middling results.

The Sunday before we needed to head out to the appointment, we accepted a dinner invitation to a home we were not very familiar with. I spent the time wrestling with my small son, swallowing mouthfuls of pride and comfort while doing so. Meanwhile, Sterling talked with the men about our struggles with Judson, referencing the idea of his fearfulness and the route of therapy.

“Have you ever thought about how Judson must feel when you discipline him in the way I observed your wife do earlier?” one of the men questioned gently. “I noticed the expression in Judson’s eyes as she restrained him, covering his mouth. He looked terrified. If you really think he has this issue with fear, perhaps you should try looking at discipline from his point of view. One of our children also responded unreasonably to our regular methods of training until I began to describe to them what I was about to do…” With discretion, this brother shared an experience with their child.

Sterling was stunned and blessed by the gentle insight. The men shared a little more. It was as if we had been too close to the situation to fully see it, and the Lord had given us perspective from a wise onlooker. We agreed to cancel the childhood development appointment and rethink our training methods. We decided to try clearly explaining to Judson our expectations and the consequences of disobedience. Instead of restraining him, demanding surrender to our desires, we agreed to use repeated small switches to reprimand his willfulness.

“I’m going to take this week to completely focus on mealtimes,” Sterling decided. “Of course, that means you will take the brunt of this, since you feed Judson two out of three meals. But I will try to take the heavier load. I’m also going to fast and pray for answers for this child. We’ve tried to train him at mealtimes before but have never stuck it out more than a day or two. There’s always ‘something going on’ and we slack off. But this is important. Too important to keep letting ‘life’ interfere.”

I agreed with him. My spirit rose with hope and rest in this decision. Something about the therapy route had not seemed correct, yet we had been desperate for an answer.

That week was tough. The other boys ate alone while I spent extended time at the table with Judson. He screamed at my clear expectation of sitting still and eating. He writhed, he gagged, he cried. I prayed and switched. At supper time, Sterling took over. Judson resisted this still more wildly. The first evening it was three hours before our child obeyed and swallowed a small amount of food for his father. Several more evenings passed with similar time frames. Sterling worked with Judson gently and firmly, speaking to him, spanking, holding. I tried to block out the sound. My commitment to stand behind my husband in this all tussled with my emotions, but I didn’t give in this time when Judson looked at me with begging eyes.

By the end of the first week, Judson showed steps of improvement. He stopped crying at mealtimes. He sat in his highchair, eating a few bites for us obediently. With a comically pathetic expression, he would offer Sterling and I each one of his little paddies to hold while he ate, as if that gave him courage. We continued with intentional training in this area alone. By the end of the second week, his behavior all around had improved. He began to let loose of me, seeking entertainment on his own, toddling around the house with happy babbling. I watched in amazement while he did normal baby things: exploring the toy box, climbing on sofas, dabbling in toilets. He ventured outside alone, soon learning to play with balls and trucks. I stopped giving him the various supplements since he was doing so well.

Then one gladsome day when the boys chorused “Daddy’s home!”, Judson squealed in delight. The next evening when Sterling arrived, he squealed again, this time happily heading for the door. I opened it for him. He toddled to the truck where Sterling was. Sterling carried him into the house. Judson looked at me triumphantly from his daddy’s arms with a burbling comment on the situation. He made no move for me. We knew then Sterling had won his heart. From that time until now, he has been a different child.

Now we watch him with delight. His little countenance is bright and beaming, his eyes clear and content. He is evidently secure. He has become a joy to have around, charming our family with his toddling antics. Not only has he bonded with Sterling, he has widened his circle of acceptance to others as well. He interacts well with his brothers. He responds reasonably to training in other areas. We love him, this third little son of ours.

So what really was wrong with Judson? I think he had a physical abnormality in the first months of his life, causing him discomfort. His was a rocky babyhood. In retrospect, I see that spoiling him crept in unawares.

Somewhere in the transition between need and demand, I began to cater to his little self. It was sneakily gradual. Incredibly early on, he obviously realized that crying controlled me. I couldn’t see it. We couldn’t see it. We couldn’t see it until after we began to take back the parental control in his training. We still don’t know when it happened or how. But this we do know: God’s way works.

Prayer works. The rod of correction works. A wife standing behind her husband as he disciplines his child in love works. In a plan that defies human reasoning, let alone worldly teaching, the process of molding Judson’s will firmly bonded him to his father. This created security in his small world. Sterling is in charge. Judson is at rest and safe in this. It removed from him the burden of controlling his world. He is free to relate to either of us, free from the tyrannical demands of his small selfish nature. Something about the clarity of his daddy being the authority in his life has also established my authority over him.

Over two years have passed since Sterling began turning Judson’s heart and will towards his own. Today, Judson is a joyful, well-adjusted boy. He sits quietly in church and devotions; he enjoys fellowship meals and his friends; he eagerly spends time with either Daddy or Mommy. Stubbornness, anxiety, and mealtimes are three areas that require daily diligence in training him—more diligence than our previous two children needed, combined! But the good news is Judson responds well to discipline. Some days it feels like we aren’t getting anywhere until we look back at how far our son has truly come. We praise the Lord for His intervention in our lives by using a perceptive brother to speak into the situation. God’s Word, God’s way, has the keys for raising a happy child.

Pedimos ao Senhor por ele, nosso terceiro filho, o terceiro menino. Ele chegou com a primavera, a obra-prima da nova vida, lamentando as mudanças ao seu redor. As pessoas comentavam sobre seu choro: achavam-no adorável. Nós também. Nós o amávamos, aconchegávamos e o chamamos de Judson.

Sterling e eu havíamos nos comprometido, antes do nascimento de Judson, a levar nosso grupo de jovens a uma viagem missionária ao México. A data de partida seria cinco semanas depois da chegada de Judson. Como esposa do líder, eu era responsável por levar comida suficiente para alimentar o grupo durante toda a viagem. Fazer listas e comprar os alimentos me absorveu nos preparativos.

Judson fez seus próprios preparativos. Desenvolveu problemas intestinais. Passou sete dias sem sujar a fralda. Perguntei à minha parteira, mas ela não se abalou com aquilo. Quando passaram outros sete dias até a próxima fralda cheia, perguntei ao pediatra. Ela também não se preocupou. Então, partimos para o México: Sterling e eu, nosso bebê de cinco semanas e dois veículos cheios de jovens.

Embora os preparativos tivessem sido cansativos para mim, o tempo no México foi como férias. Minhas únicas obrigações ali eram cuidar do bebê e supervisionar as refeições. Mas Judson não gostou nem um pouco da viagem. Eu o aconchegava por horas, sentada sob uma lona numa encosta impressionante, de frente para o canteiro de obras onde nosso grupo trabalhava. Judson se mostrava inquieto e desconfortável comigo. Chorava se outra pessoa o segurasse. Eu sentia que algo estava errado, mas não havia sinais concretos do quê, exceto que dia após dia se passava sem uma fralda suja.

Na sexta noite no México, deitei Judson no berço. Mas o Senhor me fez voltar, levando-me a tirá-lo dali e colocá-lo na cama ao meu lado. Senti claramente esse impulso e obedeci, embora Judson tivesse dormido no berço nas outras noites. Dormimos. Em algum momento da noite, Judson acordou e não se deixava acalmar. Tentei isto e aquilo, eu mesma meio adormecida. De repente, ele gritou, mas engasgou no meio do grito e ficou mole.

“Sterling!”, exclamei. “Acenda a lanterna! Ele não está respirando!” Sentei-me na cama e examinei meu bebê à luz da lanterna. Seu rostinho se contorcia desesperadamente, mas não saía nenhum sopro nem som. Em segundos, voltou a respirar e gritou de novo. Então engasgou. Como se uma mão invisível apertasse seu frágil pescoço, sua respiração cessou e seus olhos se arregalaram de terror. Passei o dedo pela boca dele, procurando algo preso em suas vias respiratórias, mas não encontrei nada. Tremendo, Judson arfou e chorou. As lágrimas brotaram de seus olhos. “Ah, ore”, implorei. Sterling orou, amontoando súplicas ao céu enquanto nosso bebê parava de respirar outra vez. O episódio se repetiu várias vezes: segundos de gritos aterrorizados, seguidos por segundos de silêncio angustiante. O rosto de Judson ficou coberto de suor. Era agonizante assistir àquilo. Os pensamentos disparavam em minha mente: Nosso bebê vai morrer. Assim mesmo. Sem aviso. Aqui, sem assistência médica. Ó Deus! Ajuda-nos, ajuda-nos, ajuda-nos! Como alguém pode simplesmente ficar olhando o bebê morrer?

“Vou chamar a esposa do missionário”, decidiu Sterling. Eu balbuciava orações enquanto sustentava Judson. Quando a esposa do missionário apareceu, entreguei-lhe o bebê, grata pela presença de uma mulher mais velha do que eu. Oramos juntas, suplicando a Deus que interviesse. Judson começou a chorar e a respirar normalmente enquanto ela o examinava. Ela o devolveu a mim quando ele se acalmou.

“Não sei o que é”, disse ela, depois que lhe contamos o ocorrido. Agradecemos por ter se levantado no meio da noite e voltamos ao nosso quarto. Chorei enquanto Judson dormia tranquilamente em meus braços.

“Sinto que foi uma manifestação demoníaca”, declarou Sterling. “Se o diabo conseguir nos assustar com o que poderia acontecer ao nosso bebê enquanto estamos no meio do nada, poderá nos fazer juntar todo o grupo e ir embora. O diabo sabe que coisas boas estão acontecendo aqui, espiritualmente; esta não é a hora de fugir. Não podemos deixar que ele nos encha de medo.”

Concordei. A maneira incomum como a respiração de Judson parava e recomeçava parecia a ação de uma mão maligna apertando seu pescoço. Não parecia haver outra explicação natural para aquele acontecimento horrível. Sterling pôs a mão sobre Judson e orou, repreendendo especificamente o diabo e buscando a proteção de Deus. Deitamo-nos em paz e segurança e dormimos.

De manhã, Judson parecia não ter sido afetado pelo episódio, embora sua inquietação aumentasse. Passaram-se oito, nove e depois dez dias sem evacuação. Ele chorava, e seu choro suave e adorável agitava meu coração. Enquanto viajávamos de volta aos Estados Unidos, eu me preocupava ao vê-lo afastar-se do peito, contorcendo-se e resmungando até adormecer.

Então começou a regurgitar. Quando finalmente regurgitou um líquido amarelo-vivo, fiquei alarmada. No décimo primeiro dia, fomos consultar uma enfermeira especializada numa colônia menonita no México. Ela examinou Judson, ouviu meu relato e respondeu calmamente: “E este é seu primeiro filho?”

“Não”, respondi, mantendo a calma. “Este é o meu terceiro.” Então ela me olhou nos olhos, em silêncio, e examinou Judson novamente. Deu-lhe um supositório, sugerindo que todos os bebês são diferentes. E são mesmo. Aquele era, sem dúvida, diferente! Com o alívio local proporcionado pelo supositório, Judson pareceu sentir-se melhor.

Ele tinha sete semanas quando chegamos em casa. Dos três meses aos sete meses, teve dificuldades intestinais.

Aos domingos, as pessoas tocavam em seu rostinho, comentando sobre seu chorinho doce. Nos outros dias, eu me encolhia na cadeira de balanço, ouvindo sem ouvir seu chorinho doce. Alguns dias, parecia que ele nunca parava. Eu o segurava, exceto quando tirava uma soneca. Familiarizei-me com seu ciclo: vários dias sem sujar a fralda, durante os quais ficava cada vez mais irritadiço, mamava menos e, por fim, chorava abertamente até que eu lhe desse o alívio temporário de um supositório. Ao contrário do que se suspeitava com frequência, ele não estava constipado. Minha intuição materna dizia que algo dentro dele não acionava naturalmente o funcionamento do intestino.

“Sem cereais”, sugeria um livro. “Pode ser doença de Hirschsprung, que pode ser tratada naturalmente eliminando os cereais da dieta.” Então, deixei de comer cereais. Cinco semanas se arrastaram com minha dieta alterada. Judson parecia não notar meus esforços.

O pediatra ouviu meu relato da rotina dele e pediu um exame para detectar a doença de Hirschsprung.

O resultado do exame foi normal. Retomei, agradecida, o consumo de cereais, mas no domingo seguinte recebi um novo conselho. Uma mãe experiente me procurou no berçário, onde eu me refugiava do salão barulhento de convívio, embalando meu filhinho, embalando, embalando, embalando. “Já pensou em eliminar os laticínios?”

Bem, não, não tinha pensado.

“Acho que você deveria experimentar uma dieta sem laticínios”, concluiu ela. Como um manual médico muito consultado, enumerou os motivos para seguir esse caminho.

O pediatra não aprovava a ideia de eliminar os laticínios. Fui ao consultório dela depois de três semanas seguindo a dieta. “Você precisa das gorduras dos laticínios para manter a produção de leite”, repreendeu-me. “Além disso, o primeiro sinal de intolerância ao leite é sangue nas fezes, não a ausência de fezes.”

Não me importei em interromper a dieta sem laticínios. Tentamos outras coisas. Judson resistia obstinadamente aos enemas. Uma dose prescrita de laxante não deu resultado. Em certa ocasião, o médico me orientou a simplesmente esperar com Judson, convencido de que o intestino dele funcionaria por conta própria. Judson teve mais paciência do que eu. Quando já haviam se passado 17 dias, recorri a supositórios para aliviar meu bebê infeliz.

Mas não era apenas o mistério digestivo que nos causava sofrimento por causa do bebê. Mesmo com o intestino recém-esvaziado, ele era irritadiço. As refeições se tornavam um tormento. Judson protestava quando eu me sentava à mesa para comer com a família. Acostumei-me a prendê-lo ao meu ombro enquanto comia depressa, com uma só mão. Quer dizer, não me acostumei. Nunca me habituei à inquietação dele. Aprendi a fazer as tarefas domésticas enquanto ele dormia, pois, quando estava acordado, era impossível fazer qualquer coisa além de cuidar dele.

A igreja também era um ponto difícil. Judson se comportava pior em qualquer lugar movimentado, mas na igreja ficava impossível. Eu lutava com ele até que adormecesse, geralmente a tempo de ouvir a parte final do sermão.

As refeições de convívio eram um desastre. Judson gritava. Não deixava ninguém tocá-lo além de mim e, mesmo assim, eu não conseguia acalmá-lo. Quando finalmente servíamos os pratos e alimentávamos nossa pequena família, eu estava exausta e pronta para ir para casa. Parecia que ele tinha medo de alguma coisa. Não conseguia descobrir do que.

Aos poucos, percebi que ele também parecia ter medo de Sterling. Nessa idade, nossos outros meninos já haviam aprendido a reconhecer Sterling como “mais divertido do que a mamãe”; Judson, não. Afastava-se do pai. Resistia às tentativas de Sterling de se reconciliar com ele e se agarrava a mim com força.

E meu instinto materno, profundamente enraizado sob as ondas de cansaço, reagia. Numa contradição de emoções, mal eu entregava Judson a outra pessoa e sua evidente aflição por mim já tocava meu coração; então eu o pegava de volta, aconchegava-o junto a mim e o acalmava. Parecia que, mesmo enquanto ele me dominava, repreendia e esgotava, sua necessidade intensa me preenchia. Eu não entendia.

“Acho que você deveria dar a ele um probiótico de qualidade”, sugeriu minha sogra. A ideia pareceu boa, pelo menos na noite de domingo. De algum modo, as semanas passaram e não encontrei tempo para procurar um probiótico de qualidade.

“Experimente um bom multivitamínico”, aconselhou outra amiga depois de nos observar durante a reunião de oração. “Pode mesmo ser verme. Conheci uma menininha que era completamente incontrolável; gritava e gritava, e, depois que a trataram para vermes, o problema desapareceu por completo...”

A ideia também pareceu boa. Mas parecia dar muito trabalho. Eu não sabia por onde começar a pesquisar sobre “vermes”, nem tinha espaço mental para isso.

Quando ele tinha cerca de seis meses, passamos pela pior fase: quase uma semana em que chorava sem parar, recusando-se a mamar ou a ser consolado. Pedimos que os irmãos do ministério o ungissem. Depois da unção, aguardamos com expectativa. Em poucas horas, Judson voltou à sua inquietação habitual. Esperamos mais alguns dias antes de informar o pediatra. Seguindo a recomendação dela, Sterling e eu o levamos ao hospital, onde um especialista em gastroenterologia pediátrica poderia nos ajudar. Tínhamos medo de levar nosso bebê vulnerável e tão enigmático ao hospital. “Orem por nós”, pedimos ao contar à família e à irmandade.

Quando fizemos a admissão no hospital, Judson já estava mais animado. A enfermeira nos mostrou um quarto. Deitou Judson na cama fria e cercada do hospital e vestiu nele uma camisola áspera. Enquanto esperávamos a chegada do médico, Sterling e eu nos admirávamos com a mudança em nosso filho. Ele ficava quieto na cama, mexendo nas grades e olhando ao redor. Não por três minutos, nem por 30, mas por uma hora, até finalmente adormecer. Esse comportamento era inédito para Judson. Olhamos um para o outro, sem jeito.

“Estou me sentindo bastante tola”, confessei a Sterling. “O que os médicos vão pensar quando encontrarem esse menininho saudável? E a enorme conta do hospital?” Cobri o rosto com as mãos.

Sterling deu de ombros, tão perplexo quanto eu. “Acho que as pessoas devem ter orado.”

Aquele foi o ponto de virada na saúde física de Judson. O hospital nos liberou no dia seguinte, registrando em seu relatório que Judson estava com boa saúde. Não conseguiram encontrar nada de errado com nosso filho. Pouco depois, o problema intestinal desapareceu. Ele passou a evacuar com a regularidade do nascer do sol — até demais para a mãe que, até então, não precisava de fraldas, lenços umedecidos ou roupas extras. Louvamos o Senhor por responder à oração.

Mas ele ainda chorava. Os meses passaram, e aguardávamos cada nova conquista: talvez quando nascesse aquele dente, talvez quando começasse a engatinhar, talvez quando começasse a andar. Judson engatinhou aos seis meses, andou aos dez, comia — ou, mais precisamente, não comia — comida da mesa e continuava inquieto. Em alguns dias, eu andava com uma pequena “sanguessuga” agarrada à minha saia. Em outros, nem andava. Sterling tentava segurá-lo enquanto eu jantava, mas Judson detestava isso ainda mais do que detestava sentar-se comigo à mesa, e logo eu cedia aos seus choros suplicantes. Quase a única ocasião em que ficava tranquilo era enquanto dormia. O mais intrigante era seu aparente medo de Sterling e seu comportamento irracional na igreja.

“Será que estamos simplesmente mimando-o?”, perguntei a Sterling. “Talvez ele só não queira ficar quieto na igreja, como qualquer outro bebê.”

Sterling refletiu. “Se fosse isso, por que resistiria tanto às refeições de convívio? Deveria ser um momento divertido. Ou, se você o estivesse mimando, por que ele não gostaria de fazer coisas divertidas, como sair comigo ou comer lanches?”

Eu não sabia. Não achava que o estivesse mimando, mas não tinha certeza. Pensava que até um bebê mimado deveria gostar de ficar longe da mãe de vez em quando. Judson, não. Andava comigo o tempo todo, com uma mão agarrada ao decote da minha blusa e a outra empurrando-se para trás para ver para onde íamos. Se não gostasse da direção, muitas vezes tentava me guiar com investidas surpreendentemente fortes. Suas atitudes ansiosas e excessivamente alertas me intrigavam. Talvez houvesse algo mais errado, algo relacionado ao sistema nervoso.

“Sabe, quando acolhemos minha sobrinha, ela tinha dificuldades de vínculo”, contou-me uma irmã durante a refeição de convívio. Judson estava com a boca aberta, virado para o outro lado, por isso conversávamos em meio à algazarra do salão. “Ela nunca havia criado vínculo com ninguém por causa da situação difícil em casa. Comecei a carregá-la comigo aonde quer que fosse, até que criou vínculo comigo. O jeito inseguro de Judson, mesmo quando está com você, me faz pensar que ele ainda não criou vínculo. Talvez seja por isso que entra em pânico sempre que você o põe no chão.” Talvez. Mas onde e quando ele teria desenvolvido dificuldades de vínculo?

“Ele teve um parto traumático?”, perguntou a mulher.

Pensei um pouco. “Bem, não...” Lembrei-me do episódio assustador no México. Talvez tivesse interrompido o processo natural de vínculo. Ou talvez fosse o tempo no hospital. Talvez a coqueluche que teve aos oito meses. Enquanto essas lembranças passavam pela minha mente, percebi que a primeira infância de Judson realmente havia sido difícil. Talvez houvesse uma boa razão para seu equilíbrio emocional estar abalado. Agora ele parecia inseguro. Assustado. Em “modo de sobrevivência” o tempo todo, sendo eu sua duvidosa fonte de segurança momentânea. Se ele tivesse dificuldades de vínculo, eu teria feito tudo errado durante toda a primeira infância dele. Repetidas vezes, tentei deixar que outras pessoas, como as avós, o segurassem, na esperança de que percebesse que estava bem com elas. Não funcionou. A conversa com aquela mulher me fez olhar com dúvida para minhas estratégias, preocupada que eu tivesse prejudicado ainda mais Judson fazendo aquilo. Pelo menos, carregá-lo o tempo todo não custaria nada.

Arranjei um carregador de bebê e passei a carregá-lo comigo enquanto trabalhava. Ele adorava, mas minhas costas, não. Logo abandonei também essa prática, pois não surgiram sinais promissores de criação de vínculo. Se cuidar daquela criança fosse desgastar meu espírito, pelo menos não era preciso desgastar também minhas costas.

Tentamos discipliná-lo. Afinal, estávamos criando outros dois meninos, e a disciplina não era novidade em nossa casa. Não parecia que tivéssemos feito algo diferente com Judson do que fizéramos com os outros meninos, mas os resultados eram certamente diferentes. Judson reagia com terror incontrolável. O chorinho suave da infância já havia desaparecido. Não sabíamos como ensiná-lo a ficar feliz sob os cuidados de Sterling, pois a disciplina só parecia aumentar sua aflição. E como se ensina uma criança a brincar longe da mãe? Depois de algumas sessões exaustivas na igreja, nas quais ele não respondia, começamos a achar que uma palmada não era o meio de chegar até ele. Na verdade, parecia que nunca conseguíamos chegar até ele. Mas, se a palmada não funcionava, como poderíamos ensiná-lo? Eu me lembrava de ver outras mães taparem a boca dos filhos pequenos com a mão para ensiná-los que berrar não lhes daria o que queriam. Talvez ele precisasse aprender a parar de chorar. Tentei fazer isso por algum tempo.

Pouco depois de Judson completar um ano, seu comportamento chegou a um clímax terrível. Ele já tinha tamanho suficiente para resistir a orientações ou tentativas de acalmá-lo. A disciplina parecia deixá-lo enlouquecido. Por fim, peguei um livro sobre desenvolvimento infantil. Uma descrição de uma condição chamada reflexo de medo retido descrevia nosso filho com exatidão. Com exercícios terapêuticos simples, prometia o livro, poderíamos corrigir o problema. No entanto, precisaríamos da ajuda de um especialista nessa área, que nos ensinasse a terapia.

“O que você acha?”, perguntei a Sterling depois de compartilhar com ele as informações do livro.

Seu rosto parecia inseguro. “Não sei”, ponderou em voz alta. “Não foi assim que me ensinaram a criar uma criança. Sempre pensei que amor, oração e disciplina constante fossem as chaves para cuidar normalmente de uma criança. Não temos provas de que haja algo de errado com Judson além da inquietação. Hesito em rotulá-lo.”

Eu também hesitava. Embora ambos reconhecêssemos as necessidades especiais de algumas crianças e o valor de cuidadores com formação especializada, não queríamos atribuir precipitadamente um rótulo que justificasse o comportamento de Judson.

Mas, no dia seguinte, o cansaço de cuidar dele voltou como neblina. Voltamos a conversar sobre o reflexo de medo retido. O amor, com certeza, já havíamos tentado. A oração, ao menos em certa medida. A disciplina constante era outra questão. Ao contrário do que acontecia com nossos outros meninos, ela parecia não funcionar com Judson. De acordo com o texto sobre reflexos de medo retido, a disciplina poderia estar produzindo o efeito contrário ao pretendido.

“Você pode ligar e marcar uma consulta com a terapeuta”, decidiu Sterling. “Vale a pena tentar. Ela também é cristã e não está sugerindo nada além de exercícios físicos para reeducar o cérebro.”

Foi o que fiz. A terapeuta morava a oito horas de distância, algo que não podíamos ignorar. Mas a promessa de ajuda parecia valer a viagem. Enquanto isso, contei a algumas pessoas o que estávamos pensando. Algumas prometeram orar por nós. Minha sogra ofereceu um suplemento infantil para acalmar e melhorar a concentração. Também consegui ir à loja de produtos naturais e comprei um probiótico e um multivitamínico. A data da consulta com a terapeuta se aproximava.

“Não vejo como podemos ir”, disse Sterling alguns dias antes. “Nossas semanas têm sido muito atarefadas e estamos todos cansados. Não consigo ver como encaixar uma viagem de carro de dois dias só para uma consulta rápida. Mas acho que teremos de ir. Se ajudar Judson, valerá a pena.”

Também senti a tensão no pescoço só de pensar na viagem. Naquela semana, fizemos um esforço concentrado para treinar Judson. Lidamos com ele com firmeza, tentando alinhar sua vontade à nossa. Ele detestava isso. Sempre que Sterling o pegava, ele reagia violentamente. Reservei momentos todos os dias para me sentar com ele no sofá, segurando suas mãos e exigindo silêncio, com resultados medianos.

No domingo anterior à data em que deveríamos partir para a consulta, aceitamos um convite para jantar numa casa que não conhecíamos muito bem. Passei o tempo lutando com meu filhinho, engolindo meu orgulho e meu conforto a cada mordida. Enquanto isso, Sterling conversou com os homens sobre nossas dificuldades com Judson, mencionando a ideia de que ele sentia medo e a possibilidade de fazer terapia.

“Já pensou em como Judson deve se sentir quando você o disciplina da maneira que vi sua esposa usar mais cedo?”, perguntou gentilmente um dos homens. “Notei a expressão nos olhos de Judson quando ela o conteve, tapando-lhe a boca. Ele parecia aterrorizado. Se vocês realmente acham que ele tem esse problema de medo, talvez devam tentar ver a disciplina do ponto de vista dele. Um de nossos filhos também reagia de maneira desproporcional aos nossos métodos habituais de educação, até que comecei a explicar-lhe o que eu estava prestes a fazer...” Com discrição, aquele irmão compartilhou uma experiência com o filho deles.

Sterling ficou impressionado e grato por aquela percepção gentil. Os homens compartilharam um pouco mais. Era como se estivéssemos perto demais da situação para enxergá-la plenamente, e o Senhor nos tivesse dado a perspectiva de um observador sábio. Concordamos em cancelar a consulta sobre desenvolvimento infantil e repensar nossos métodos de educação. Decidimos tentar explicar claramente a Judson o que esperávamos dele e quais seriam as consequências da desobediência. Em vez de contê-lo, exigindo que se submetesse à nossa vontade, concordamos em usar repetidas palmadas leves para repreender sua obstinação.

“Vou dedicar esta semana inteiramente às refeições”, decidiu Sterling. “É claro que você vai ficar com a parte mais pesada, já que alimenta Judson em duas das três refeições. Mas vou tentar assumir a maior parte do trabalho. Também vou jejuar e orar por respostas para esse filho. Já tentamos ensiná-lo à mesa, mas nunca persistimos por mais de um ou dois dias. Sempre há ‘alguma coisa acontecendo’ e acabamos relaxando. Mas isto é importante. Importante demais para continuarmos deixando que a ‘vida’ interfira.”

Concordei com ele. Essa decisão fez meu espírito se encher de esperança e alívio. Algo na possibilidade de fazer terapia não parecia certo, mas estávamos desesperados por uma resposta.

Aquela semana foi difícil. Os outros meninos comiam sozinhos enquanto eu passava muito tempo à mesa com Judson. Ele gritava diante da minha expectativa clara de que se sentasse quieto e comesse. Contorcia-se, engasgava, chorava. Eu orava e lhe dava palmadas. Na hora do jantar, Sterling assumia. Judson resistia ainda mais ferozmente. Na primeira noite, foram três horas até nosso filho obedecer e engolir um pouco de comida para o pai. Nas noites seguintes, a situação durou tempos semelhantes. Sterling lidava com Judson com gentileza e firmeza, falando com ele, dando-lhe palmadas e segurando-o. Eu tentava não ouvir. Meu compromisso de apoiar meu marido em tudo isso lutava com minhas emoções, mas dessa vez não cedi quando Judson me olhou com olhos suplicantes.

Ao final da primeira semana, Judson começou a melhorar. Parou de chorar durante as refeições. Sentava-se na cadeirinha e comia obedientemente algumas colheradas para nós. Com uma expressão comicamente desamparada, oferecia a Sterling e a mim uma de suas pequenas raquetes para segurarmos enquanto comia, como se isso lhe desse coragem. Continuamos a trabalhar intencionalmente apenas nessa área. Ao final da segunda semana, seu comportamento em geral havia melhorado. Começou a soltar-se de mim, buscando diversão por conta própria, caminhando pela casa e balbuciando alegremente. Eu o observava, admirada, enquanto fazia coisas normais de bebê: explorava a caixa de brinquedos, subia nos sofás e mexia nos vasos sanitários. Aventurou-se a sair sozinho e logo aprendeu a brincar com bolas e caminhõezinhos. Parei de lhe dar os vários suplementos, pois ele estava indo tão bem.

Então, num dia feliz, quando os meninos cantaram em coro “O papai chegou!”, Judson soltou um gritinho de alegria. Na noite seguinte, quando Sterling chegou, ele gritou de novo, dessa vez indo feliz até a porta. Abri-a para ele. Caminhou até o caminhão onde Sterling estava. Sterling o carregou para dentro de casa. Nos braços do pai, Judson olhou para mim triunfante e fez um comentário balbuciado sobre o que estava acontecendo. Não fez menção de vir até mim. Então soubemos que Sterling havia conquistado seu coração. Desde então, ele tem sido uma criança diferente.

Agora o observamos com alegria. Seu rostinho é radiante e luminoso, e seus olhos, claros e tranquilos. É evidente que se sente seguro. Tornou-se uma alegria tê-lo por perto, encantando nossa família com suas travessuras de criança pequena. Não só criou vínculo com Sterling, como também ampliou seu círculo de aceitação para incluir outras pessoas. Interage bem com os irmãos. Responde de maneira razoável à educação em outras áreas. Nós o amamos, esse nosso terceiro filhinho.

Então, o que realmente havia de errado com Judson? Acho que ele tinha uma anomalia física nos primeiros meses de vida, que lhe causava desconforto. Sua primeira infância foi difícil. Olhando para trás, vejo que comecei a mimá-lo sem perceber.

Em algum momento da transição entre necessidade e exigência, comecei a satisfazer todos os desejos do meu pequeno. Isso aconteceu de maneira sorrateira e gradual. Desde muito cedo, ele percebeu claramente que o choro me controlava. Eu não percebia. Nós não percebíamos. Só percebemos depois que começamos a retomar o controle dos pais na educação dele. Ainda não sabemos quando aconteceu nem como. Mas isto sabemos: o caminho de Deus funciona.

A oração funciona. A vara da correção funciona. A esposa que apoia o marido quando ele disciplina o filho com amor também funciona. Num plano que desafia a razão humana, para não falar dos ensinamentos do mundo, o processo de moldar firmemente a vontade de Judson o uniu profundamente ao pai. Isso criou segurança em seu pequeno mundo. Sterling está no comando. Judson encontra descanso e segurança nisso. Isso o livrou do peso de controlar seu mundo. Ele está livre para se relacionar com qualquer um de nós, livre das exigências tirânicas de sua pequena natureza egoísta. A clareza de que seu pai é a autoridade em sua vida também parece ter estabelecido minha autoridade sobre ele.

Já se passaram mais de dois anos desde que Sterling começou a voltar o coração e a vontade de Judson para si. Hoje, Judson é um menino alegre e bem ajustado. Fica sentado em silêncio na igreja e nos momentos devocionais; gosta das refeições de convívio e dos amigos; passa com entusiasmo o tempo com o papai ou com a mamãe. Teimosia, ansiedade e refeições são três áreas que exigem empenho diário para educá-lo — mais empenho do que foi necessário com nossos dois filhos anteriores somados! Mas a boa notícia é que Judson responde bem à disciplina. Alguns dias parece que não estamos avançando, até olharmos para trás e vermos o quanto nosso filho realmente progrediu. Louvamos o Senhor por sua intervenção em nossa vida, usando um irmão perspicaz para falar à nossa situação. A Palavra de Deus, o caminho de Deus, contém as chaves para criar uma criança feliz.

He was born in a stable, meant for beasts of the field.
It was from the beginning that His will He would yield.

He was never well-liked; despised by all men;
Laughed to scorn, reviled—again, and again.

Yes, His mission on this earth was unusual indeed,
Not seeking money and friends or trying to succeed.

He knew His purpose was to please His Father,
With the trifles of earth, He would not bother.

It surely wasn’t easy, to be the King of kings.
And suffer as a criminal, taking what that brings.

Ten thousand angels, He could have summoned south,
But the stricken Savior opened not His mouth.

With His eyes on the reward, He persevered the pain;
Was cruelly stripped and beaten, and ultimately slain.

But why would He suffer so willingly there;
Enduring the cross, all the pain He did bear?

Because He treasured us, an atonement for our sin
He made when He bled and died there to make us His kin!

I thank God now for that sacrifice so great;
Providing the Lamb and transforming my fate.

I say, “A wonderful Savior, is Jesus my Lord;”
Now the Father and I—a relationship restored!

–Barry Grant

Hij werd geboren in een stal, bedoeld voor de dieren van het veld.
Vanaf het begin gaf Hij Zich over aan Gods wil, zoals die voor Hem gold.

Hij was nooit geliefd; door alle mensen veracht;
Bespot en gehoond—keer op keer, zonder erbarmen.

Ja, Zijn missie op aarde was werkelijk ongewoon,
Hij zocht geen geld en vrienden, geen succes of aanzien.

Hij wist dat Zijn doel was Zijn Vader te behagen,
Om aardse kleinigheden zou Hij Zich niet bekommeren.

Het was vast niet gemakkelijk, de Koning der koningen te zijn.
En als een misdadiger te lijden, met alles wat daarbij komt.

Tienduizend engelen had Hij naar het zuiden kunnen roepen,
Maar de gekwelde Heiland opende Zijn mond niet.

Met Zijn blik op de beloning verdroeg Hij de pijn;
Wreed ontkleed en geslagen, en uiteindelijk gedood.

Maar waarom zou Hij daar zo gewillig lijden;
Het kruis verdragen, al die pijn dragen?

Omdat Hij ons koesterde, bracht Hij verzoening voor onze zonde
Toen Hij daar bloedde en stierf om ons tot de Zijnen te maken!

Nu dank ik God voor dat zo grote offer;
Hij gaf het Lam en veranderde mijn lot.

Ik zeg: ‘Een wonderbare Heiland is Jezus, mijn Heer;’
Nu is de band tussen de Vader en mij hersteld!

–Barry Grant
