It is August 2020, over four months since the coronavirus pandemic started, and it is still affecting our lives. People are still getting sick. The government and its decisions continue to be at the center of a lot of our conversations. The cause and cure are ongoing topics. The difference between those that believe the coronavirus to be a real threat and those that believe it to be primarily an agenda of political nature are becoming more distinct as this virus slowly makes its way through our communities, churches, and society as a whole.

The mandates being issued by the governors of many of our states are forcing God’s people to make decisions on issues we have not faced before. At what point does the government cross the line of interfering in our religious freedoms by putting in place mandates that will affect how we do church? How should we relate to the differences among us concerning the mandates? Should we or should we not follow them? What should our attitude be towards those in authority when we feel that they are doing things that are politically motivated? What should we do with all the “unbelievable things” that are being passed around, even from well-meaning Christians from what they would consider to be very valid and from legitimate sources? What should we do with the many, what seem to be, “conspiracy theories” that are being propagated and peddled from one person to another in such a manner that makes it hard to refute them? I, in no way, am going to attempt to answer how a church should relate to the specific mandates but would like to address some concerning attitudes and other responses that have been observed throughout our plain communities.

One of the most concerning issues is the attitude that people have had and are having toward the government. In 1 Peter, the apostle Peter calls us to “honor the king” and the Apostle Paul admonishes us in Romans 13 to be “subject to the higher Powers, for there is no power but of God”. The word honour, as used in 1 Peter 2, in reference to the king, means to “prize” or to “fix valuation upon.” A verse like this and others would indicate that when we speak of our government and, for that matter, others, our attitude should be one of respect. The words and the tone of voice we use should reflect that commitment. Our choice of words and the tone we use will speak volumes. They reflect our attitude.

I personally believe that we as the plain community have done a lot of damage to our “light” and “witness” by refusing to wear the mask in required public settings. But God looks deeper than our actions and we should too. The remarks like “no one will tell me I have to wear that thing” and others similar to that have their roots in a “lack of respect.” God clearly tells us, though we may not be able to always obey in every situation, respect and honor is always to be seen and heard in our attitudes and speech.

The apostle Paul is a good example of one who had a heart to honor those in authority and repented when he failed to do so. When Ananias the high priest asked the ones by him to smite him, he called the high priest a “whited wall”. When told that he had reviled the high priest, he was very quick to apologize for his wrong even though the high priest was wrong in asking them to hit him. It might remind us of the little saying, “Two wrongs do not make a right.”

Having a bad attitude because the government is making what we think are wrong decisions will not bring about right! As we find our way through these mandates, let’s make sure we do not sin against those in authority by speaking about them in a disrespectful manner. Let us repent of any bad attitudes and make sure our heart is in a position to honor and then the words and tone we use will convey the same.

Another area that is extremely hard to know how to respond to is that of all the negative information that is floating around surrounding Covid–19. Many of the plain community tend to distrust the government’s way of handling the situation. Because of this we are quick to believe and pass on negative information as fact. How do we know what is true and what is not? We need to be so careful, even when the information comes from what we believe to be a reliable source, because the more this negative information is passed along, the more folks will distrust the government. Case in point, there have been numerous deaths that were not directly connected to Covid–19; however, it was reported that Covid–19 was marked on the death certificate as being the cause of these deaths. After fact checking some of these supposed cases, it was found that some of these reports were not true. Since several reports have been verified as untrue, I no longer know what to believe. I think we should all be very careful what we do with the information we come across and do all we can to verify the information before passing it on as fact. If it is hard to believe, it is all the more important to check the facts or not pass it on until it has been proven.

Throughout this time period it seems that the conspiracy theories have just escalated. A lot of speculation surrounds the origin of Covid–19, the possible underlying motives, and secrecies the government has in how they are handling the whole Covid–19 dilemma. How do we know if the many propagated theories are true? If they are true, how will that affect the way I live for the other kingdom now? Will it change the way I live? Will it somehow help me prepare for these supposed difficulties that are coming?

In Luke 21, we have a verse talking about future events: “Men’s hearts failing them for fear of things that are coming on the earth.” Are we going to respond to the future in faith or in fear? The media proclaims Covid–19 to be a very dangerous, infectious virus. This perception has caused many in our world to start buying and hoarding for fear of things coming on the face of the earth. We now have articles and theories being peddled by many that seemingly will cause fear of the government and what they are planning to do and ultimately men’s hearts will fail for fear.

The Apostle Peter said that …God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind –2 Timothy 1:7. Whether these claims are true or not, the Bible still calls us in Philippians to think on …whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report… –Philippians 4:8. To spend even a little time following these theories will have a negative and spiritually draining effect on our lives and the lives around us. Thinking about them not only promotes fear but also makes it even more difficult to respect and honor the government. In reality, some or many of these things may not even be true. As Christians we try to be a peaceful and trusting people, yet this tends to make us vulnerable to be quite gullible. We are quite willing to believe negative claims, allegations, and theories without checking the facts to see whether they could even be true or not. My appeal would be to continue to seek those things that are above, to think on the things that are noble and virtuous.

As believers, we are facing another challenge. The unity within our groups is being challenged in ways it has not been before. We differ in thought on how much the government should interfere in our services. Should we even be having church if the governor would rather that we would not? What about the wearing of masks in our services? Some feel one way and others think differently. These mandates and how we should respond to them can be quite controversial! Now, as much as ever before, we need to extend lots of grace as we sort these things through with each other. We must give some room to each other to understand and relate to it a bit differently. We need much grace with one another and dare not allow these things to become a point of contention. I believe God wants to use these difficulties to draw us closer to Him and each other, but the enemy of our souls is doing his best to have it destroy our love and commitment to each other. Let us seek peace and ensue it!

2020년 8월, 코로나바이러스 대유행이 시작된 지 넉 달이 넘었지만 여전히 우리의 삶에 영향을 미치고 있습니다. 사람들은 계속 병에 걸리고 있습니다. 정부와 정부의 결정은 여전히 우리 대화의 상당 부분을 차지합니다. 원인과 치료법은 계속해서 화제가 되고 있습니다. 이 바이러스가 우리 공동체와 교회, 그리고 사회 전체로 서서히 퍼져 나가면서, 코로나바이러스를 실제 위협으로 여기는 사람들과 주로 정치적 의도에 따른 것이라고 여기는 사람들 사이의 차이가 더욱 뚜렷해지고 있습니다.

많은 주의 주지사들이 내리는 명령은 하나님의 백성에게 이전에는 마주한 적 없는 문제들에 관해 결정을 내리도록 하고 있습니다. 교회 활동 방식에 영향을 미치는 명령을 시행함으로써 정부가 어느 지점에서 종교의 자유를 침해하는 선을 넘게 될까요? 명령에 관한 우리 사이의 견해 차이에 어떻게 대처해야 할까요? 우리는 그 명령을 따라야 할까요, 따르지 말아야 할까요? 권위 있는 사람들이 정치적 동기에 따라 행동한다고 느낄 때, 우리는 그들을 어떤 태도로 대해야 할까요? 선의의 그리스도인들조차 매우 타당하고 합법적인 출처에서 나온 것이라고 여기는 “믿기 어려운 이야기들”을 퍼뜨릴 때, 우리는 어떻게 해야 할까요? 반박하기 어려운 방식으로 한 사람에게서 다른 사람에게로 전해지고 유포되는, 이른바 “음모론”은 어떻게 해야 할까요? 저는 교회가 구체적인 명령에 어떻게 대처해야 하는지 답하려는 것이 결코 아닙니다. 다만 우리 소박한 공동체 곳곳에서 목격된 몇 가지 우려스러운 태도와 다른 반응들에 대해 말씀드리고자 합니다.

가장 우려되는 문제 가운데 하나는 사람들이 정부를 대하는 태도였고 지금도 그러하다는 점입니다. 베드로전서에서 사도 베드로는 우리에게 “왕을 공경하라”고 권하고, 사도 바울은 로마서 13장에서 “위에 있는 권세들에게 복종하라. 권세는 하나님께로부터 나지 않음이 없다”고 권면합니다. 베드로전서 2장에서 왕을 두고 사용된 ‘공경하다’라는 말은 “귀하게 여기다” 또는 “가치를 매기다”라는 뜻입니다. 이 구절과 그 밖의 구절들은 우리가 정부와, 더 나아가 다른 사람들에 대해 말할 때 존중하는 태도를 지녀야 한다는 것을 보여 줍니다. 우리가 쓰는 말과 목소리의 어조에는 그러한 다짐이 드러나야 합니다. 우리가 선택하는 말과 어조는 많은 것을 말해 줍니다. 그것은 우리의 태도를 드러냅니다.

저는 개인적으로 우리 소박한 공동체가 공공장소에서 의무화된 마스크 착용을 거부함으로써 우리의 “빛”과 “증거”에 큰 손상을 입혔다고 믿습니다. 그러나 하나님께서는 우리의 행동보다 더 깊은 곳을 보시며, 우리도 그래야 합니다. “누구도 나더러 그걸 쓰라고 할 수 없다”와 같은 말은 “존중심의 부족”에서 비롯됩니다. 모든 상황에서 언제나 순종할 수 있는 것은 아니지만, 존중과 공경은 우리의 태도와 말에서 언제나 드러나고 들려야 한다고 하나님께서는 분명히 말씀하십니다.

사도 바울은 권위 있는 이들을 공경하려는 마음을 지녔고, 그렇게 하지 못했을 때 회개한 좋은 본보기입니다. 대제사장 아나니아가 곁에 있는 사람들에게 바울을 치라고 하자, 바울은 대제사장을 “회칠한 담”이라고 불렀습니다. 대제사장을 모욕했다는 말을 듣자, 대제사장이 사람들에게 자신을 치라고 한 것은 잘못이었지만 바울은 자신의 잘못을 매우 서둘러 사과했습니다. “두 가지 잘못이 옳은 일을 만들지는 않는다”라는 짧은 격언이 떠오를 수도 있습니다.

정부가 우리가 보기에 잘못된 결정을 내린다는 이유로 나쁜 태도를 갖는다고 해서 올바른 결과가 생기지는 않습니다! 이러한 명령들을 헤쳐 나가는 동안, 권위 있는 이들에 대해 무례한 방식으로 말함으로써 그들에게 죄를 짓지 않도록 합시다. 좋지 않은 태도가 있다면 회개하고, 우리의 마음이 공경하는 자세를 갖추도록 합시다. 그러면 우리가 사용하는 말과 어조에도 같은 태도가 드러날 것입니다.

어떻게 대응해야 할지 알기가 매우 어려운 또 다른 분야는 코로나19를 둘러싸고 떠도는 모든 부정적인 정보입니다. 소박한 공동체의 많은 사람은 정부의 대처 방식을 불신하는 경향이 있습니다. 이 때문에 우리는 부정적인 정보를 사실이라고 쉽게 믿고 전합니다. 무엇이 사실이고 무엇이 사실이 아닌지 어떻게 알 수 있을까요? 우리가 믿기에 믿을 만한 출처에서 나온 정보라 하더라도 매우 조심해야 합니다. 이러한 부정적인 정보가 더 많이 퍼질수록 정부를 불신하는 사람들도 더 많아질 것이기 때문입니다. 한 가지 사례를 들자면, 코로나19와 직접 관련되지 않은 사망 사례가 여럿 있었는데, 이 사망들의 원인이 코로나19라고 사망진단서에 기재되었다는 보도가 있었습니다. 이른바 그런 사례 가운데 몇 가지를 사실 확인해 보니, 그 보도 중 일부는 사실이 아닌 것으로 드러났습니다. 여러 보도가 사실이 아닌 것으로 확인된 뒤로는 무엇을 믿어야 할지 더는 모르겠습니다. 우리 모두 접하는 정보를 어떻게 다룰지 매우 조심하고, 사실이라고 전하기 전에 정보를 확인하기 위해 할 수 있는 일을 다 해야 한다고 생각합니다. 믿기 어렵다면 사실을 확인하거나, 입증될 때까지 전하지 않는 일이 더욱 중요합니다.

이 기간 내내 음모론이 계속 확산된 것 같습니다. 코로나19의 기원과 그 밑에 깔렸을지도 모르는 동기, 그리고 정부가 코로나19라는 난제를 다루는 방식에 숨겨진 비밀을 둘러싸고 많은 추측이 나돌고 있습니다. 널리 퍼지는 여러 이론이 사실인지 어떻게 알 수 있을까요? 그것이 사실이라면, 지금 다른 나라를 위해 살아가는 나의 방식에는 어떤 영향을 미칠까요? 내 삶의 방식을 바꾸게 될까요? 다가온다고들 하는 이러한 어려움에 대비하는 데 어떤 식으로든 도움이 될까요?

누가복음 21장에는 미래에 일어날 일에 대해 말하는 구절이 있습니다. “땅에 임할 일을 생각하고 무서워하므로 사람들의 마음이 기절하리니.” 우리는 미래에 믿음으로 반응할까요, 두려움으로 반응할까요? 언론은 코로나19가 매우 위험하고 전염성이 높은 바이러스라고 알립니다. 이러한 인식으로 인해 세상 많은 사람이 땅에 닥칠 일을 두려워하여 물건을 사서 쌓아 두기 시작했습니다. 이제 많은 이들이 정부와 정부가 계획하는 일에 대한 두려움을 불러일으키고, 결국 사람들의 마음이 두려움으로 무너지게 할 것 같은 기사와 이론을 유포하고 있습니다.

사도 베드로는 이렇게 말했습니다. …하나님이 우리에게 주신 것은 두려워하는 마음이 아니요 오직 능력과 사랑과 절제하는 마음이니 –디모데후서 1:7. 이러한 주장들이 사실이든 아니든, 성경은 여전히 빌립보서에서 우리에게 …무엇에든지 참되며 무엇에든지 경건하며 무엇에든지 옳으며 무엇에든지 정결하며 무엇에든지 사랑받을 만하며 무엇에든지 칭찬받을 만하며… 이것들을 생각하라 –빌립보서 4:8.라고 말씀합니다. 이러한 이론들을 따라가는 데 조금이라도 시간을 쓰면 우리의 삶과 우리 주변 사람들의 삶에 부정적이고 영적으로 소진시키는 영향을 미칩니다. 그런 것들을 생각하는 일은 두려움을 부추길 뿐 아니라 정부를 존중하고 공경하기도 더욱 어렵게 만듭니다. 실제로는 이런 일들 가운데 일부 또는 많은 것이 사실이 아닐 수도 있습니다. 그리스도인으로서 우리는 화평하고 신뢰하는 사람이 되려고 하지만, 그러다 보면 쉽게 속아 넘어갈 수 있습니다. 우리는 부정적인 주장과 혐의, 이론이 사실일 수 있는지조차 확인하지 않은 채 기꺼이 믿습니다. 제가 호소하고 싶은 것은 위에 있는 것들을 계속 구하고, 고결하고 덕스러운 것들을 생각하자는 것입니다.

믿는 이로서 우리는 또 다른 도전에 직면하고 있습니다. 우리 모임 안의 연합이 이전에는 겪지 못한 방식으로 시험받고 있습니다. 정부가 예배에 얼마나 개입해야 하는지에 대해 생각이 다릅니다. 주지사가 원하지 않는다면 교회 모임을 가져도 될까요? 예배 때 마스크를 쓰는 문제는 어떻습니까? 어떤 이들은 이렇게 생각하고 다른 이들은 다르게 생각합니다. 이러한 명령과 그에 대한 대응 방식은 상당히 논란이 될 수 있습니다! 지금처럼 서로에게 넉넉한 은혜를 베풀어야 할 때는 일찍이 없었습니다. 서로가 이 일을 조금 다르게 이해하고 대처할 수 있도록 어느 정도 여지를 주어야 합니다. 우리는 서로에게 많은 은혜를 베풀어야 하며, 이러한 일들이 다툼의 불씨가 되도록 내버려 두어서는 안 됩니다. 하나님께서 이러한 어려움을 사용해 우리를 그분과 서로에게 더 가까이 이끄시기를 원하신다고 믿습니다. 그러나 우리 영혼의 원수는 이러한 일로 우리의 사랑과 서로에 대한 헌신을 무너뜨리려고 최선을 다하고 있습니다. 화평을 구하고 그것을 좇읍시다!

A verse that has always caught my attention, one that has caused my spine to tingle is found in Matthew chapter seven. Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works? –Matthew 7:22.

Jesus gives us a picture of a large group of people standing before Him on Judgment Day. They thought they lived their lives for Him. They were gifted people—prophesying, casting out devils, and doing many wonderful things in the name of Jesus—they seemed like good Christians. However, in the next verse we read that Jesus will say to them that He never knew them. Jesus even tells them to depart from Him. He sends them to hell, forever.

I remember an account that reminds me of these verses. Years ago, I was working for a steel joist company. It was a normal Friday morning, we were working hard, as was required of each of us. The line boss came out and announced a meeting with the whole plant after the shift was over. We all wondered what the meeting was about. We asked around but it seemed that no one knew. After the shift, we all stood in a large circle and waited for the boss. He soon entered the room with another man. It was the manager of the whole company. Prior to these men coming in, we were all talking casually with each other, there was laughter and loud voices. The boss had a large stack of envelopes, and I heard a buzz go around about bonus checks. Everyone looked excited, except for the boss.

Then the boss started talking, “We have been watching all of you very closely over the past four weeks. We have been looking at your work ethic, how hard you try, and whether you’re on time. We have been looking at many different areas. Your supervisors will give each of you an envelope with your name on it. Do not open this letter until you are off the premises. When you do open it, you will find some instructions. For most, it will say to return to work at the normal time on Monday. But for 27 of you, it will say that you are fired. For those included in that number, we did not like what we saw during our time of evaluation, so we decided that we need to release you from your employment here.”

You could hear a pin drop. Fear was seen on every face. I remember wishing I had worked harder, been more involved. I regretted taking my job for granted. It was a terrible feeling, I had worked there for years, but did that matter?

I wasn’t fired that day, but 27 others were. They thought they had done enough. They thought they were safe since they had put in their time. But they were wrong, and now nothing could be done. It was over.

What about us? Do we gauge our walk with God based on eternity? Do we wonder what will happen on the day of judgement? How can we know?

Jesus says a few verses earlier that we will know each other by our fruits. There is much talk in the Word of God about fruit. We know what type of tree one is, by examining its fruit. When we first moved to Haiti, we didn’t know what kinds of trees were there. I remember looking up at a large tree on our property and wondering what kind it was. Then something gave it away. There were small avocados hanging from its branches. In the church today, it seems that people do not want to talk about this. But I assure you that we should talk about it before it is forever too late. Looking back, we would have loved to talk about this at the factory before that day when some of the employees were fired.

So, what is the fruit of a Christian? We know that being a good person and dressing in a certain way are not determining factors of a godly life. It is not the church we attend, the family we were born into, our culture, or the color of our skin. Many would agree that these things are not what identifies us as Christians. Some may think that the fruit of a Christian is being a good, morally upright, and loving citizen of society. There are many people who are law-abiding citizens, loving and peaceful, taking care of their own needs and the needs of others. Yet it is still possible for them to do all these good things and still go to hell.

We hear the world (and some in the church) proclaiming loudly that it’s only the heart that matters. We know they are saying this so they can excuse the lack of visible fruit. Even though their outside is bad, they want people to think that their heart is good, and that that’s all that really matters.

They are correct about the heart being important. You can’t change or fix anything simply by putting on a form when the heart is still selfish and wicked. However, they are wrong about the heart being good and the outside being bad. This is impossible. Jesus says, Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also –Matthew 23:26.

You cannot have a clean heart and a sinful appearance. However, on the flip side, you can have a clean appearance and yet still have an ungodly heart. So how do we tell? What is this fruit that Jesus is talking about?

We will talk about the fruit of the Spirit shortly, but first I would like to talk about something else that I believe defines a Christian. Something that can separate the sheep from the wolves, even if they both appear to be the same.

A desire to serve Jesus. When God converts a person’s soul, that individual is a new creature, and desires to serve God with his whole being. That person does not need to be forced to do what pleases God. There is much talk today in the church about structure and rules, however, this was not always the case. So why is this such a big issue today? Maybe there are unconverted people in the church. Perhaps people are too independent and do not want to be told what to do. You can tell a church member to dress modestly, but if their heart is not changed, you will face problems. They will try to be as worldly as they can, and still be within the ‘law’ of the church. Or they will simply refuse to do it and the church soon gives in and no longer requires their people to dress and live modestly. Should the church need to force its people to be modest? Should the church need to force its people to be Christ-like? Absolutely not. When a soul has been redeemed and transformed by the blood of Christ, that person, in return, will, because of his changed nature, live a sacrificial life for Him. We obey His commandments with grateful hearts!

For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous –1 John 5:3.

A heart that has not been made new by God’s Spirit will not passionately desire to live for God. One can religiously go to church—many unbelievers attend church services regularly. One can dress right and act right, but if their heart does not pant after the things of God, these things will have no profit. Much of what they do is to receive the praise of men, not the glory of God. It is no wonder that many churches of today are accepting drift.

It is a beautiful thing to see someone truly desire to live for God. They desire to seek the face of their Creator, their Savior. They live for the Kingdom, for the brotherhood. To obey God and serve Him is a necessity; it is the only thing that really matters to them. Their ‘all’ truly is on the altar. They love reading the Word and spending time alone with God. Their desires and their will have been sacrificed on the altar of their God.

People have told me that we need to give a new Christian some room. “Some room for what?” I ask. Some room for sin… for carnality? Absolutely not. Every example in the Bible says differently. Every conversion brought a tremendous change, a new creature. Many people confuse ‘grace to learn and to grow’ in the faith as an ‘excuse for sin’. The Scriptures define new Christians… As newborn babes, and commands each of us to desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby: –1 Peter 2:2. So new Christians don’t need space to continue for a time in their ungodly ways, but they do need space to grow …in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man –Luke 2:52.

When someone comes declaring they have been converted, it is easy to find out. We simply go over some scriptures that explain practical, foundational doctrines like non-conformity, non-resistance, and such like. Some see it as God’s Word and soak it in. Many folks sit in astonishment as I read such verses to them—Scripture verses they have never heard before. Usually they simply believe what they just heard from God’s word, and it changes them. That is a Christian who wants to be taught, who wants to be discipled. They tend to come with a teachable attitude asking questions about that which they have read in God’s Word and don’t understand.

But what about so many others? They hear the same scriptures and they argue—they argue with the Bible and the person sharing the Scripture with them, but ultimately, they are arguing with God. They will usually admit that it’s what the Bible says but they want to know why it says that. They are not wanting to change their life for God. They want to be a Christian, yes, but they also want to live how they want. They do not desire to obey God. We can continue working with them, but it is clear: their heart pants after the things of the world and the pleasures of this life.

Picture with me a man living 1,000 years ago. He is locked in a dungeon, where everything is as black as coal. It is musty and stinks. He has been arrested for preaching the gospel. His ankles and wrists are raw and bloody from the large, heavy chains that keep him bound in the tiny cell. He’s claustrophobic, weary, and worn. His back is bloody. His aching limbs have been stretched to the breaking point. He talks to God, but God does not answer. He pleads for deliverance but hears nothing in return. He thinks back on his life, his faith. Then he wonders the dreaded thought: “God, are you there? Are you real?” Silence. His faith is being tried to the extreme. He knows that if he continues to hold to his beliefs, a fire awaits him. Why? Why die for a God that allows him to go through this agony? Why die for a God that will not speak? “My God, my God, why hast Thou forsaken me?”

Now picture this man… is you.

Do we really believe in God, a God who’s not seen and often not heard? If our faith does not exist, then God will not exist when we really need Him.

God wants us to put all our faith in Him, all the time. We walk by faith, NOT by sight… even when things are going well. When we find ourselves in terrible times, God is still near, leading us and giving us courage to go on! We are used to simply trusting in Him, in His word.

For if they do these things in a green tree, what shall be done in the dry? –Luke 23:31.

God loves a heart that is turned toward Him, fully yielded, and surrendered. He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek Him!

Do we have the fruit of the Spirit of God? Do we act like Christians? Do we look like Christians?

I was asked to preach for a large church that I had never been to before. I went with my family and sat while the seats filled up with hundreds of people. I was amazed at how these people were dressed. There were short miniskirts and skimpy tops, much worldly fashion and style. The service began and I realized quickly that this was not a good place for my family, so I took them home and returned by myself. The rock music was still going, and the dancing was pushing my limits. After two hours it was time for the message. I stood and told the large crowd that I was the new President of America. Laughter filled the auditorium. I then asked them if they believed me. “No!” they shouted. I asked why they didn’t believe me, and they responded with different answers. One yelled, “You don’t look or dress like the president!” Another said, “You wouldn’t be here if you were the president!” Yet another said that I didn’t sound like the president. I told them that I didn’t understand. I asked how they can say that they are Christians—They don’t look like it! They don’t act like it! They don’t sound like it!—Yet everyone believes them!

It seems that we judge everything by its fruit, except for Christians. For Christians we are expected to judge by what they claim. This world thinks they can simply imagine what Jesus wants and then please Him in any way they personally choose. However, the Bible is clear: Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles? Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit. A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire. Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them –Matthew 7:16-20.

The Bible says that …the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance… –Galatians 5:22-23. Are these the things that people see when they look at you and I? I know it is easy to justify not having one or more of these fruits by saying, “I’m working on it,” or “I’m praying about it.” Jesus does not say that this fruit is something that Christians should work to attain. He simply says that these are the fruits, or product, of the indwelling Spirit of God. If we pursue worldly ambitions, or if we desire to fit in with the world, we cannot expect this fruit to be evident in our lives. I believe this is the fruit of a suffering man, a person that has been giving his all, and desires to give his all to the Lamb that was slain.

Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire –Matthew 7:19.

When we give something our all, whether it’s our work, our school, or raising a family, it feels good—it is fulfilling. When we serve God with all our being, the same is true. There is a very rewarding feeling, a feeling of peace that passes all understanding.

Un versículo que siempre ha llamado mi atención, uno que me ha hecho estremecer, se encuentra en el capítulo siete de Mateo. Muchos me dirán en aquel día: Señor, Señor, ¿no profetizamos en tu nombre, y en tu nombre echamos fuera demonios, y en tu nombre hicimos muchos milagros? –Mateo 7:22.

Jesús nos presenta la imagen de un gran grupo de personas de pie delante de Él en el Día del Juicio. Pensaban que habían vivido para Él. Eran personas talentosas: profetizaban, echaban fuera demonios y hacían muchas cosas maravillosas en el nombre de Jesús; parecían buenos cristianos. Sin embargo, en el versículo siguiente leemos que Jesús les dirá que nunca los conoció. Jesús incluso les dice que se aparten de Él. Los envía al infierno para siempre.

Recuerdo un suceso que me hace pensar en estos versículos. Hace años trabajaba para una empresa de viguetas de acero. Era un viernes por la mañana normal; trabajábamos duro, como se exigía de cada uno de nosotros. El jefe de línea salió y anunció que habría una reunión con toda la planta al terminar el turno. Todos nos preguntábamos de qué se trataría. Preguntamos por ahí, pero parecía que nadie lo sabía. Al terminar el turno, nos pusimos todos en un gran círculo y esperamos al jefe. Pronto entró en la sala acompañado de otro hombre. Era el gerente de toda la empresa. Antes de que entraran, todos conversábamos despreocupadamente; había risas y voces fuertes. El jefe llevaba una gran pila de sobres, y oí que corría el rumor de que eran cheques de bonificación. Todos parecían entusiasmados, menos el jefe.

Entonces el jefe empezó a hablar: «Los hemos estado observando muy de cerca durante las últimas cuatro semanas. Hemos estado evaluando su ética de trabajo, cuánto se esfuerzan y si llegan a tiempo. Hemos examinado muchos aspectos diferentes. Sus supervisores les entregarán a cada uno un sobre con su nombre. No abran esta carta hasta que hayan salido de las instalaciones. Cuando la abran, encontrarán algunas instrucciones. A la mayoría les dirá que regresen a trabajar el lunes a la hora habitual. Pero a 27 de ustedes les dirá que están despedidos. En cuanto a los incluidos en ese número, no nos gustó lo que vimos durante el período de evaluación, así que decidimos que debemos poner fin a su empleo aquí».

Se podía oír caer un alfiler. El miedo se veía en todos los rostros. Recuerdo que deseé haber trabajado más duro, haber participado más. Me arrepentí de haber dado mi trabajo por sentado. Fue una sensación terrible. Había trabajado allí durante años, pero ¿eso importaba?

A mí no me despidieron ese día, pero a otros 27 sí. Pensaban que habían hecho lo suficiente. Pensaban que estaban a salvo porque habían cumplido su tiempo. Pero se equivocaban, y ahora ya no se podía hacer nada. Todo había terminado.

¿Y nosotros? ¿Evaluamos nuestro andar con Dios a la luz de la eternidad? ¿Nos preguntamos qué ocurrirá el día del juicio? ¿Cómo podemos saberlo?

Jesús dice unos versículos antes que nos conoceremos unos a otros por nuestros frutos. La Palabra de Dios habla mucho del fruto. Sabemos qué clase de árbol es uno examinando su fruto. Cuando nos mudamos a Haití, no sabíamos qué clases de árboles había allí. Recuerdo que miraba un árbol grande en nuestra propiedad y me preguntaba de qué especie era. Entonces algo lo reveló: de sus ramas colgaban pequeños aguacates. En la iglesia de hoy, parece que la gente no quiere hablar de esto. Pero les aseguro que deberíamos hablar de ello antes de que sea demasiado tarde para siempre. Al mirar atrás, nos habría gustado hablar de esto en la fábrica antes de aquel día en que despidieron a algunos empleados.

Entonces, ¿cuál es el fruto de un cristiano? Sabemos que ser una buena persona y vestir de cierta manera no son factores determinantes de una vida piadosa. No lo son la iglesia a la que asistimos, la familia en la que nacimos, nuestra cultura ni el color de nuestra piel. Muchos estarían de acuerdo en que estas cosas no son lo que nos identifica como cristianos. Algunos podrían pensar que el fruto de un cristiano consiste en ser un ciudadano bueno, moralmente recto y afectuoso. Hay muchas personas que respetan la ley, son afectuosas y pacíficas, y atienden sus propias necesidades y las de los demás. Sin embargo, aun así es posible que hagan todas estas cosas buenas y terminen en el infierno.

Oímos al mundo (y a algunos en la iglesia) proclamar a gritos que lo único que importa es el corazón. Sabemos que dicen esto para justificar la falta de fruto visible. Aunque su exterior sea malo, quieren que la gente piense que su corazón es bueno y que eso es lo único que realmente importa.

Tienen razón al decir que el corazón es importante. No se puede cambiar ni arreglar nada simplemente adoptando una apariencia cuando el corazón sigue siendo egoísta y perverso. Sin embargo, se equivocan al decir que el corazón es bueno y el exterior malo. Eso es imposible. Jesús dice: ¡Fariseo ciego! Limpia primero lo de dentro del vaso y del plato, para que también lo de fuera quede limpio –Mateo 23:26.

No se puede tener un corazón limpio y una apariencia pecaminosa. Sin embargo, a la inversa, se puede tener una apariencia limpia y aun así un corazón impío. Entonces, ¿cómo podemos distinguirlo? ¿Cuál es este fruto del que habla Jesús?

Pronto hablaremos del fruto del Espíritu, pero primero quisiera hablar de otra cosa que creo que define a un cristiano: algo que puede separar a las ovejas de los lobos, aunque ambos parezcan iguales.

El deseo de servir a Jesús. Cuando Dios convierte el alma de una persona, esa persona es una nueva criatura y desea servir a Dios con todo su ser. No hace falta obligarla a hacer lo que agrada a Dios. Hoy se habla mucho en la iglesia de estructura y reglas; sin embargo, no siempre fue así. Entonces, ¿por qué es hoy un problema tan grande? Quizás haya personas inconversas en la iglesia. Tal vez la gente sea demasiado independiente y no quiera que le digan qué hacer. Se le puede decir a un miembro de la iglesia que vista con modestia, pero si su corazón no ha cambiado, surgirán problemas. Intentará ser tan mundano como pueda y, aun así, mantenerse dentro de la «ley» de la iglesia. O simplemente se negará a hacerlo, y pronto la iglesia cederá y dejará de exigir que su gente vista y viva con modestia. ¿Debería la iglesia tener que obligar a su gente a ser modesta? ¿Debería tener que obligarla a ser como Cristo? En absoluto. Cuando un alma ha sido redimida y transformada por la sangre de Cristo, esa persona, a su vez, por causa de su naturaleza cambiada, vivirá una vida de sacrificio por Él. ¡Obedecemos sus mandamientos con corazones agradecidos!

Porque este es el amor de Dios: que guardemos sus mandamientos; y sus mandamientos no son gravosos –1 Juan 5:3.

Un corazón que no ha sido renovado por el Espíritu de Dios no deseará fervientemente vivir para Dios. Se puede ir religiosamente a la iglesia; muchos incrédulos asisten con regularidad a los cultos. Se puede vestir y comportar correctamente, pero si el corazón no anhela las cosas de Dios, todo esto será inútil. Gran parte de lo que hacen busca recibir la alabanza de los hombres, no la gloria de Dios. No es de extrañar que muchas iglesias de hoy acepten el desviarse del camino.

Es hermoso ver a alguien que de verdad desea vivir para Dios. Desea buscar el rostro de su Creador, su Salvador. Vive para el Reino, para la hermandad. Obedecer a Dios y servirle es una necesidad; es lo único que realmente le importa. De verdad ha puesto todo sobre el altar. Ama leer la Palabra y pasar tiempo a solas con Dios. Sus deseos y su voluntad han sido sacrificados en el altar de su Dios.

Algunos me han dicho que debemos darle un poco de margen a un cristiano nuevo. «¿Margen para qué?», pregunto. ¿Margen para pecar… para vivir según la carne? En absoluto. Todos los ejemplos de la Biblia dicen lo contrario. Toda conversión produjo un cambio tremendo, una nueva criatura. Muchos confunden la «gracia para aprender y crecer» en la fe con una «excusa para pecar». Las Escrituras describen a los cristianos nuevos como niños recién nacidos y nos mandan a cada uno a desear, como niños recién nacidos, la leche espiritual pura, para que por ella crezcan: –1 Pedro 2:2. Así que los cristianos nuevos no necesitan espacio para seguir por un tiempo en sus caminos impíos, pero sí necesitan espacio para crecer …en sabiduría y en estatura, y en gracia para con Dios y los hombres –Lucas 2:52.

Cuando alguien viene declarando que se ha convertido, es fácil averiguarlo. Simplemente repasamos algunos pasajes que explican doctrinas prácticas y fundamentales, como la inconformidad con el mundo, la no resistencia y otras semejantes. Algunos reconocen que es la Palabra de Dios y la reciben con avidez. Muchos se quedan asombrados mientras les leo versículos como estos: pasajes de las Escrituras que nunca habían oído antes. Por lo general, simplemente creen lo que acaban de oír de la Palabra de Dios, y eso los transforma. Ese es un cristiano que quiere que le enseñen, que quiere ser discipulado. Suele venir con una actitud dispuesta a aprender, haciendo preguntas sobre lo que ha leído en la Palabra de Dios y no entiende.

Pero ¿qué pasa con tantos otros? Oyen los mismos pasajes y discuten; discuten con la Biblia y con la persona que comparte las Escrituras con ellos, pero, en última instancia, están discutiendo con Dios. Por lo general admitirán que eso es lo que dice la Biblia, pero quieren saber por qué lo dice. No quieren cambiar su vida por Dios. Sí, quieren ser cristianos, pero también quieren vivir como les dé la gana. No desean obedecer a Dios. Podemos seguir trabajando con ellos, pero está claro: su corazón anhela las cosas del mundo y los placeres de esta vida.

Imaginen conmigo a un hombre que vive hace 1.000 años. Está encerrado en un calabozo donde todo es negro como el carbón. Huele a humedad y apesta. Lo arrestaron por predicar el evangelio. Tiene los tobillos y las muñecas en carne viva y ensangrentados por las pesadas cadenas que lo mantienen atado en la diminuta celda. Es claustrofóbico, está agotado y exhausto. Tiene la espalda ensangrentada. Sus miembros doloridos han sido estirados hasta casi quebrarse. Habla con Dios, pero Dios no responde. Suplica que lo libre, pero no recibe respuesta. Recuerda su vida, su fe. Entonces se le ocurre el pensamiento temido: «Dios, ¿estás ahí? ¿Eres real?». Silencio. Su fe está siendo probada al extremo. Sabe que, si sigue aferrado a sus creencias, lo espera el fuego. ¿Por qué? ¿Por qué morir por un Dios que permite que pase por esta agonía? ¿Por qué morir por un Dios que no hablará? «Dios mío, Dios mío, ¿por qué me has desamparado?»

Ahora imaginen a este hombre… ese eres tú.

¿De verdad creemos en Dios, un Dios que no se ve y a menudo no se oye? Si nuestra fe no existe, Dios tampoco existirá cuando realmente lo necesitemos.

Dios quiere que pongamos toda nuestra fe en Él, en todo momento. Andamos por fe, NO por vista… incluso cuando todo va bien. Cuando nos encontramos en momentos terribles, Dios sigue cerca, guiándonos y dándonos valor para seguir adelante. Estamos acostumbrados a confiar sencillamente en Él, en su palabra.

Porque si hacen estas cosas en el árbol verde, ¿qué no se hará en el seco? –Lucas 23:31.

Dios ama un corazón vuelto hacia Él, plenamente entregado y rendido. ¡Él recompensa a quienes lo buscan diligentemente!

¿Tenemos el fruto del Espíritu de Dios? ¿Nos comportamos como cristianos? ¿Parecemos cristianos?

Me pidieron que predicara en una iglesia grande en la que nunca había estado. Fui con mi familia y me senté mientras cientos de personas llenaban los asientos. Me sorprendió cómo vestía aquella gente. Había minifaldas cortas y blusas diminutas, mucha moda y estilo mundanos. Comenzó el servicio y pronto me di cuenta de que aquel no era un buen lugar para mi familia, así que los llevé a casa y regresé solo. Seguía sonando la música rock, y el baile estaba poniendo a prueba mis límites. Después de dos horas llegó el momento del mensaje. Me puse de pie y le dije a la multitud que yo era el nuevo presidente de Estados Unidos. El auditorio estalló en risas. Entonces les pregunté si me creían. «¡No!», gritaron. Les pregunté por qué no me creían, y respondieron con distintas razones. Uno gritó: «¡No pareces ni vistes como el presidente!». Otro dijo: «¡Si fueras el presidente, no estarías aquí!». Otro más dijo que no hablaba como el presidente. Les dije que no entendía. Les pregunté cómo podían decir que eran cristianos: ¡no parecían cristianos!, ¡no se comportaban como cristianos!, ¡no hablaban como cristianos! Sin embargo, ¡todos les creen!

Parece que juzgamos todo por su fruto, excepto a los cristianos. En el caso de los cristianos, se espera que juzguemos por lo que afirman. Este mundo piensa que basta con imaginar lo que Jesús quiere y luego agradarle de cualquier manera que cada uno elija. Sin embargo, la Biblia es clara: Por sus frutos los conocerán. ¿Acaso se recogen uvas de los espinos, o higos de los abrojos? Así, todo buen árbol da buenos frutos, pero el árbol malo da frutos malos. No puede el buen árbol dar malos frutos, ni el árbol malo dar frutos buenos. Todo árbol que no da buen fruto es cortado y echado al fuego. Así que, por sus frutos los conocerán –Mateo 7:16-20.

La Biblia dice que …el fruto del Espíritu es amor, gozo, paz, paciencia, benignidad, bondad, fe, mansedumbre, templanza… –Gálatas 5:22-23. ¿Son estas las cosas que la gente ve cuando nos mira a ti y a mí? Sé que es fácil justificar la falta de uno o más de estos frutos diciendo: «Estoy trabajando en ello» o «Estoy orando por ello». Jesús no dice que estos frutos sean algo que los cristianos deban esforzarse por alcanzar. Simplemente dice que estos son los frutos, o el producto, del Espíritu de Dios que mora en nosotros. Si perseguimos ambiciones mundanas o deseamos encajar en el mundo, no podemos esperar que este fruto se haga evidente en nuestra vida. Creo que este es el fruto de un hombre que sufre, de una persona que lo ha dado todo y desea entregarlo todo al Cordero que fue inmolado.

Todo árbol que no da buen fruto es cortado y echado al fuego –Mateo 7:19.

Cuando damos todo de nosotros en algo, ya sea nuestro trabajo, nuestros estudios o la crianza de una familia, se siente bien; resulta gratificante. Lo mismo ocurre cuando servimos a Dios con todo nuestro ser. Se siente una gran satisfacción, una paz que sobrepasa todo entendimiento.

As a young man I remember hearing a popular slogan about faith: “Faith begins when reason ends.” As a young Christian, I thought it was a great life slogan. As I mature in my walk with Jesus, I look back on this particular slogan and shake my head. I can think of no better way to misrepresent faith than by claiming it exists apart from reason.

One simple reason for rejecting this view is because it misrepresents faith. A quick search on Google turns up this definition of faith: “complete trust or confidence in someone or something.” We use this definition all the time. I might tell you I have faith in my wife, I have faith in my employer to give me a paycheck, or I have no faith in alcohol to give me a good time. This is the same way the Bible defines faith.

Hebrews 11:1 affirms that faith is “confidence in what we hope for and assurance about what we do not see.” Biblical faith is simply a state of mind that has confidence and trust in the Lord. I have confidence that I will one day walk on the new Earth, and I have confidence that the Holy Spirit is working in the hearts of Christians. My confidence is based on, not apart from, reason. The more Jesus shows himself trustworthy, the more I trust (have confidence in) Him.

One aspect of Christ’s dependability is His word. The Old Testament was written by prophets and leaders who correctly predicted future events and ruled nations. The New Testament was written by Apostles or people that were closely associated with the apostles. We have more manuscripts of the Bible than any other work in antiquity. The Bible gives an honest portrayal of its heroes and correctly describes ancient leaders and places. In short, I trust in the Bible because it stands alone above all other books in terms of its authorship, preservation, honesty, and accuracy. The more I read it and read about it, the more my faith—and trust—increases.

Luke bases his whole Gospel on the premise that more knowledge gives more faith. He begins his book with this introduction: Many have undertaken to draw up an account of the things that have been fulfilled [or been surely believed] among us, just as they were handed down to us by those who from the first were eyewitnesses and servants of the word. With this in mind, since I myself have carefully investigated everything from the beginning, I too decided to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught. –Luke 1:1-4. (NIV)

The apostle Paul argues that faith in God is so grounded in reality that no one has a legitimate claim against God’s existence. He writes, The wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of people, who suppress the truth by their wickedness, since what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities—his eternal power and divine nature—have been clearly seen, being understood from what has been made, so that people are without excuse –Romans 1:18-20. (NIV)

Knowledge of nature builds my faith in Jesus. Scripture teaches that God created all life in six days, that there was a global flood, and that animals produce after their own kind. All across our earth, the rocks cry out their testimony of the global flood. People have uncovered billions of fossils—mostly marine animals—in rock layers that were laid down by water. Animals too, live out what the Bible teaches about kinds. We can observe animals changing all around us. They change sizes, colors, and eating habits. Fish in caves lose their ability to see. Birds’ beaks adjust to the environment. In all this intricate change, all animals exist within the Biblical framework of their own kind. Sharks remain sharks; frogs remain frogs; iguanas remain iguanas; and gibbons remain gibbons. The more I learn and observe about nature, the more my faith (confidence) increases.

In some discussions of faith, it is natural for the words of Jesus to come up. After His resurrection, Jesus visits Thomas and tells him, …Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed –John 20:29. (ESV) From this, it is tempting to define faith as “believing without seeing.” That would be missing the point. I’m not claiming any superiority to Thomas, but he should have believed without seeing Jesus. All the evidence pointed to it. First, his good friends, who had proved themselves trustworthy, said Jesus was alive. Second, Jesus had plainly said He would be resurrected (see Matthew 16:21). Third, Jesus had already proven He was divine by His ability to raise the dead, control the weather, heal the sick, and multiply food. Thomas had all he needed to believe Jesus rose from the dead. Yet, he went against all reasoning and said he needed more evidence.

When confronted with the resurrected Christ, Thomas repented of his disbelief and followed Christ into martyrdom. Unfortunately, the spirit of disbelief in the face of evidence still lingers in our world. Atheists claim, in spite of all evidence to the contrary, that life can come from nothing. They claim, without any evidence, that fish turned into frogs. They blindly cling to various theories such as: The Big Bang, Punctuated Equilibrium, and Descent with Modification. They have NO workable evidence, yet they still claim to base all their thoughts on observable, repeatable reality. Christians, who with good intentions, tell them that faith begins where reason ends, unwittingly play right into their hands. This world does not need a social media definition of faith. They need to see faith for what it is: confidence in the living God based firmly in reason.

Quando era jovem, lembro-me de ouvir um slogan popular sobre a fé: “A fé começa quando a razão termina.” Quando jovem cristão, achei que era um excelente lema de vida. À medida que amadureço em minha caminhada com Jesus, olho para trás e balanço a cabeça diante desse slogan em particular. Não consigo pensar em maneira melhor de deturpar a fé do que afirmar que ela existe à parte da razão.

Uma razão simples para rejeitar essa visão é que ela deturpa a fé. Uma rápida pesquisa no Google apresenta esta definição de fé: “confiança ou convicção completa em alguém ou alguma coisa”. Usamos essa definição o tempo todo. Eu poderia dizer que tenho fé em minha esposa, que tenho fé em meu empregador para me pagar, ou que não tenho fé no álcool para me proporcionar bons momentos. É assim também que a Bíblia define a fé.

Hebreus 11:1 afirma que a fé é “confiança naquilo que esperamos e convicção a respeito do que não vemos”. A fé bíblica é simplesmente um estado de espírito que tem confiança e confia no Senhor. Tenho confiança de que um dia caminharei na nova Terra e tenho confiança de que o Espírito Santo está agindo no coração dos cristãos. Minha confiança se baseia na razão, e não à parte dela. Quanto mais Jesus se mostra digno de confiança, mais confio nele (tenho confiança nele).

Um aspecto da confiabilidade de Cristo é a sua palavra. O Antigo Testamento foi escrito por profetas e líderes que previram corretamente acontecimentos futuros e governaram nações. O Novo Testamento foi escrito por apóstolos ou por pessoas estreitamente associadas aos apóstolos. Temos mais manuscritos da Bíblia do que de qualquer outra obra da Antiguidade. A Bíblia apresenta honestamente seus heróis e descreve corretamente líderes e lugares antigos. Em suma, confio na Bíblia porque ela se destaca acima de todos os outros livros em termos de autoria, preservação, honestidade e exatidão. Quanto mais a leio e leio a respeito dela, mais minha fé — e confiança — aumenta.

Lucas baseia todo o seu Evangelho na premissa de que mais conhecimento produz mais fé. Ele começa seu livro com esta introdução: Muitos empreenderam fazer um relato dos fatos que se cumpriram [ou nos quais se creu firmemente] entre nós, conforme nos foram transmitidos por aqueles que desde o princípio foram testemunhas oculares e servos da palavra. Por isso, visto que eu mesmo investiguei cuidadosamente todas as coisas desde o princípio, também decidi escrever-te um relato ordenado, excelentíssimo Teófilo, para que conheças a certeza das coisas que te foram ensinadas. –Lucas 1:1-4. (NIV)

O apóstolo Paulo argumenta que a fé em Deus está tão firmemente alicerçada na realidade que ninguém tem uma alegação legítima contra a existência de Deus. Ele escreve: A ira de Deus está sendo revelada do céu contra toda a impiedade e injustiça das pessoas que suprimem a verdade por meio de sua injustiça, pois o que se pode conhecer a respeito de Deus lhes é evidente, porque Deus lhes tornou isso evidente. Pois, desde a criação do mundo, as qualidades invisíveis de Deus — seu poder eterno e sua natureza divina — são claramente percebidas, sendo compreendidas por meio das coisas criadas, de modo que as pessoas ficam sem desculpa –Romanos 1:18-20. (NIV)

O conhecimento da natureza fortalece minha fé em Jesus. As Escrituras ensinam que Deus criou toda a vida em seis dias, que houve um dilúvio global e que os animais se reproduzem segundo a sua própria espécie. Por toda a Terra, as rochas proclamam o testemunho do dilúvio global. As pessoas descobriram bilhões de fósseis — em sua maioria, de animais marinhos — em camadas de rocha depositadas pela água. Os animais também vivem de acordo com o que a Bíblia ensina sobre as espécies. Podemos observar animais mudando ao nosso redor. Eles mudam de tamanho, de cor e de hábitos alimentares. Peixes das cavernas perdem a capacidade de enxergar. Os bicos das aves se ajustam ao ambiente. Em meio a todas essas mudanças intrincadas, todos os animais se mantêm dentro do modelo bíblico de sua própria espécie. Os tubarões continuam sendo tubarões; as rãs continuam sendo rãs; as iguanas continuam sendo iguanas; e os gibões continuam sendo gibões. Quanto mais aprendo e observo a natureza, mais minha fé (confiança) aumenta.

Em algumas conversas sobre fé, é natural que venham à tona as palavras de Jesus. Após sua ressurreição, Jesus visita Tomé e lhe diz: …Você creu porque me viu? Bem-aventurados os que não viram e creram –João 20:29. (ESV) Diante disso, é tentador definir fé como “crer sem ver”. Isso seria não entender o ponto. Não estou afirmando ser superior a Tomé, mas ele deveria ter crido sem ver Jesus. Todas as evidências apontavam nessa direção. Primeiro, seus bons amigos, que haviam provado ser dignos de confiança, disseram que Jesus estava vivo. Segundo, Jesus havia dito claramente que ressuscitaria (ver Mateus 16:21). Terceiro, Jesus já havia provado que era divino por sua capacidade de ressuscitar os mortos, controlar o clima, curar os doentes e multiplicar alimentos. Tomé tinha tudo de que precisava para crer que Jesus ressuscitara dos mortos. Ainda assim, foi contra todo o raciocínio e disse que precisava de mais evidências.

Ao se deparar com Cristo ressuscitado, Tomé se arrependeu de sua incredulidade e seguiu Cristo até o martírio. Infelizmente, o espírito de incredulidade diante das evidências ainda persiste em nosso mundo. Os ateus afirmam, apesar de todas as evidências em contrário, que a vida pode surgir do nada. Afirmam, sem qualquer evidência, que os peixes se transformaram em rãs. Apegam-se cegamente a várias teorias, como: o Big Bang, o Equilíbrio Pontuado e a Descendência com Modificação. Não têm NENHUMA evidência viável, mas ainda afirmam basear todos os seus pensamentos na realidade observável e repetível. Os cristãos que, com boas intenções, lhes dizem que a fé começa onde a razão termina, acabam, sem perceber, fazendo exatamente o jogo deles. Este mundo não precisa de uma definição de fé das redes sociais. Precisa ver a fé como ela é: confiança no Deus vivo, firmemente alicerçada na razão.

That our sons may be as plants grown up in their youth; that our daughters may be as corner stones, polished after the similitude of a palace –Psalm 144:12.

The vision of every godly parent is to see their children grow into mature adulthood. We want our children to develop biblical convictions that will govern their lives and allow them to become independent of parental guidance.

This was the vision of every Jewish father. To celebrate their child’s transition to personal responsibility, a ceremony was held called bar mitzvah for boys, and bat mitzvah for girls. This was traditionally done at the age of thirteen. Bar mitzvah means “a son of the commandment” and bat mitzvah “a daughter of the commandment”. After bar mitzvah a son was considered to be “under the law” and responsible for his own actions. Prior to this event, his parents were accountable for his actions.

Most of us are not of Jewish descent; however, our Lord Jesus was. We find him at the age of twelve sitting in the temple visiting with the doctors, both hearing them and asking them questions. And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers. (see Luke 2:47) Jesus demonstrated an amazing level of maturity at the age of twelve. Even his parents were amazed. Yes, he was divine, yet as a human he demonstrated the potential for early maturity given the right set of values and disciplines.

The teen years are transitional years. Teens are transitioning from childhood to adulthood; from being dependent on parents to learning to be independent. This transition is a process that must be understood by both the parents and the child. Too much freedom too soon, can leave the child feeling insecure and can result in bad choices that can have life-long consequences. Too little freedom can squelch a child’s character growth and can become fertile ground for rebellion.

The teen years are growing years. Just as a plant needs diligent cultivation throughout its life cycle, so a child needs ongoing direction throughout his teen years. After Jesus’ episode in the temple we read, And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them… –Luke 2:51. We will look at some things that parents can do to nurture maturity in their children, but first we will consider several relationships that are foundational to healthy maturity.

Happy is that people, that is in such a case: yea, happy is that people, whose God is the LORD –Psalm 144:15.

Parental relationship

The relationship between the parent and the child in the teen years is largely a reaping of what that relationship was throughout the formative years of childhood. Unless there is a major spiritual crisis that dynamically changes the relationship—such as an evangelical conversion on the part of either the parent or the child—we (as parents) reap during the child’s teen years that which we have sown during their childhood.

Raising teens is a rewarding experience if there has been a healthy foundational relationship established throughout childhood. If the parent has been physically and emotionally present; if the parent and child have been communicating openly and freely; and if the parent has lovingly maintained the role of authority and control, then a foundation has been laid for a more mature level of relating during the teen years.

In the absence of this kind of parental relationship, the child entering the teen years will try to fill this void with other relationships. Most often, if a parental relationship is lacking, a child will seek to fill that void through relationships with their peers. Peers are great friends but are a poor substitute for a parent. We have been created to be relational. Teens especially crave significance through relationship.

There are two things that every teen is looking for in parental relationship. One is identity and the other is affirmation. Two burning questions in the heart of every teen are “Who am I?” and “Am I OK?”.

The identity factor

When children are young, they assume their family identity. As children grow into adolescence and become more independent, they begin to view themselves as someone more than merely Dad’s son. They begin to develop an identity of their own. This movement toward “being my own person” becomes evident in many of the choices that they make such as:

  • How they dress
  • Their choice of music
  • Their choice of friends
  • Whether or not they choose to serve their parent’s God
  • Whether or not they choose to worship in the church of their upbringing

Admittedly, there are other influences that can affect a teen’s choices in these areas, but for the most part these choices reflect the relationship between the child and the parent. Where the parent has exerted a positive influence on the child, that child will be more inclined to adopt the values of the parent.

When the parental relationship has broken down or has never been nurtured, or if the relationship has been nothing more than a master/slave relationship, that child will seek to identify with someone other than the parent. This will manifest itself in choices of dress, music, friends, and activities that the parent will not approve of. This is often called “teenage rebellion”.

Is “teenage rebellion” always the fault of the parent? No, but if you are not actively involved in building and maintaining a relationship with your teen, it is likely to happen. It is important to note that there is a rebel in the heart of every person. In my last article I stressed the importance of confronting that rebel spirit when our children are young and impressionable.

This rebel spirit will not be fully conquered until it is surrendered to God through an evangelical conversion experience. Only a work of the grace of God upon the heart can subdue the inborn rebellion against God and parental authority.

Know the heart of your child and seek to lead them into loving submission to the Lord Jesus Christ. Only in a relationship with Jesus Christ can our children find their true and lasting identity. Parental authority has a place in shaping and controlling our children when they are young. As our children grow into adulthood, we come to realize that parental authority has limitations and our children need to be controlled by an influence beyond ourselves.

It is never too late to build a relational bridge. If you are feeling that you have failed in your relationship with your children, it’s never too late to call them to your side and humbly seek to restore what is missing. Even if your children are gone from home, I can assure you that they long for a relationship with mom and dad.

The affirmation factor

Every teen longs to be affirmed by their parents, especially their father. You can affirm your teen by looking for and acknowledging positive character traits. There is a place for corrective criticism from parent to child, but criticism that demeans is not constructive; it’s destructive. For every critical comment you should have several positive compliments. In other words, you earn the right to criticize what is wrong by blessing what is right.

You can affirm your teen by treating them with dignity and respect. You can ask, “How do you feel about…?” Or “What do you think we should do…?” You are not surrendering your parental responsibility by probing your son’s or daughter’s mind for their perspective. You are actually causing them to be “grown up in their youth” by forcing them to think as adults.

You can affirm your teen by treating him with common courtesy. Simple things like “please” and “thank you”,” I’m sorry”, “pardon me”, “good bye”, “have a good day”, “drive safely”, and “God bless you”, expresses worth and value to your teen. If these simple courtesies are common in your home your children will return them to you. Think about how you feel when someone says to you, “Oh, excuse me, I’m sorry.” You feel a sense of respect, value, and dignity. That is a simple gift that every parent can give to his child.

You can affirm your teen by entrusting him with responsibility. I grew up on a dairy farm. We had plenty of opportunity to develop character and skills. I remember one day when I was 16 years of age, my dad needed a concrete block wall built out in the barn. I volunteered for the job. Dad provided the blocks and the mortar and got me started. Then I was on my own. Did I build a professional-looking wall? No, but I was quite proud of the outcome and that wall lasted for many years. Dad trusted me to do a man’s job and I did it.

Affirming is not flattery. Flattery is praise that is not sincere and often is not true. Affirming is recognizing and encouraging the good that you see in another. I have encountered grown men who have wept bitterly because they had never received affirmation from their father. Even Jesus received affirmation from His Father when His Father said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

(2) Relationship with God

Our first responsibility in evangelization is to our children. If we cannot evangelize our children, how can we expect to win others to the Lord? We have a distinct advantage in relating our faith to our children in that we are living with our children. They can and do observe how our faith is lived out in everyday life. This should be the most convincing evidence for the validity of our faith.

Unfortunately, how parents live out their faith, or rather fail to live out their faith, can become a huge stumbling block to their children. Our children are keenly aware of any inconsistency in our Christian profession.

Conversely, if our children see that the power of God is evident in our lives, if they see their parents demonstrating faith in God that carries them through difficult times, if they see their parents demonstrating a graceful rest in the Lord, and if, in the home Jesus Christ is exalted and worshipped, they will be convinced to make their parents’ God, their God.

It is the reality of the gospel lived out in daily life that is the most convincing evidence for the validity of our faith. Our children should be our first witnesses to the transformational work of the gospel in our hearts.

How does a parent lead his child to salvation? Salvation is a work of God; however, God uses human instrumentality to accomplish His work. Parents play a major role in leading their children to Christ. Be aware of evidence of conviction. If a child is quiet and withdrawn, or irritable and restless, or belligerent and defiant, it may be that the spirit of God is working in their heart.

Hopefully, you have nurtured a relationship that allows you to probe their heart and gently lead them to Jesus for forgiveness and cleansing. Most of our children’s conversions were initiated by a parent. We recognized signs of conviction and lead them to brokenness and repentance and to receive salvation through faith in Christ.

The early teen years are an ideal time for a child to surrender his/her life to Jesus if he has not already done so. When active rebellion sets in, a teen often makes choices that lead to painful reaping and sometimes irrevocable consequences. A life of dedicated service to God is the only life of blessing and fulfilment.

Relationship with the church

There is one more relationship that dramatically affects the formation of a teen’s life and convictions and that is the local church. We gain both our sense of identity and our understanding of the reality of the Christian faith through our experience of worship and relationship within the local church. After parental relationship, this is the next most significant influence in a teen’s life.

It is important that we worship in a church that presents the gospel as a transformational relationship with God through faith in Jesus. It is also important that our church life consists of warm, loving relationships in a close–knit community.

The reason that I mention this is that some parents have the mistaken idea that they can provide all the spiritual direction and relationships that their children need. This may seem to work when the children are small and close at hand, but as our children grow into adulthood, they will seek a broader world of relationships. The local church and community of associated churches provides this broader base of fellowship.

It is important to worship in a church that you can support and that you can encourage your children to support. Many children have been lost to the faith because mom and dad were not supportive of the church where they were worshipping. It is far better to move on and find a church that you can support than to stay in a church and be in a state of constant opposition.

I am not encouraging church hopping. It is important to children, especially your teens, that there is stability in church life. Find a church that you are comfortable with, hopefully while your children are young, and stick with it. There are always logistical exceptions and your children will adapt to these, but for the most part a stable church life produces youth who have a strong sense of identity and purpose.

As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man; so are children of the youth –Psalm 127:4. This verse reminds us that our children are a mighty defense against the enemy. If properly honed (trained) and balanced (taught disciplines) our children will have the potential to outlive us both in years and in usefulness. When you release the arrow your children will go places both in time and in the world that you will never see. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them: they shall not be ashamed, but they shall speak with the enemies in the gate –Psalm 127:5.

Så att våra söner må vara som plantor, uppvuxna i sin ungdom, och våra döttrar som hörnstenar, polerade efter mönstret av ett palats – Psaltaren 144:12.

Varje gudfruktig förälders vision är att se sina barn växa upp till mogna vuxna. Vi vill att våra barn ska utveckla bibliska övertygelser som vägleder deras liv och gör det möjligt för dem att bli självständiga från föräldrarnas vägledning.

Detta var varje judisk fars vision. För att fira barnets övergång till personligt ansvar hölls en ceremoni som kallades bar mitzva för pojkar och bat mitzva för flickor. Traditionellt ägde detta rum vid tretton års ålder. Bar mitzva betyder ”en son av budet” och bat mitzva ”en dotter av budet”. Efter bar mitzva ansågs en son stå ”under lagen” och vara ansvarig för sina egna handlingar. Före denna händelse var hans föräldrar ansvariga för hans handlingar.

De flesta av oss har inte judisk härkomst, men vår Herre Jesus hade det. Vi finner honom vid tolv års ålder sittande i templet och samtala med de lärda, både lyssna på dem och ställa frågor till dem. Och alla som hörde honom häpnade över hans förstånd och svar. (se Lukasevangeliet 2:47) Jesus visade en förbluffande mognad vid tolv års ålder. Till och med hans föräldrar häpnade. Ja, han var gudomlig, men som människa visade han på möjligheten till tidig mognad när rätt värderingar och vanor finns på plats.

Tonåren är en övergångsperiod. Tonåringar går från barndom till vuxenliv, från att vara beroende av sina föräldrar till att lära sig bli självständiga. Denna övergång är en process som både föräldrarna och barnet behöver förstå. För mycket frihet för tidigt kan göra att barnet känner sig otryggt och leda till dåliga val som kan få konsekvenser för resten av livet. För lite frihet kan hämma barnets karaktärsutveckling och bli en grogrund för uppror.

Tonåren är en tid av utveckling. Precis som en planta behöver omsorgsfull odling genom hela sin livscykel behöver ett barn fortlöpande vägledning under tonåren. Efter Jesu vistelse i templet läser vi: Han följde med dem ner till Nasaret och lydde dem … – Lukasevangeliet 2:51. Vi ska se på några saker som föräldrar kan göra för att främja sina barns mognad, men först ska vi begrunda några relationer som utgör grunden för en sund mognad.

Saligt är det folk som har det så, ja, saligt är det folk vars Gud är Herren – Psaltaren 144:15.

Relationen till föräldrarna

Relationen mellan förälder och barn under tonåren är till stor del en skörd av den relation de hade under barndomens formativa år. Om inte en allvarlig andlig kris förändrar relationen på ett genomgripande sätt – till exempel genom att någon av föräldrarna eller barnet blir evangeliskt omvänd – skördar vi (som föräldrar) under barnets tonår det vi sådde under barndomen.

Att uppfostra tonåringar är en givande erfarenhet om en sund grundläggande relation har etablerats under barndomen. Om föräldern har varit fysiskt och känslomässigt närvarande, om förälder och barn har kommunicerat öppet och fritt, och om föräldern kärleksfullt har upprätthållit sin roll som den som har auktoritet och bestämmer, då har en grund lagts för en mognare relation under tonåren.

Om en sådan föräldrarelation saknas kommer barnet som går in i tonåren att försöka fylla tomrummet med andra relationer. Oftast försöker barnet, när en föräldrarelation brister, fylla tomrummet genom relationer till jämnåriga. Jämnåriga kan vara goda vänner, men de är en dålig ersättning för en förälder. Vi är skapade för relationer. Tonåringar längtar särskilt efter att känna sig betydelsefulla genom relationer.

Det finns två saker som varje tonåring söker i relationen till sina föräldrar. Den ena är identitet och den andra bekräftelse. Två brännande frågor i varje tonårings hjärta är: ”Vem är jag?” och ”Är jag okej?”

Identitetsfaktorn

När barn är små tar de till sig familjens identitet. När barn växer in i tonåren och blir mer självständiga börjar de se sig själva som någon mer än bara pappas son. De börjar utveckla en egen identitet. Denna rörelse mot att ”vara min egen person” blir tydlig i många av deras val, till exempel:

  • Hur de klär sig
  • Vilken musik de väljer
  • Vilka vänner de väljer
  • Om de väljer att tjäna sina föräldrars Gud eller inte
  • Om de väljer att tillbe i den kyrka där de växte upp eller inte

Det finns naturligtvis andra faktorer som kan påverka en tonårings val på dessa områden, men för det mesta återspeglar valen relationen mellan barnet och föräldern. När föräldern har haft ett positivt inflytande på barnet är det mer sannolikt att barnet tar till sig förälderns värderingar.

När föräldrarelationen har brutit samman eller aldrig har vårdats, eller om relationen inte har varit något annat än en herre/slav-relation, kommer barnet att söka sin identitet hos någon annan än föräldern. Detta kommer till uttryck i val av kläder, musik, vänner och aktiviteter som föräldern inte godkänner. Detta kallas ofta ”tonårsrevolt”.

Är ”tonårsrevolt” alltid förälderns fel? Nej, men om du inte aktivt arbetar på att bygga upp och upprätthålla en relation till din tonåring är det sannolikt att det händer. Det är viktigt att komma ihåg att det finns en upprorsmakare i varje människas hjärta. I min förra artikel betonade jag hur viktigt det är att konfrontera denna upproriska ande när våra barn är små och formbara.

Denna upproriska ande kommer inte att besegras helt förrän den överlämnas åt Gud genom en evangelisk omvändelse. Endast Guds nådverk i hjärtat kan kuva den medfödda upproret mot Gud och föräldrarnas auktoritet.

Lär känna ditt barns hjärta och försök leda det till kärleksfull underkastelse under Herren Jesus Kristus. Endast i en relation med Jesus Kristus kan våra barn finna sin sanna och bestående identitet. Föräldrarnas auktoritet har en roll i att forma och styra våra barn när de är små. När våra barn växer upp till vuxna inser vi att föräldrarnas auktoritet har sina begränsningar och att våra barn behöver ledas av ett inflytande som sträcker sig bortom oss själva.

Det är aldrig för sent att bygga en bro mellan er. Om du känner att du har misslyckats i relationen till dina barn är det aldrig för sent att kalla dem till dig och ödmjukt försöka återställa det som saknas. Även om dina barn har flyttat hemifrån kan jag försäkra dig om att de längtar efter en relation med mamma och pappa.

Bekräftelsefaktorn

Varje tonåring längtar efter bekräftelse från sina föräldrar, särskilt sin far. Du kan bekräfta din tonåring genom att lägga märke till och erkänna positiva karaktärsdrag. Det finns en plats för korrigerande kritik från förälder till barn, men kritik som förödmjukar är inte konstruktiv; den är destruktiv. För varje kritisk kommentar bör du ge flera positiva komplimanger. Med andra ord förtjänar du rätten att kritisera det som är fel genom att uppmuntra det som är rätt.

Du kan bekräfta din tonåring genom att behandla honom eller henne med värdighet och respekt. Du kan fråga: ”Hur känner du inför …?” eller ”Vad tycker du att vi borde göra …?” Du avsäger dig inte ditt föräldraansvar genom att ta reda på din sons eller dotters perspektiv. Du hjälper dem faktiskt att ”växa upp i sin ungdom” genom att få dem att tänka som vuxna.

Du kan bekräfta din tonåring genom att behandla honom eller henne med vanlig artighet. Enkla ord som ”snälla” och ”tack”, ”förlåt”, ”ursäkta mig”, ”hej då”, ”ha en bra dag”, ”kör försiktigt” och ”Gud välsigne dig” förmedlar att din tonåring är värdefull och betydelsefull. Om sådana enkla artighetsfraser är vanliga i ert hem kommer dina barn att använda dem mot dig också. Tänk på hur du känner dig när någon säger till dig: ”Åh, ursäkta mig, förlåt.” Du känner dig respekterad och uppskattad och att din värdighet tas på allvar. Det är en enkel gåva som varje förälder kan ge sitt barn.

Du kan bekräfta din tonåring genom att anförtro honom eller henne ansvar. Jag växte upp på en mjölkgård. Vi hade gott om möjligheter att utveckla karaktär och färdigheter. Jag minns en dag när jag var 16 år och pappa behövde få en betongblocksvägg byggd ute i ladan. Jag erbjöd mig att göra jobbet. Pappa ordnade fram blocken och murbruket och satte i gång mig. Sedan fick jag klara mig själv. Byggde jag en vägg som såg professionell ut? Nej, men jag var ganska stolt över resultatet, och väggen stod i många år. Pappa litade på att jag skulle klara ett vuxenjobb, och jag gjorde det.

Att bekräfta är inte att smickra. Smicker är beröm som inte är uppriktigt och ofta inte heller sant. Att bekräfta är att uppmärksamma och uppmuntra det goda man ser hos någon annan. Jag har träffat vuxna män som gråtit bittert för att de aldrig fått bekräftelse från sin far. Till och med Jesus fick bekräftelse från sin Fader när Fadern sade: ”Detta är min älskade Son, han är min glädje.”

(2) Relationen till Gud

Vårt första ansvar när det gäller evangelisation är gentemot våra barn. Om vi inte kan evangelisera våra barn, hur kan vi då förvänta oss att vinna andra för Herren? Vi har ett särskilt försteg när vi förmedlar vår tro till våra barn, eftersom vi lever tillsammans med dem. De kan se, och ser faktiskt, hur vår tro tar sig uttryck i vardagen. Detta borde vara det mest övertygande beviset på att vår tro är sann.

Tyvärr kan föräldrarnas sätt att leva ut sin tro, eller snarare deras misslyckande med att göra det, bli en stor stötesten för barnen. Våra barn lägger noga märke till varje brist på överensstämmelse mellan vår kristna bekännelse och vårt liv.

Omvänt kommer våra barn att bli övertygade om att göra sina föräldrars Gud till sin Gud om de ser att Guds kraft är uppenbar i våra liv, om de ser sina föräldrar visa tro på Gud som bär dem genom svåra tider, om de ser sina föräldrar vila fridfullt i Herren, och om Jesus Kristus upphöjs och tillbes i hemmet.

Det är evangeliets verklighet, levd ut i vardagen, som är det mest övertygande beviset på att vår tro är sann. Våra barn borde vara de första som får bevittna evangeliets förvandlande verk i våra hjärtan.

Hur leder en förälder sitt barn till frälsning? Frälsningen är Guds verk, men Gud använder människor för att utföra sitt verk. Föräldrar spelar en viktig roll när det gäller att leda sina barn till Kristus. Var uppmärksam på tecken på överbevisning. Om ett barn är tyst och tillbakadraget, lättirriterat och rastlöst, eller stridslystet och trotsigt, kan det vara så att Guds Ande verkar i dess hjärta.

Förhoppningsvis har du vårdat en relation som gör det möjligt för dig att utforska deras hjärta och varsamt leda dem till Jesus för förlåtelse och rening. De flesta av våra barns omvändelser tog sin början genom en förälder. Vi såg tecken på överbevisning och ledde dem till förkrosselse och omvändelse och till att ta emot frälsningen genom tro på Kristus.

De tidiga tonåren är en idealisk tid för ett barn att överlämna sitt liv åt Jesus, om det inte redan har gjort det. När aktivt uppror tar vid gör en tonåring ofta val som leder till en smärtsam skörd och ibland oåterkalleliga konsekvenser. Ett liv i hängiven tjänst för Gud är det enda liv som är välsignat och meningsfullt.

Relationen till kyrkan

Det finns ytterligare en relation som i hög grad påverkar hur en tonårings liv och övertygelser formas: den lokala kyrkan. Vi får både vår känsla av identitet och vår förståelse av den kristna trons verklighet genom vår erfarenhet av gudstjänst och gemenskap i den lokala kyrkan. Efter relationen till föräldrarna är detta det näst mest betydelsefulla inflytandet i en tonårings liv.

Det är viktigt att vi tillber i en kyrka som förkunnar evangeliet som en förvandlande relation till Gud genom tron på Jesus. Det är också viktigt att kyrkolivet präglas av varma, kärleksfulla relationer i en nära gemenskap.

Jag nämner detta eftersom en del föräldrar felaktigt tror att de själva kan ge sina barn all den andliga vägledning och gemenskap de behöver. Det kan verka fungera när barnen är små och nära till hands, men när våra barn växer upp till vuxna kommer de att söka en bredare gemenskap. Den lokala kyrkan och gemenskapen av samverkande kyrkor ger denna bredare bas av gemenskap.

Det är viktigt att tillbe i en kyrka som du kan stödja och som du kan uppmuntra dina barn att stödja. Många barn har gått förlorade för tron eftersom mamma och pappa inte stödde kyrkan där de firade gudstjänst. Det är mycket bättre att gå vidare och hitta en kyrka som du kan stödja än att stanna i en kyrka och ständigt vara motståndare.

Jag uppmuntrar inte till att hoppa mellan kyrkor. Det är viktigt för barnen, särskilt tonåringarna, att kyrkolivet är stabilt. Hitta en kyrka som ni trivs i, helst medan barnen är små, och håll fast vid den. Det finns alltid praktiska undantag, och barnen kommer att anpassa sig till dem, men för det mesta leder ett stabilt kyrkoliv till ungdomar med en stark känsla av identitet och mening.

Som pilar i en hjältes hand är söner man får i sin ungdom – Psaltaren 127:4. Denna vers påminner oss om att våra barn är ett mäktigt försvar mot fienden. Om de slipas (tränas) och balanseras (undervisas i disciplin) på rätt sätt kommer våra barn att kunna överleva oss både i antal år och i vad de uträttar. När du släpper pilen kommer dina barn att komma till platser, både i tiden och i världen, som du aldrig kommer att få se. Lycklig den man som har sitt koger fullt av dem. De kommer inte på skam, när de går till rätta med fiender i porten – Psaltaren 127:5.
