We asked the Lord for him, our third child, third son. He came with the springtime, the crowning creation of new life, bewailing his shuffled surroundings. Folks commented on his wail: they thought it was adorable. We thought so, too. We loved him, we snuggled him, and we called him Judson.

Sterling and I had committed, prior to Judson’s birth, to take our youth group on a mission trip to Mexico. The date to leave for this trip fell five weeks after Judson came. As the leader’s wife, I was responsible to take food along to feed our group for the entire time. Making lists and shopping for it consumed me with preparation.

Judson did his own preparing. He developed bowel trouble. He went seven days without a messy pamper. I asked my midwife about it, but she was unruffled by the occurrence. When it went another seven days until the next full diaper, I asked his pediatrician. She, too, was unconcerned. So, we headed for Mexico: Sterling and I, our five-week-old baby, and two vanloads of youth.

Although the preparation had been taxing for me, the time in Mexico was like vacation. My only requirements while there were to take care of my baby and oversee mealtimes. But Judson didn’t like the trip at all. I cuddled him for hours, sitting under a tarp on a dramatic hillside, overlooking the construction site where our group was laboring. Judson acted restless and uncomfortable with me. He cried if anyone else held him. I felt something was amiss, but I had no definite signs of what, except that day after day passed without a dirty diaper.

On our sixth night in Mexico, I laid Judson on his cot. But the Lord drew me back, prompting me to pull him into bed beside me. I felt this nudge distinctly and obeyed, although I had let Judson sleep in the cot the other nights. We slept. Somewhere in the night, Judson awoke, refusing to be pacified. I tried this and that, half asleep myself. Suddenly he screamed out, only to choke mid-scream and then go limp.

“Sterling!” I yelped. “Turn on the flashlight! He’s not breathing!” I sat up in bed, examining my baby in the flashlight’s beam. His little face worked desperately, but no breath or sound came forth. Within seconds, his breath returned, and he screamed again. Then he choked. As surely as an invisible hand clutching his fragile neck, his breath ceased, and his eyes bulged in terror. I swiped my finger through his mouth, checking for something lodged in his airway, finding nothing. Shuddering, Judson gasped and cried. Tears forced themselves out of his eyes. “Oh, pray,” I begged. Sterling prayed, jumbling pleas together in a heavenward heap as our baby ceased breathing again. The episode repeated itself several more times: seconds of terrified screaming, then seconds of tortured silence. Sweat popped out on Judson’s face. It was agonizing to watch. Thoughts flew through my head: Our baby’s going to die. Just like that. No warning. Out here with no medical aid. Oh God! Help us, help us, help us! How does one just watch their baby die?

“I’m getting the missionary’s wife,” Sterling decided. I stammered dangling prayers while supporting Judson. When the missionary’s wife appeared, I handed him to her, grateful for the presence of a woman older than I. We prayed together, begging God to intervene. Judson began to cry and breath normally while she examined him. She handed him back to me as he calmed down.

“I don’t know what it is,” she said, after we told her the story. We thanked her for rousing in the night, then returned to our room. I cried while Judson peacefully slept in my arms.

“I sense it was a demoniac display,” Sterling stated. “If the devil can get us scared over what could happen to our baby while we are out in the boondocks, then he can get us to pack up our whole group and leave. The devil knows there are good things happening here, spiritually; this is not the time to flee. We can’t let him fill us with fear.”

I agreed. The unusual way Judson’s breath came and went looked as if an evil hand was gripping his neck. There seemed to be no natural explanation otherwise for the horrifying event. Sterling laid his hand on Judson and prayed, specifically rebuking the devil, and seeking the protection of God. We laid us down in peace and safety and slept.

In the morning, Judson seemed untroubled by the episode, although his restlessness increased. Eight, nine, and then ten days passed with no bowel movement. He cried, his soft, adorable cry agitating my heart. As we traveled back to the States, I fretted over the way he drew back from nursing, squirming and fussing until he fell asleep instead.

Then he began spitting up. When he finally spit up bright yellow liquid, I was alarmed. On the eleventh day, we visited a nurse practitioner in a Mennonite colony in Mexico. She examined Judson, listened to my report, and calmly replied, “And this is your first child?”

“No,” I responded, matching calm with calm. “This is my third.” She met my eyes then, silently, and reexamined Judson. She gave him a suppository, suggesting all babies are different. And so, they are. This one certainly was! With the topical relief of the suppository, Judson seemed to feel better.

He was seven weeks old when we came home. From the time he was three weeks until he was seven months, he struggled with his bowels.

On Sundays, people fingered his tiny face, commenting on his sweet little cry. Other days, I huddled in the rocker, hearing but not hearing his sweet little cry. Some days it seemed it never stopped. I held him except while he napped. I became familiar with his cycle: a span of days with no mess in which he gradually grew grumpier, a slacking off nursing, and finally, outright crying until I gave him the temporary relief of a suppository. Contrary to regular suspicion, he was not constipated. It appeared to my mother-sense that something within him did not naturally trigger his bowels to move.

“Grain free,” prompted one book. “It could be Hirschsprung’s, which can be naturally treated by going grain-free.” So, I ate grain-free. Five weeks dragged by on my altered diet. Judson didn’t seem to notice my efforts.

His pediatrician listened to my recital of his routine, then ordered a test for Hirschsprung’s.

The test came back clear. I gratefully resumed eating grains, only to meet with new advice the next Sunday. An experienced mother sought me out in the nursery where I took refuge from the noisy fellowship hall, rocking my sonny, rocking, rocking, rocking. “Have you considered dairy-free?”

Well, no, I hadn’t.

“I think you should try dairy-free,” she decided. Like a well-thumbed medical manual, she recounted the reasons for this route.

His pediatrician didn’t approve of the dairy-free idea. I visited her office after three weeks of it. “You need the fats in dairy to keep up your milk supply,” she scolded. “Besides, the first sign of a milk intolerance is blood in the stool, not lack of stool.”

I didn’t mind stopping the dairy-free diet. We tried other things. Judson held enemas in stubbornly. A prescribed dosage of laxative didn’t produce results. At one point, the doctor instructed me to just wait it out with Judson, convinced his bowels would move on their own. Judson outwaited me. By 17 days along, I resorted to suppositories to give my miserable baby relief.

But it wasn’t only the digestive mystery that gave us heartache over my baby. Even on a freshly emptied system, he was cantankerous. Mealtimes became misery. Judson fought when I sat down at the table to join the family for a meal. I became used to pinning him over my shoulder while I quickly ate, one-handed. Except I didn’t become used to it. I never became accustomed to his fussing. I learned to do the housework while he napped, as anything other than tending him was impossible when he was awake.

Church was also a sore spot. Judson acted worse in any place of activity, but he became unreasonable at church. I wrestled with him until he fell asleep, usually in time for me to hear the last part of the sermon.

Fellowship meals were a disaster. Judson screamed. He would let no one touch him other than me, and even then, I couldn’t calm him down. By the time we had fixed plates and fed our little family, I was exhausted and ready to go home. It seemed like he was afraid of something. What it was, I couldn’t figure out.

Gradually I became aware he even acted afraid of Sterling. Whereas our other boys by this age had learned to recognize Sterling as “more fun than Mommy”, Judson didn’t. He pulled away from his daddy. He resisted Sterling’s efforts to make up, clinging to me fiercely.

And my mother-instinct, grounded deep beneath the waves of weariness, responded. In an oxymoron of emotions, I no sooner handed Judson to someone else than his obvious desperation for me tugged at my heart; and I would take him back, nestling him close, calming him down. It seemed even as he ruled and berated and emptied me, his intense need fulfilled me. I didn’t understand it.

“I think you need to get him on a quality probiotic,” my mother-in-law suggested. That sounded good, at least on Sunday evening. Somehow the weeks passed, and I didn’t find time to locate a quality probiotic.

“Try a good multivitamin,” another friend advised after observing us during prayer meeting. “It really could be worms. I knew this little girl who was totally unreasonable; she just screamed and screamed, and once they treated her for worms, it totally cleared up…”

That sounded good, too. It also sounded huge. I didn’t know where to begin research on “worms”, nor did I have the mental space.

When he was about six months old, we had the worst stint with him: almost a week wherein he cried and cried, refusing to nurse or be comforted. We requested an anointing by our ministry. We waited expectantly after the anointing. Within hours Judson was back to his restless fussing. We waited a couple more days before updating his pediatrician. Per her advice, Sterling & I took him to the hospital, where a specialist in pediatric gastroenterology could help us. It frightened us to take our puzzling, vulnerable baby to the hospital. “Pray for us,” we requested as we told our families and brotherhood about it.

By the time we checked in to the hospital, Judson had perked up. The nurse showed us to a room. She laid Judson in the cold, caged hospital bed and dressed him in a coarse gown. While we waited for the doctor to come in, Sterling and I marveled at the change in our son. He lay in the bed quietly, fingering the rails and looking around. Not for three minutes, not for 30, but for an hour, finally drifting off to sleep. This was unheard-of behavior for Judson. We looked at each other sheepishly.

“I feel pretty foolish,” I confessed to Sterling. “What are the doctors going to think when they find this healthy little fellow? What about the huge hospital bill?” I covered my face with my hands.

Sterling shrugged, as puzzled as I. “I think people must have been praying.”

That was the turning point in Judson’s physical wellbeing. The hospital released us the next day, signing a bill of good health in Judson’s report. They couldn’t find anything wrong with our child. Soon thereafter, his bowel trouble cleared up. He became regular as the sunrise, all too regular for the lady who hitherto had needed no extra diapers, wipes, or clothes. We praised the Lord for answered prayer.

But he still cried. Months passed while we looked ahead to each accomplishment: maybe when this tooth comes in, maybe when he starts crawling, maybe when he starts walking. Judson crawled at six months, walked at ten months, ate—or more accurately didn’t eat—table food, and still he fussed. I walked around with a little “leech” on my skirt some days. Other days I didn’t walk. Sterling attempted to hold him while I ate supper, but Judson hated that worse than he hated sitting with me for meals, and I would soon relent to his pleading cries. About the only time he was content was while he slept. Most puzzling was his apparent fear of Sterling and his irrational behavior at church.

“Are we just spoiling him?” I asked Sterling. “Maybe he just doesn’t want to sit still in church like any other baby.”

Sterling thought. “If that was so, then why would he resist fellowship meals so fiercely? That should be a fun time. Or if you were spoiling him, why wouldn’t he want to do fun things like come outside with me, or eat snacks?”

I didn’t know. I didn’t think I was spoiling him, but I couldn’t tell. I thought even a spoiled baby should enjoy being away from its mother occasionally. Not Judson. He rode around with me continually, one hand clutching my neckline, the other hand pushing himself away to see where we were headed. If he didn’t like our direction, he often attempted to steer me by surprisingly strong lunging. His anxious, overly alert actions puzzled me. Perhaps something more was wrong, something relating to his nervous system.

“You know, when we took in my niece, she had bonding issues,” one sister told me over fellowship meal. Judson had his open mouth turned away from her, so we were actually visiting over the hubbub in the hall. “She had never bonded with anyone due to her poor home situation. I took to carrying her around with me everywhere I went until she bonded with me. The way Judson acts insecure, even when he is with you, makes me think he hasn’t bonded. Perhaps that’s why he panics whenever you put him down.” Maybe. But where and when would he have gotten bonding issues?

“Did he have a traumatic birth?” the lady inquired.

I thought it over. “Well, no…” I glanced back at the scary episode in Mexico. Perhaps that had undone the natural bonding process. Or maybe the time in the hospital. Maybe his stint with whooping cough as an eight-month-old. As these moments scrolled through my mind, I realized Judson’s babyhood really had been difficult. Maybe there was good reason his emotional balance was off kilter. He did seem insecure now. Frightened. On “survival mode” all the time, me being his dubious source of momentary safety. If he did have bonding issues, then I would have been doing the wrong thing his entire baby life. I repeatedly tried to let other people, like his grandmothers, hold him, hoping he would realize he was fine with them. It didn’t work. Talking with this lady caused me to look doubtfully at my tactics, worried I had hurt Judson worse by doing this. At least carrying him around all the time would be free.

I procured a baby carrier and took to wearing him as I worked. He loved it, but my back did not. I soon gave that practice up, too, after no hopeful signs of bonding occurred. If my spirit was going to be worn down by caring for this child, at least my back didn’t need to be.

We tried discipline. After all, we were working on raising two other boys, and discipline was not a new thing in our home. It didn’t seem we had done anything different with Judson than we did with the other boys, but the results were certainly different. Judson responded with uncontrollable terror. The soft infant cry was long gone. We were unsure how to teach him to be happy in Sterling’s care, for discipline only seemed to heighten his distress. And how does one teach a child to play away from his mother? After a few exhausting sessions at church, wherein he refused to respond, we began to feel a spanking wasn’t the tool to get through to him. Indeed, it felt we never got through to him. But if a spanking didn’t work, how else could we teach him? I recalled seeing other mothers clamp their hands over their toddler’s mouth to teach them that wailing didn’t bring the desired result. Perhaps he needed to be taught how to stop crying. I tried it for a while.

Shortly after Judson turned one, his behavior reached a terrible climax. He was big enough to refuse direction or pacification. Discipline seemed to make him go crazy. Finally, I reached for a book about child development. One description on a condition called retained fear reflex described our child exactly. With simple therapeutic practice, the book promised, we could correct this. However, we would need an expert in this field to work with us, teaching us the therapy.

“What do you think?” I asked Sterling after sharing the book’s information with him.

His face looked unsure. “I don’t know,” he pondered aloud. “This isn’t what I would have been taught about raising a child. I always thought love, prayer, and consistent discipline were the keys to normal childcare. We have no proof other than fussiness that something is wrong with Judson. I hesitate to label him.”

I did, too. While we both acknowledged the special needs of some children, and the gift of specially trained caregivers, we didn’t want to hastily tack an excusing name on Judson’s behavior.

But the exhaustion of caring for him rolled back in like a fog the next day. We talked about the retained fear reflex again. We’d tried the love, definitely. We’d tried prayer, at least in a measure. The consistent discipline was another matter. Unlike our other boys, it didn’t seem to work with Judson. According to the text on retained fear reflexes, discipline could be accomplishing the opposite of its intention.

“You may call and get an appointment with the therapist,” Sterling decided. “It’s worth a try. She’s a Christian, too, and isn’t suggesting anything beyond physical exercises to retrain the brain.”

So I did. The therapist lived eight hours away, which was nothing to brush aside. But the promise of help seemed worth the drive to us. In the meantime, I shared with a few people what we were thinking. A few of them promised to pray for us. My mother-in-law offered a children’s supplement for calming and focus. I also made it to the health food store and procured a probiotic and multivitamin. The time for the therapist appointment drew close.

“I don’t see how we can go,” Sterling said a few days before. “Our weeks have been super busy, and we are all tired. I can’t see how we can fit in a two-day road trip just for one short appointment. But I guess we’ll have to. If it helps Judson, that will be worth it.”

Tension tugged at my neck, too, just thinking about the trip. That week we made a concentrated effort on Judson’s training. We worked with him firmly, attempting to bring his will into line with ours. He despised it. Any time Sterling took him, he reacted violently. I set aside times each day to sit with him on the sofa, holding his hands and requiring silence, with middling results.

The Sunday before we needed to head out to the appointment, we accepted a dinner invitation to a home we were not very familiar with. I spent the time wrestling with my small son, swallowing mouthfuls of pride and comfort while doing so. Meanwhile, Sterling talked with the men about our struggles with Judson, referencing the idea of his fearfulness and the route of therapy.

“Have you ever thought about how Judson must feel when you discipline him in the way I observed your wife do earlier?” one of the men questioned gently. “I noticed the expression in Judson’s eyes as she restrained him, covering his mouth. He looked terrified. If you really think he has this issue with fear, perhaps you should try looking at discipline from his point of view. One of our children also responded unreasonably to our regular methods of training until I began to describe to them what I was about to do…” With discretion, this brother shared an experience with their child.

Sterling was stunned and blessed by the gentle insight. The men shared a little more. It was as if we had been too close to the situation to fully see it, and the Lord had given us perspective from a wise onlooker. We agreed to cancel the childhood development appointment and rethink our training methods. We decided to try clearly explaining to Judson our expectations and the consequences of disobedience. Instead of restraining him, demanding surrender to our desires, we agreed to use repeated small switches to reprimand his willfulness.

“I’m going to take this week to completely focus on mealtimes,” Sterling decided. “Of course, that means you will take the brunt of this, since you feed Judson two out of three meals. But I will try to take the heavier load. I’m also going to fast and pray for answers for this child. We’ve tried to train him at mealtimes before but have never stuck it out more than a day or two. There’s always ‘something going on’ and we slack off. But this is important. Too important to keep letting ‘life’ interfere.”

I agreed with him. My spirit rose with hope and rest in this decision. Something about the therapy route had not seemed correct, yet we had been desperate for an answer.

That week was tough. The other boys ate alone while I spent extended time at the table with Judson. He screamed at my clear expectation of sitting still and eating. He writhed, he gagged, he cried. I prayed and switched. At supper time, Sterling took over. Judson resisted this still more wildly. The first evening it was three hours before our child obeyed and swallowed a small amount of food for his father. Several more evenings passed with similar time frames. Sterling worked with Judson gently and firmly, speaking to him, spanking, holding. I tried to block out the sound. My commitment to stand behind my husband in this all tussled with my emotions, but I didn’t give in this time when Judson looked at me with begging eyes.

By the end of the first week, Judson showed steps of improvement. He stopped crying at mealtimes. He sat in his highchair, eating a few bites for us obediently. With a comically pathetic expression, he would offer Sterling and I each one of his little paddies to hold while he ate, as if that gave him courage. We continued with intentional training in this area alone. By the end of the second week, his behavior all around had improved. He began to let loose of me, seeking entertainment on his own, toddling around the house with happy babbling. I watched in amazement while he did normal baby things: exploring the toy box, climbing on sofas, dabbling in toilets. He ventured outside alone, soon learning to play with balls and trucks. I stopped giving him the various supplements since he was doing so well.

Then one gladsome day when the boys chorused “Daddy’s home!”, Judson squealed in delight. The next evening when Sterling arrived, he squealed again, this time happily heading for the door. I opened it for him. He toddled to the truck where Sterling was. Sterling carried him into the house. Judson looked at me triumphantly from his daddy’s arms with a burbling comment on the situation. He made no move for me. We knew then Sterling had won his heart. From that time until now, he has been a different child.

Now we watch him with delight. His little countenance is bright and beaming, his eyes clear and content. He is evidently secure. He has become a joy to have around, charming our family with his toddling antics. Not only has he bonded with Sterling, he has widened his circle of acceptance to others as well. He interacts well with his brothers. He responds reasonably to training in other areas. We love him, this third little son of ours.

So what really was wrong with Judson? I think he had a physical abnormality in the first months of his life, causing him discomfort. His was a rocky babyhood. In retrospect, I see that spoiling him crept in unawares.

Somewhere in the transition between need and demand, I began to cater to his little self. It was sneakily gradual. Incredibly early on, he obviously realized that crying controlled me. I couldn’t see it. We couldn’t see it. We couldn’t see it until after we began to take back the parental control in his training. We still don’t know when it happened or how. But this we do know: God’s way works.

Prayer works. The rod of correction works. A wife standing behind her husband as he disciplines his child in love works. In a plan that defies human reasoning, let alone worldly teaching, the process of molding Judson’s will firmly bonded him to his father. This created security in his small world. Sterling is in charge. Judson is at rest and safe in this. It removed from him the burden of controlling his world. He is free to relate to either of us, free from the tyrannical demands of his small selfish nature. Something about the clarity of his daddy being the authority in his life has also established my authority over him.

Over two years have passed since Sterling began turning Judson’s heart and will towards his own. Today, Judson is a joyful, well-adjusted boy. He sits quietly in church and devotions; he enjoys fellowship meals and his friends; he eagerly spends time with either Daddy or Mommy. Stubbornness, anxiety, and mealtimes are three areas that require daily diligence in training him—more diligence than our previous two children needed, combined! But the good news is Judson responds well to discipline. Some days it feels like we aren’t getting anywhere until we look back at how far our son has truly come. We praise the Lord for His intervention in our lives by using a perceptive brother to speak into the situation. God’s Word, God’s way, has the keys for raising a happy child.

Vi ba Herren om ham, vårt tredje barn, vår tredje sønn. Han kom med våren, kronen på verket i det nye livet, og gråt over de uvante omgivelsene sine. Folk kommenterte gråten hans: De syntes den var bedårende. Det syntes vi også. Vi elsket ham, koste med ham og kalte ham Judson.

Sterling og jeg hadde før Judson ble født forpliktet oss til å ta ungdomsgruppen vår med på misjonstur til Mexico. Avreisedatoen for turen var fem uker etter at Judson kom. Som lederens kone hadde jeg ansvar for å ta med mat til hele gruppen under hele oppholdet. Jeg brukte all min tid på forberedelsene, med lister og innkjøp.

Judson forberedte seg på sin egen måte. Han fikk problemer med tarmene. Han gikk sju dager uten en skitten bleie. Jeg spurte jordmoren min om det, men hun lot seg ikke uro av det. Da det gikk enda sju dager før neste fulle bleie, spurte jeg barnelegen hans. Hun var heller ikke bekymret. Så dro vi til Mexico: Sterling og jeg, den fem uker gamle babyen vår og to varebillass med ungdommer.

Selv om forberedelsene hadde tæret på meg, føltes tiden i Mexico som ferie. Det eneste jeg trengte å gjøre der, var å ta vare på babyen min og ha ansvar for måltidene. Men Judson likte ikke turen i det hele tatt. Jeg holdt ham inntil meg i timevis mens jeg satt under en presenning i en dramatisk åsside med utsikt over byggeplassen der gruppen vår arbeidet. Judson virket urolig og utilpass hos meg. Han gråt hvis noen andre holdt ham. Jeg følte at noe var galt, men hadde ingen tydelige tegn på hva det kunne være, bortsett fra at dagene gikk uten en skitten bleie.

Den sjette natten vår i Mexico la jeg Judson i den lille sengen hans. Men Herren fikk meg til å gå tilbake og la ham ned ved siden av meg i sengen. Jeg kjente tydelig denne tilskyndelsen og adlød, selv om jeg de andre nettene hadde latt Judson sove i den lille sengen. Vi sov. En gang i løpet av natten våknet Judson og lot seg ikke trøste. Jeg prøvde det ene og det andre, halvt sovende selv. Plutselig skrek han, men satte så skriket i halsen og ble slapp.

«Sterling!» ropte jeg. «Slå på lommelykten! Han puster ikke!» Jeg satte meg opp i sengen og undersøkte babyen min i lyset fra lommelykten. Det lille ansiktet hans arbeidet desperat, men det kom verken pust eller lyd. Etter noen sekunder begynte han å puste igjen og skrek. Så satte han det i halsen. Som om en usynlig hånd grep rundt den skjøre halsen hans, stanset pusten, og øynene hans sto skrekkslagne ut. Jeg stakk fingeren inn i munnen hans for å se om noe hadde satt seg fast i luftveiene, men fant ingenting. Judson skalv, gispet etter luft og gråt. Tårene presset seg ut av øynene hans. «Å, be!» tryglet jeg. Sterling ba, og ordene i bønnene hans hopet seg opp mot himmelen mens babyen vår igjen sluttet å puste. Dette gjentok seg flere ganger: noen sekunder med skrekkskrik, så noen sekunder med pinefull stillhet. Svetten piplet frem i ansiktet til Judson. Det var forferdelig å se på. Tankene føk gjennom hodet mitt: Babyen vår kommer til å dø. Sånn helt plutselig. Uten varsel. Her ute, uten medisinsk hjelp. Å Gud! Hjelp oss, hjelp oss, hjelp oss! Hvordan kan man bare se på at babyen sin dør?

«Jeg henter misjonærens kone», bestemte Sterling. Jeg mumlet frem bønner mens jeg holdt Judson. Da misjonærens kone kom, ga jeg ham til henne, takknemlig for at en kvinne som var eldre enn meg, var der. Vi ba sammen og tryglet Gud om å gripe inn. Judson begynte å gråte og puste normalt mens hun undersøkte ham. Hun ga ham tilbake til meg da han hadde roet seg.

«Jeg vet ikke hva det er», sa hun etter at vi hadde fortalt henne hva som hadde skjedd. Vi takket henne for at hun hadde stått opp midt på natten, og gikk så tilbake til rommet vårt. Jeg gråt mens Judson sov fredelig i armene mine.

«Jeg har en følelse av at dette var et demonisk angrep», sa Sterling. «Hvis djevelen kan skremme oss med det som kan skje med babyen vår mens vi er langt ute på landet, kan han få oss til å pakke sammen hele gruppen og dra. Djevelen vet at det skjer gode ting her, åndelig sett; dette er ikke tiden for å flykte. Vi kan ikke la ham fylle oss med frykt.»

Jeg var enig. Den uvanlige måten Judson sluttet å puste og begynte igjen på, så ut som om en ond hånd grep rundt halsen hans. Det virket ikke som det fantes noen naturlig forklaring på den fryktelige hendelsen. Sterling la hånden på Judson og ba, tok uttrykkelig et oppgjør med djevelen og søkte Guds beskyttelse. Vi la oss ned i fred og trygghet og sov.

Om morgenen virket Judson uberørt av det som hadde skjedd, selv om uroen hans økte. Åtte, ni og så ti dager gikk uten avføring. Han gråt, den myke, bedårende gråten hans uroet hjertet mitt. På reisen tilbake til USA bekymret jeg meg over at han trakk seg unna når han skulle ammes, vred seg og klynket helt til han sovnet i stedet.

Så begynte han å gulpe. Da han til slutt gulpet opp en klar gul væske, ble jeg redd. Den ellevte dagen oppsøkte vi en sykepleier med videreutdanning ved en mennonittkoloni i Mexico. Hun undersøkte Judson, lyttet til det jeg fortalte og svarte rolig: «Og dette er deres første barn?»

«Nei», svarte jeg, like rolig som henne. «Dette er mitt tredje.» Da møtte hun blikket mitt, uten å si noe, og undersøkte Judson på nytt. Hun ga ham et stikkpiller og sa at alle babyer er forskjellige. Og det er de. Denne var i hvert fall det! Etter den lokale lindringen fra stikkpillen virket Judson bedre.

Han var sju uker gammel da vi kom hjem. Fra han var tre uker til han var sju måneder, hadde han problemer med tarmene.

På søndagene tok folk på det lille ansiktet hans og kommenterte den søte, lille gråten. Andre dager satt jeg krøket sammen i gyngestolen og hørte, men hørte likevel ikke, den søte, lille gråten hans. Noen dager virket det som om den aldri tok slutt. Jeg holdt ham bortsett fra når han sov. Jeg ble kjent med mønsteret hans: flere dager uten avføring, hvor han gradvis ble mer gretten, ammet mindre og til slutt gråt høylytt helt til jeg ga ham den midlertidige lindringen en stikkpille ga. Til tross for den vanlige mistanken var han ikke forstoppet. Morsinstinktet mitt sa meg at noe i ham ikke naturlig satte tarmene i gang.

«Kutt ut korn», foreslo en bok. «Det kan være Hirschsprungs sykdom, som kan behandles naturlig ved å unngå korn.» Så jeg spiste ikke korn. Fem lange uker gikk på det endrede kostholdet mitt. Judson så ikke ut til å merke innsatsen min.

Barnelegen hans lyttet til beskrivelsen min av rutinene hans og bestilte så en test for Hirschsprungs sykdom.

Testen viste ingen tegn til sykdommen. Takknemlig begynte jeg å spise korn igjen, men allerede neste søndag fikk jeg nye råd. En erfaren mor oppsøkte meg på barnerommet, dit jeg hadde trukket meg tilbake fra den støyende kirkesalen. Jeg satt og gynget sønnen min, gynget, gynget, gynget. «Har du vurdert å kutte ut meieriprodukter?»

Nei, det hadde jeg ikke.

«Jeg synes du skal prøve å kutte ut meieriprodukter», sa hun bestemt. Som en medisinsk håndbok som var lest mange ganger, ramset hun opp grunnene til denne fremgangsmåten.

Barnelegen hans syntes ikke det var noen god idé å kutte ut meieriprodukter. Jeg besøkte kontoret hennes etter tre uker med det kostholdet. «Du trenger fettet i meieriprodukter for å opprettholde melkeproduksjonen», irettesatte hun meg. «Dessuten er det første tegnet på melkeintoleranse blod i avføringen, ikke fravær av avføring.»

Jeg hadde ikke noe imot å slutte med kostholdet uten meieriprodukter. Vi prøvde andre ting. Judson holdt klysteret inne med stahet. En foreskrevet dose avføringsmiddel ga ingen resultater. På et tidspunkt ba legen meg bare vente det ut sammen med Judson, overbevist om at tarmene hans ville komme i gang av seg selv. Judson holdt ut lenger enn jeg gjorde. Da det hadde gått 17 dager, tydde jeg til stikkpiller for å lindre plagene til den stakkars babyen min.

Men det var ikke bare mysteriet med fordøyelsen som gjorde oss fortvilet over babyen min. Selv når tarmene var tømt, var han gretten. Måltidene ble en prøvelse. Judson protesterte når jeg satte meg ved bordet for å spise sammen med familien. Jeg ble vant til å holde ham over skulderen mens jeg spiste raskt med én hånd. Nei, jeg ble ikke vant til det. Jeg ble aldri vant til at han klynket. Jeg lærte meg å gjøre husarbeidet mens han sov, for det var umulig å gjøre noe annet enn å stelle ham når han var våken.

Kirken var også en kilde til bekymring. Judson oppførte seg verre alle steder der det skjedde noe, men i kirken ble han helt umulig. Jeg strevde med ham til han sovnet, som regel tidsnok til at jeg fikk høre den siste delen av prekenen.

Fellesskapsmåltidene var en katastrofe. Judson skrek. Han lot ingen andre enn meg ta på seg, og selv jeg klarte ikke å roe ham. Innen vi hadde laget tallerkener og matet den lille familien vår, var jeg utslitt og klar til å dra hjem. Det virket som om han var redd for noe. Hva det var, klarte jeg ikke å finne ut av.

Gradvis ble jeg klar over at han til og med virket redd for Sterling. Da de andre guttene våre var på denne alderen, hadde de lært å se på Sterling som «morsommere enn mamma». Det gjorde ikke Judson. Han trakk seg unna pappaen sin. Han avviste Sterlings forsøk på å bli venner igjen og klamret seg febrilsk til meg.

Og morsinstinktet mitt, dypt forankret under bølgene av utmattelse, reagerte. I et følelsesmessig paradoks hadde jeg knapt rukket å gi Judson til noen andre før den tydelige fortvilelsen hans etter meg grep hjertet mitt; og jeg tok ham tilbake, holdt ham tett inntil meg og roet ham ned. Det virket som om hans intense behov fylte meg, selv mens han styrte, skjelte ut og tappet meg for krefter. Jeg forsto det ikke.

«Jeg tror du bør gi ham et godt probiotikum», foreslo svigermoren min. Det hørtes lurt ut, i hvert fall søndag kveld. På et eller annet vis gikk ukene, og jeg fant ikke tid til å skaffe et godt probiotikum.

«Prøv et godt multivitamin», rådet en annen venninne etter å ha sett oss på bønnemøtet. «Det kan virkelig være mark. Jeg kjente ei lita jente som var helt umulig; hun bare skrek og skrek, og da de behandlet henne for mark, forsvant det helt …»

Det hørtes også lurt ut. Men det virket omfattende. Jeg visste ikke hvor jeg skulle begynne å undersøke «mark», og jeg hadde heller ikke overskudd til det.

Da han var rundt seks måneder gammel, hadde vi den verste perioden med ham: nesten en uke hvor han gråt og gråt og nektet å ammes eller trøstes. Vi ba menigheten vår salve ham med olje. Etter salvingen ventet vi forventningsfullt. I løpet av noen timer var Judson tilbake til å klynke urolig. Vi ventet enda et par dager før vi ga barnelegen hans beskjed. Etter rådet hennes tok Sterling og jeg ham med til sykehuset, der en spesialist i barnemedisinsk mage- og tarmsykdom kunne hjelpe oss. Vi ble skremt av å ta den gåtefulle, sårbare babyen vår med til sykehuset. «Be for oss», ba vi da vi fortalte familiene våre og brødrene og søstrene i menigheten om det.

Da vi ble innlagt på sykehuset, hadde Judson kviknet til. Sykepleieren viste oss til et rom. Hun la Judson i den kalde sykehussengen med sengehester og kledde ham i en grov sykehusskjorte. Mens vi ventet på at legen skulle komme inn, undret Sterling og jeg oss over forandringen hos sønnen vår. Han lå stille i sengen, tok på sengehestene og så seg rundt. Ikke i tre minutter, ikke i 30, men i en hel time, før han omsider sovnet. Slik hadde Judson aldri oppført seg før. Vi så forlegent på hverandre.

«Jeg føler meg ganske dum», innrømmet jeg overfor Sterling. «Hva kommer legene til å tenke når de ser denne friske lille karen? Og hva med den enorme sykehusregningen?» Jeg dekket ansiktet med hendene.

Sterling trakk på skuldrene, like forvirret som jeg. «Jeg tror folk må ha bedt.»

Det ble et vendepunkt for Judsons fysiske helse. Sykehuset skrev oss ut dagen etter og skrev i rapporten at Judson var frisk. De kunne ikke finne noe galt med barnet vårt. Kort tid etter gikk tarmproblemene hans over. Han fikk regelmessig avføring, like regelmessig som soloppgangen, noe som var altfor ofte for hun som til nå ikke hadde trengt ekstra bleier, våtservietter eller klær. Vi takket Herren for at han hadde hørt bønnene våre.

Men han gråt fortsatt. Månedene gikk mens vi så frem til hver ny milepæl: kanskje når denne tannen kommer, kanskje når han begynner å krabbe, kanskje når han begynner å gå. Judson krabbet da han var seks måneder, gikk da han var ti måneder, spiste – eller rettere sagt, spiste ikke – vanlig mat, og likevel klynket han. Noen dager gikk jeg rundt med en liten «igle» hengende i skjørtet mitt. Andre dager gikk jeg ikke. Sterling prøvde å holde ham mens jeg spiste kveldsmat, men Judson mislikte det enda mer enn å sitte sammen med meg under måltidene, og jeg ga snart etter for de bønnfallende skrikene hans. Nesten den eneste gangen han var fornøyd, var når han sov. Det mest forvirrende var at han virket redd for Sterling, og at han oppførte seg irrasjonelt i kirken.

«Skjemmer vi ham bare bort?» spurte jeg Sterling. «Kanskje han bare ikke vil sitte stille i kirken, som alle andre babyer.»

Sterling tenkte seg om. «Hvis det var slik, hvorfor ville han da protestere så voldsomt mot fellesskapsmåltidene? Det burde jo være hyggelig. Og hvis du skjemte ham bort, hvorfor ville han ikke gjøre morsomme ting som å gå ut med meg eller spise snacks?»

Det visste jeg ikke. Jeg trodde ikke at jeg skjemte ham bort, men jeg kunne ikke være sikker. Jeg tenkte at selv en bortskjemt baby burde like å være borte fra moren sin innimellom. Men ikke Judson. Han satt stadig på meg, med den ene hånden knyttet i halsåpningen på klærne mine og den andre hånden mot meg, så han kunne se hvor vi var på vei. Hvis han ikke likte retningen, prøvde han ofte å styre meg med overraskende kraftige utfall. De engstelige, overdrevent årvåkne bevegelsene hans forvirret meg. Kanskje det var noe mer galt, noe som hadde med nervesystemet hans å gjøre.

«Du vet, da vi tok til oss niesen min, hadde hun problemer med tilknytning», sa en søster til meg under et fellesskapsmåltid. Judson hadde vendt den åpne munnen sin bort fra henne, så vi snakket egentlig sammen midt i levenet i salen. «Hun hadde aldri knyttet seg til noen på grunn av de dårlige forholdene hjemme. Jeg begynte å bære henne med meg overalt jeg gikk, helt til hun knyttet seg til meg. Måten Judson virker utrygg på, selv når han er sammen med deg, får meg til å tro at han ikke har knyttet seg til deg. Kanskje det er derfor han får panikk hver gang du setter ham ned.» Kanskje. Men hvor og når skulle han ha fått tilknytningsproblemer?

«Hadde han en traumatisk fødsel?» spurte kvinnen.

Jeg tenkte meg om. «Nei, det hadde han ikke …» Jeg tenkte tilbake på den skremmende episoden i Mexico. Kanskje den hadde forstyrret den naturlige tilknytningsprosessen. Eller kanskje tiden på sykehuset. Kanskje perioden med kikhoste da han var åtte måneder. Mens disse øyeblikkene rullet gjennom tankene mine, innså jeg at Judsons første leveår virkelig hadde vært vanskelige. Kanskje det var en god grunn til at følelseslivet hans var ute av balanse. Han virket virkelig utrygg nå. Redd. Som om han hele tiden var i «overlevelsesmodus», og jeg var hans tvilsomme kilde til et øyeblikks trygghet. Hvis han hadde tilknytningsproblemer, hadde jeg gjort alt feil gjennom hele spedbarnstiden hans. Jeg hadde gang på gang prøvd å la andre, som bestemødrene hans, holde ham, i håp om at han skulle forstå at han hadde det fint hos dem. Det fungerte ikke. Samtalen med denne kvinnen fikk meg til å tvile på fremgangsmåten min, og jeg var redd for at jeg hadde skadet Judson enda mer ved å gjøre dette. Å bære ham rundt hele tiden ville i det minste være gratis.

Jeg skaffet meg en bæresele og begynte å bære ham mens jeg arbeidet. Han elsket det, men ryggen min gjorde det ikke. Snart sluttet jeg også med det, siden det ikke viste seg noen tegn til at han knyttet seg bedre til meg. Hvis omsorgen for dette barnet skulle bryte meg ned, trengte i det minste ikke ryggen min å bli det også.

Vi prøvde med disiplin. Vi holdt tross alt på å oppdra to andre gutter, og disiplin var ikke noe nytt hjemme hos oss. Det virket ikke som om vi hadde gjort noe annerledes med Judson enn med de andre guttene, men resultatene var absolutt annerledes. Judson reagerte med ukontrollerbar redsel. Den myke spedbarnsgråten var for lengst borte. Vi visste ikke hvordan vi skulle lære ham å være glad når Sterling passet ham, for disiplinen så bare ut til å gjøre ham enda mer fortvilet. Og hvordan lærer man et barn å leke borte fra moren sin? Etter noen utmattende forsøk i kirken, hvor han ikke ville høre etter, begynte vi å føle at ris ikke var veien inn til ham. Det føltes faktisk som om vi aldri nådde inn til ham. Men hvis ris ikke fungerte, hvordan kunne vi ellers lære ham? Jeg husket at jeg hadde sett andre mødre holde hånden over munnen til småbarna sine for å lære dem at gråt ikke førte til det de ønsket. Kanskje han trengte å lære seg å slutte å gråte. Jeg prøvde det en stund.

Kort tid etter at Judson fylte ett år, nådde oppførselen hans et fryktelig høydepunkt. Han var stor nok til å nekte å følge beskjeder eller la seg trøste. Disiplinen så ut til å gjøre ham helt fra seg. Til slutt fant jeg frem en bok om barns utvikling. En beskrivelse av en tilstand som kalles vedvarende fryktrefleks, beskrev barnet vårt nøyaktig. Boken lovet at vi kunne rette opp i dette med enkle terapeutiske øvelser. Men vi ville trenge en ekspert på området til å arbeide sammen med oss og lære oss terapien.

«Hva synes du?» spurte jeg Sterling etter å ha fortalt ham om det som sto i boken.

Han så usikker ut. «Jeg vet ikke», funderte han høyt. «Dette er ikke det jeg ville ha lært om barneoppdragelse. Jeg har alltid trodd at kjærlighet, bønn og konsekvent disiplin var nøklene til normal barneomsorg. Vi har ingen andre bevis på at noe er galt med Judson enn at han er urolig. Jeg nøler med å sette en merkelapp på ham.»

Det gjorde jeg også. Selv om vi begge anerkjente at noen barn har spesielle behov, og at det er en gave å ha omsorgspersoner med spesialopplæring, ønsket vi ikke å skynde oss med å sette et unnskyldende navn på oppførselen til Judson.

Men neste dag kom utmattelsen ved å ta vare på ham tilbake som en tåke. Vi snakket igjen om den vedvarende fryktrefleksen. Vi hadde i hvert fall prøvd kjærlighet. Vi hadde også prøvd bønn, om enn i en viss grad. Den konsekvente disiplinen var en annen sak. I motsetning til med de andre guttene våre så den ikke ut til å fungere med Judson. Ifølge teksten om vedvarende fryktreflekser kunne disiplinen ha motsatt virkning av det vi ønsket.

«Du kan ringe og bestille time hos terapeuten», bestemte Sterling. «Det er verdt et forsøk. Hun er også kristen og foreslår ikke noe annet enn fysiske øvelser for å trene hjernen på nytt.»

Det gjorde jeg. Terapeuten bodde åtte timer unna, noe som ikke var noen liten sak. Men vi syntes løftet om hjelp var verdt kjøreturen. I mellomtiden fortalte jeg noen få mennesker hva vi tenkte. Noen av dem lovet å be for oss. Svigermoren min tilbød et kosttilskudd for barn som skulle virke beroligende og hjelpe konsentrasjonen. Jeg fikk også dratt innom helsekostbutikken og skaffet et probiotikum og et multivitamin. Timen hos terapeuten nærmet seg.

«Jeg skjønner ikke hvordan vi skal få dratt», sa Sterling noen dager før. «Ukene våre har vært veldig travle, og vi er alle slitne. Jeg kan ikke se hvordan vi skal få presset inn en to dagers kjøretur bare for én kort time. Men jeg antar at vi må. Hvis det hjelper Judson, er det verdt det.»

Jeg kjente også spenningen stramme i nakken bare ved tanken på turen. Den uken gjorde vi en målrettet innsats for å lære opp Judson. Vi var bestemte med ham og prøvde å få viljen hans til å føye seg etter vår. Han hatet det. Hver gang Sterling tok seg av ham, reagerte han voldsomt. Hver dag satte jeg av tid til å sitte med ham i sofaen, holde hendene hans og kreve at han var stille. Resultatene var blandede.

Søndagen før vi skulle dra til timen, takket vi ja til middagsinvitasjon hjem til noen vi ikke kjente særlig godt. Jeg brukte tiden på å streve med den lille sønnen min og svelget stoltheten og ubehaget mens jeg gjorde det. Samtidig snakket Sterling med mennene om problemene våre med Judson og nevnte både frykten hans og terapien vi vurderte.

«Har du noen gang tenkt på hvordan Judson må føle det når du disiplinerer ham på den måten jeg så kona di gjøre tidligere?» spurte en av mennene forsiktig. «Jeg la merke til uttrykket i øynene til Judson da hun holdt ham fast og dekket munnen hans. Han så livredd ut. Hvis du virkelig tror at han har dette problemet med frykt, bør du kanskje prøve å se disiplinen fra hans ståsted. Et av barna våre reagerte også urimelig på de vanlige metodene våre for oppdragelse, helt til jeg begynte å fortelle barnet hva jeg skulle gjøre …» Denne broren fortalte diskret om en erfaring med barnet deres.

Sterling ble overrasket og takknemlig for den varsomme innsikten. Mennene sa litt mer. Det var som om vi hadde vært for nær situasjonen til å se den klart, og Herren hadde gitt oss perspektiv gjennom en klok utenforstående. Vi ble enige om å avlyse timen for vurdering av barns utvikling og tenke gjennom oppdragelsesmetodene våre på nytt. Vi bestemte oss for å prøve å forklare Judson tydelig hva vi forventet av ham, og hva konsekvensene av ulydighet ville være. I stedet for å holde ham fast og kreve at han føyde seg etter det vi ønsket, ble vi enige om å bruke gjentatte små rapp med en tynn stokk for å irettesette egenrådigheten hans.

«Jeg skal bruke denne uken til å konsentrere meg helt om måltidene», bestemte Sterling. «Det betyr selvfølgelig at du får ta den største støyten, siden du gir Judson to av tre måltider. Men jeg skal prøve å ta den tyngste delen. Jeg skal også faste og be om svar for dette barnet. Vi har prøvd å lære ham opp under måltidene før, men har aldri holdt ut mer enn en dag eller to. Det er alltid ‘noe som skjer’, og så slapper vi av. Men dette er viktig. Altfor viktig til at vi stadig lar ‘livet’ komme i veien.»

Jeg var enig med ham. Denne beslutningen ga meg håp og ro. Det var noe ved terapifremgangsmåten som ikke hadde føltes riktig, men vi hadde vært desperate etter et svar.

Den uken var tøff. De andre guttene spiste alene mens jeg brukte lang tid ved bordet sammen med Judson. Han skrek da jeg tydelig forlangte at han skulle sitte stille og spise. Han vred seg, brekte seg og gråt. Jeg ba og brukte ris. Til kveldsmaten tok Sterling over. Judson satte seg enda mer voldsomt imot. Den første kvelden gikk det tre timer før barnet vårt adlød faren sin og svelget litt mat. Flere kvelder gikk med på lignende vis. Sterling behandlet Judson mildt, men bestemt; han snakket med ham, riset ham og holdt ham. Jeg prøvde å stenge lyden ute. Beslutningen min om å støtte mannen min i dette kjempet mot følelsene mine, men denne gangen ga jeg ikke etter da Judson så på meg med bønnfallende øyne.

Mot slutten av den første uken viste Judson tegn til bedring. Han sluttet å gråte under måltidene. Han satt i barnestolen og spiste lydig noen få biter for oss. Med et komisk ynkelig uttrykk tilbød han Sterling og meg hver vår lille bæsj å holde mens han spiste, som om det ga ham mot. Vi fortsatte med målrettet opplæring på akkurat dette området. Mot slutten av den andre uken hadde oppførselen hans bedret seg på alle måter. Han begynte å slippe taket i meg og finne på ting selv, og stabbet rundt i huset mens han bablet fornøyd. Jeg så forundret på mens han gjorde vanlige babystreker: utforsket lekekassen, klatret i sofaer og lekte med toalettene. Han våget seg ut alene og lærte snart å leke med baller og lastebiler. Jeg sluttet å gi ham de ulike kosttilskuddene siden han hadde det så bra.

Så, en gledelig dag da guttene ropte i kor: «Pappa er hjemme!», hvinte Judson av fryd. Neste kveld, da Sterling kom hjem, hvinte han igjen, denne gangen mens han glad gikk mot døren. Jeg åpnet den for ham. Han stabbet bort til lastebilen der Sterling var. Sterling bar ham inn i huset. Fra armene til pappa så Judson triumferende på meg og sa noe pludrende om situasjonen. Han gjorde ikke mine til å komme til meg. Da visste vi at Sterling hadde vunnet hjertet hans. Fra da av har han vært et annet barn.

Nå ser vi på ham med glede. Det lille ansiktet hans er lyst og strålende, øynene klare og tilfredse. Han føler seg tydeligvis trygg. Det er blitt en glede å ha ham rundt seg, og han sjarmere familien med de ustøe sprellene sine. Han har ikke bare knyttet seg til Sterling, men også utvidet kretsen av dem han føler seg trygg sammen med. Han kommer godt overens med brødrene sine. Han reagerer rimelig på opplæring på andre områder. Vi elsker ham, denne tredje lille sønnen vår.

Så hva var det egentlig som feilte Judson? Jeg tror han hadde en fysisk unormalitet de første månedene av livet, som ga ham ubehag. Den første tiden hans var vanskelig. Når jeg ser tilbake, skjønner jeg at jeg uten å merke det begynte å skjemme ham bort.

Et eller annet sted i overgangen mellom behov og krav begynte jeg å føye meg etter den lille gutten min. Det skjedde gradvis og i det skjulte. Utrolig tidlig skjønte han tydeligvis at gråten hans styrte meg. Jeg så det ikke. Vi så det ikke. Vi så det ikke før vi begynte å ta den foreldremessige kontrollen tilbake i oppdragelsen hans. Vi vet fortsatt ikke når det skjedde eller hvordan. Men dette vet vi: Guds vei virker.

Bønn virker. Riset som irettesetter, virker. Det virker når en kone støtter mannen sin mens han disiplinerer barnet sitt i kjærlighet. I en plan som trosser menneskelig fornuft, for ikke å snakke om verdslig lære, knyttet prosessen med å forme Judsons vilje ham sterkt til faren. Det skapte trygghet i den lille verdenen hans. Sterling har ansvaret. Judson finner ro og trygghet i det. Det tok fra ham byrden med å styre sin egen verden. Han står fritt til å ha et forhold til oss begge, fri fra de tyranniske kravene fra sin lille, selviske natur. Noe ved tydeligheten i at pappa har autoritet i livet hans, har også fastslått min autoritet over ham.

Det har gått over to år siden Sterling begynte å vende Judsons hjerte og vilje mot seg selv. I dag er Judson en glad og veltilpasset gutt. Han sitter stille i kirken og under andaktene; han liker fellesskapsmåltider og vennene sine; han tilbringer gjerne tid sammen med enten pappa eller mamma. Stahet, engstelse og måltider er tre områder der det kreves daglig grundighet i opplæringen hans – mer grundighet enn det de to første barna våre trengte til sammen! Men det gode er at Judson reagerer godt på disiplin. Noen dager føles det som om vi ikke kommer noen vei, helt til vi ser tilbake på hvor langt sønnen vår virkelig har kommet. Vi priser Herren for at han grep inn i livene våre ved å bruke en oppmerksom bror til å si noe inn i situasjonen. Guds ord, Guds vei, har nøklene til å oppdra et lykkelig barn.

We asked the Lord for him, our third child, third son. He came with the springtime, the crowning creation of new life, bewailing his shuffled surroundings. Folks commented on his wail: they thought it was adorable. We thought so, too. We loved him, we snuggled him, and we called him Judson.

Sterling and I had committed, prior to Judson’s birth, to take our youth group on a mission trip to Mexico. The date to leave for this trip fell five weeks after Judson came. As the leader’s wife, I was responsible to take food along to feed our group for the entire time. Making lists and shopping for it consumed me with preparation.

Judson did his own preparing. He developed bowel trouble. He went seven days without a messy pamper. I asked my midwife about it, but she was unruffled by the occurrence. When it went another seven days until the next full diaper, I asked his pediatrician. She, too, was unconcerned. So, we headed for Mexico: Sterling and I, our five-week-old baby, and two vanloads of youth.

Although the preparation had been taxing for me, the time in Mexico was like vacation. My only requirements while there were to take care of my baby and oversee mealtimes. But Judson didn’t like the trip at all. I cuddled him for hours, sitting under a tarp on a dramatic hillside, overlooking the construction site where our group was laboring. Judson acted restless and uncomfortable with me. He cried if anyone else held him. I felt something was amiss, but I had no definite signs of what, except that day after day passed without a dirty diaper.

On our sixth night in Mexico, I laid Judson on his cot. But the Lord drew me back, prompting me to pull him into bed beside me. I felt this nudge distinctly and obeyed, although I had let Judson sleep in the cot the other nights. We slept. Somewhere in the night, Judson awoke, refusing to be pacified. I tried this and that, half asleep myself. Suddenly he screamed out, only to choke mid-scream and then go limp.

“Sterling!” I yelped. “Turn on the flashlight! He’s not breathing!” I sat up in bed, examining my baby in the flashlight’s beam. His little face worked desperately, but no breath or sound came forth. Within seconds, his breath returned, and he screamed again. Then he choked. As surely as an invisible hand clutching his fragile neck, his breath ceased, and his eyes bulged in terror. I swiped my finger through his mouth, checking for something lodged in his airway, finding nothing. Shuddering, Judson gasped and cried. Tears forced themselves out of his eyes. “Oh, pray,” I begged. Sterling prayed, jumbling pleas together in a heavenward heap as our baby ceased breathing again. The episode repeated itself several more times: seconds of terrified screaming, then seconds of tortured silence. Sweat popped out on Judson’s face. It was agonizing to watch. Thoughts flew through my head: Our baby’s going to die. Just like that. No warning. Out here with no medical aid. Oh God! Help us, help us, help us! How does one just watch their baby die?

“I’m getting the missionary’s wife,” Sterling decided. I stammered dangling prayers while supporting Judson. When the missionary’s wife appeared, I handed him to her, grateful for the presence of a woman older than I. We prayed together, begging God to intervene. Judson began to cry and breath normally while she examined him. She handed him back to me as he calmed down.

“I don’t know what it is,” she said, after we told her the story. We thanked her for rousing in the night, then returned to our room. I cried while Judson peacefully slept in my arms.

“I sense it was a demoniac display,” Sterling stated. “If the devil can get us scared over what could happen to our baby while we are out in the boondocks, then he can get us to pack up our whole group and leave. The devil knows there are good things happening here, spiritually; this is not the time to flee. We can’t let him fill us with fear.”

I agreed. The unusual way Judson’s breath came and went looked as if an evil hand was gripping his neck. There seemed to be no natural explanation otherwise for the horrifying event. Sterling laid his hand on Judson and prayed, specifically rebuking the devil, and seeking the protection of God. We laid us down in peace and safety and slept.

In the morning, Judson seemed untroubled by the episode, although his restlessness increased. Eight, nine, and then ten days passed with no bowel movement. He cried, his soft, adorable cry agitating my heart. As we traveled back to the States, I fretted over the way he drew back from nursing, squirming and fussing until he fell asleep instead.

Then he began spitting up. When he finally spit up bright yellow liquid, I was alarmed. On the eleventh day, we visited a nurse practitioner in a Mennonite colony in Mexico. She examined Judson, listened to my report, and calmly replied, “And this is your first child?”

“No,” I responded, matching calm with calm. “This is my third.” She met my eyes then, silently, and reexamined Judson. She gave him a suppository, suggesting all babies are different. And so, they are. This one certainly was! With the topical relief of the suppository, Judson seemed to feel better.

He was seven weeks old when we came home. From the time he was three weeks until he was seven months, he struggled with his bowels.

On Sundays, people fingered his tiny face, commenting on his sweet little cry. Other days, I huddled in the rocker, hearing but not hearing his sweet little cry. Some days it seemed it never stopped. I held him except while he napped. I became familiar with his cycle: a span of days with no mess in which he gradually grew grumpier, a slacking off nursing, and finally, outright crying until I gave him the temporary relief of a suppository. Contrary to regular suspicion, he was not constipated. It appeared to my mother-sense that something within him did not naturally trigger his bowels to move.

“Grain free,” prompted one book. “It could be Hirschsprung’s, which can be naturally treated by going grain-free.” So, I ate grain-free. Five weeks dragged by on my altered diet. Judson didn’t seem to notice my efforts.

His pediatrician listened to my recital of his routine, then ordered a test for Hirschsprung’s.

The test came back clear. I gratefully resumed eating grains, only to meet with new advice the next Sunday. An experienced mother sought me out in the nursery where I took refuge from the noisy fellowship hall, rocking my sonny, rocking, rocking, rocking. “Have you considered dairy-free?”

Well, no, I hadn’t.

“I think you should try dairy-free,” she decided. Like a well-thumbed medical manual, she recounted the reasons for this route.

His pediatrician didn’t approve of the dairy-free idea. I visited her office after three weeks of it. “You need the fats in dairy to keep up your milk supply,” she scolded. “Besides, the first sign of a milk intolerance is blood in the stool, not lack of stool.”

I didn’t mind stopping the dairy-free diet. We tried other things. Judson held enemas in stubbornly. A prescribed dosage of laxative didn’t produce results. At one point, the doctor instructed me to just wait it out with Judson, convinced his bowels would move on their own. Judson outwaited me. By 17 days along, I resorted to suppositories to give my miserable baby relief.

But it wasn’t only the digestive mystery that gave us heartache over my baby. Even on a freshly emptied system, he was cantankerous. Mealtimes became misery. Judson fought when I sat down at the table to join the family for a meal. I became used to pinning him over my shoulder while I quickly ate, one-handed. Except I didn’t become used to it. I never became accustomed to his fussing. I learned to do the housework while he napped, as anything other than tending him was impossible when he was awake.

Church was also a sore spot. Judson acted worse in any place of activity, but he became unreasonable at church. I wrestled with him until he fell asleep, usually in time for me to hear the last part of the sermon.

Fellowship meals were a disaster. Judson screamed. He would let no one touch him other than me, and even then, I couldn’t calm him down. By the time we had fixed plates and fed our little family, I was exhausted and ready to go home. It seemed like he was afraid of something. What it was, I couldn’t figure out.

Gradually I became aware he even acted afraid of Sterling. Whereas our other boys by this age had learned to recognize Sterling as “more fun than Mommy”, Judson didn’t. He pulled away from his daddy. He resisted Sterling’s efforts to make up, clinging to me fiercely.

And my mother-instinct, grounded deep beneath the waves of weariness, responded. In an oxymoron of emotions, I no sooner handed Judson to someone else than his obvious desperation for me tugged at my heart; and I would take him back, nestling him close, calming him down. It seemed even as he ruled and berated and emptied me, his intense need fulfilled me. I didn’t understand it.

“I think you need to get him on a quality probiotic,” my mother-in-law suggested. That sounded good, at least on Sunday evening. Somehow the weeks passed, and I didn’t find time to locate a quality probiotic.

“Try a good multivitamin,” another friend advised after observing us during prayer meeting. “It really could be worms. I knew this little girl who was totally unreasonable; she just screamed and screamed, and once they treated her for worms, it totally cleared up…”

That sounded good, too. It also sounded huge. I didn’t know where to begin research on “worms”, nor did I have the mental space.

When he was about six months old, we had the worst stint with him: almost a week wherein he cried and cried, refusing to nurse or be comforted. We requested an anointing by our ministry. We waited expectantly after the anointing. Within hours Judson was back to his restless fussing. We waited a couple more days before updating his pediatrician. Per her advice, Sterling & I took him to the hospital, where a specialist in pediatric gastroenterology could help us. It frightened us to take our puzzling, vulnerable baby to the hospital. “Pray for us,” we requested as we told our families and brotherhood about it.

By the time we checked in to the hospital, Judson had perked up. The nurse showed us to a room. She laid Judson in the cold, caged hospital bed and dressed him in a coarse gown. While we waited for the doctor to come in, Sterling and I marveled at the change in our son. He lay in the bed quietly, fingering the rails and looking around. Not for three minutes, not for 30, but for an hour, finally drifting off to sleep. This was unheard-of behavior for Judson. We looked at each other sheepishly.

“I feel pretty foolish,” I confessed to Sterling. “What are the doctors going to think when they find this healthy little fellow? What about the huge hospital bill?” I covered my face with my hands.

Sterling shrugged, as puzzled as I. “I think people must have been praying.”

That was the turning point in Judson’s physical wellbeing. The hospital released us the next day, signing a bill of good health in Judson’s report. They couldn’t find anything wrong with our child. Soon thereafter, his bowel trouble cleared up. He became regular as the sunrise, all too regular for the lady who hitherto had needed no extra diapers, wipes, or clothes. We praised the Lord for answered prayer.

But he still cried. Months passed while we looked ahead to each accomplishment: maybe when this tooth comes in, maybe when he starts crawling, maybe when he starts walking. Judson crawled at six months, walked at ten months, ate—or more accurately didn’t eat—table food, and still he fussed. I walked around with a little “leech” on my skirt some days. Other days I didn’t walk. Sterling attempted to hold him while I ate supper, but Judson hated that worse than he hated sitting with me for meals, and I would soon relent to his pleading cries. About the only time he was content was while he slept. Most puzzling was his apparent fear of Sterling and his irrational behavior at church.

“Are we just spoiling him?” I asked Sterling. “Maybe he just doesn’t want to sit still in church like any other baby.”

Sterling thought. “If that was so, then why would he resist fellowship meals so fiercely? That should be a fun time. Or if you were spoiling him, why wouldn’t he want to do fun things like come outside with me, or eat snacks?”

I didn’t know. I didn’t think I was spoiling him, but I couldn’t tell. I thought even a spoiled baby should enjoy being away from its mother occasionally. Not Judson. He rode around with me continually, one hand clutching my neckline, the other hand pushing himself away to see where we were headed. If he didn’t like our direction, he often attempted to steer me by surprisingly strong lunging. His anxious, overly alert actions puzzled me. Perhaps something more was wrong, something relating to his nervous system.

“You know, when we took in my niece, she had bonding issues,” one sister told me over fellowship meal. Judson had his open mouth turned away from her, so we were actually visiting over the hubbub in the hall. “She had never bonded with anyone due to her poor home situation. I took to carrying her around with me everywhere I went until she bonded with me. The way Judson acts insecure, even when he is with you, makes me think he hasn’t bonded. Perhaps that’s why he panics whenever you put him down.” Maybe. But where and when would he have gotten bonding issues?

“Did he have a traumatic birth?” the lady inquired.

I thought it over. “Well, no…” I glanced back at the scary episode in Mexico. Perhaps that had undone the natural bonding process. Or maybe the time in the hospital. Maybe his stint with whooping cough as an eight-month-old. As these moments scrolled through my mind, I realized Judson’s babyhood really had been difficult. Maybe there was good reason his emotional balance was off kilter. He did seem insecure now. Frightened. On “survival mode” all the time, me being his dubious source of momentary safety. If he did have bonding issues, then I would have been doing the wrong thing his entire baby life. I repeatedly tried to let other people, like his grandmothers, hold him, hoping he would realize he was fine with them. It didn’t work. Talking with this lady caused me to look doubtfully at my tactics, worried I had hurt Judson worse by doing this. At least carrying him around all the time would be free.

I procured a baby carrier and took to wearing him as I worked. He loved it, but my back did not. I soon gave that practice up, too, after no hopeful signs of bonding occurred. If my spirit was going to be worn down by caring for this child, at least my back didn’t need to be.

We tried discipline. After all, we were working on raising two other boys, and discipline was not a new thing in our home. It didn’t seem we had done anything different with Judson than we did with the other boys, but the results were certainly different. Judson responded with uncontrollable terror. The soft infant cry was long gone. We were unsure how to teach him to be happy in Sterling’s care, for discipline only seemed to heighten his distress. And how does one teach a child to play away from his mother? After a few exhausting sessions at church, wherein he refused to respond, we began to feel a spanking wasn’t the tool to get through to him. Indeed, it felt we never got through to him. But if a spanking didn’t work, how else could we teach him? I recalled seeing other mothers clamp their hands over their toddler’s mouth to teach them that wailing didn’t bring the desired result. Perhaps he needed to be taught how to stop crying. I tried it for a while.

Shortly after Judson turned one, his behavior reached a terrible climax. He was big enough to refuse direction or pacification. Discipline seemed to make him go crazy. Finally, I reached for a book about child development. One description on a condition called retained fear reflex described our child exactly. With simple therapeutic practice, the book promised, we could correct this. However, we would need an expert in this field to work with us, teaching us the therapy.

“What do you think?” I asked Sterling after sharing the book’s information with him.

His face looked unsure. “I don’t know,” he pondered aloud. “This isn’t what I would have been taught about raising a child. I always thought love, prayer, and consistent discipline were the keys to normal childcare. We have no proof other than fussiness that something is wrong with Judson. I hesitate to label him.”

I did, too. While we both acknowledged the special needs of some children, and the gift of specially trained caregivers, we didn’t want to hastily tack an excusing name on Judson’s behavior.

But the exhaustion of caring for him rolled back in like a fog the next day. We talked about the retained fear reflex again. We’d tried the love, definitely. We’d tried prayer, at least in a measure. The consistent discipline was another matter. Unlike our other boys, it didn’t seem to work with Judson. According to the text on retained fear reflexes, discipline could be accomplishing the opposite of its intention.

“You may call and get an appointment with the therapist,” Sterling decided. “It’s worth a try. She’s a Christian, too, and isn’t suggesting anything beyond physical exercises to retrain the brain.”

So I did. The therapist lived eight hours away, which was nothing to brush aside. But the promise of help seemed worth the drive to us. In the meantime, I shared with a few people what we were thinking. A few of them promised to pray for us. My mother-in-law offered a children’s supplement for calming and focus. I also made it to the health food store and procured a probiotic and multivitamin. The time for the therapist appointment drew close.

“I don’t see how we can go,” Sterling said a few days before. “Our weeks have been super busy, and we are all tired. I can’t see how we can fit in a two-day road trip just for one short appointment. But I guess we’ll have to. If it helps Judson, that will be worth it.”

Tension tugged at my neck, too, just thinking about the trip. That week we made a concentrated effort on Judson’s training. We worked with him firmly, attempting to bring his will into line with ours. He despised it. Any time Sterling took him, he reacted violently. I set aside times each day to sit with him on the sofa, holding his hands and requiring silence, with middling results.

The Sunday before we needed to head out to the appointment, we accepted a dinner invitation to a home we were not very familiar with. I spent the time wrestling with my small son, swallowing mouthfuls of pride and comfort while doing so. Meanwhile, Sterling talked with the men about our struggles with Judson, referencing the idea of his fearfulness and the route of therapy.

“Have you ever thought about how Judson must feel when you discipline him in the way I observed your wife do earlier?” one of the men questioned gently. “I noticed the expression in Judson’s eyes as she restrained him, covering his mouth. He looked terrified. If you really think he has this issue with fear, perhaps you should try looking at discipline from his point of view. One of our children also responded unreasonably to our regular methods of training until I began to describe to them what I was about to do…” With discretion, this brother shared an experience with their child.

Sterling was stunned and blessed by the gentle insight. The men shared a little more. It was as if we had been too close to the situation to fully see it, and the Lord had given us perspective from a wise onlooker. We agreed to cancel the childhood development appointment and rethink our training methods. We decided to try clearly explaining to Judson our expectations and the consequences of disobedience. Instead of restraining him, demanding surrender to our desires, we agreed to use repeated small switches to reprimand his willfulness.

“I’m going to take this week to completely focus on mealtimes,” Sterling decided. “Of course, that means you will take the brunt of this, since you feed Judson two out of three meals. But I will try to take the heavier load. I’m also going to fast and pray for answers for this child. We’ve tried to train him at mealtimes before but have never stuck it out more than a day or two. There’s always ‘something going on’ and we slack off. But this is important. Too important to keep letting ‘life’ interfere.”

I agreed with him. My spirit rose with hope and rest in this decision. Something about the therapy route had not seemed correct, yet we had been desperate for an answer.

That week was tough. The other boys ate alone while I spent extended time at the table with Judson. He screamed at my clear expectation of sitting still and eating. He writhed, he gagged, he cried. I prayed and switched. At supper time, Sterling took over. Judson resisted this still more wildly. The first evening it was three hours before our child obeyed and swallowed a small amount of food for his father. Several more evenings passed with similar time frames. Sterling worked with Judson gently and firmly, speaking to him, spanking, holding. I tried to block out the sound. My commitment to stand behind my husband in this all tussled with my emotions, but I didn’t give in this time when Judson looked at me with begging eyes.

By the end of the first week, Judson showed steps of improvement. He stopped crying at mealtimes. He sat in his highchair, eating a few bites for us obediently. With a comically pathetic expression, he would offer Sterling and I each one of his little paddies to hold while he ate, as if that gave him courage. We continued with intentional training in this area alone. By the end of the second week, his behavior all around had improved. He began to let loose of me, seeking entertainment on his own, toddling around the house with happy babbling. I watched in amazement while he did normal baby things: exploring the toy box, climbing on sofas, dabbling in toilets. He ventured outside alone, soon learning to play with balls and trucks. I stopped giving him the various supplements since he was doing so well.

Then one gladsome day when the boys chorused “Daddy’s home!”, Judson squealed in delight. The next evening when Sterling arrived, he squealed again, this time happily heading for the door. I opened it for him. He toddled to the truck where Sterling was. Sterling carried him into the house. Judson looked at me triumphantly from his daddy’s arms with a burbling comment on the situation. He made no move for me. We knew then Sterling had won his heart. From that time until now, he has been a different child.

Now we watch him with delight. His little countenance is bright and beaming, his eyes clear and content. He is evidently secure. He has become a joy to have around, charming our family with his toddling antics. Not only has he bonded with Sterling, he has widened his circle of acceptance to others as well. He interacts well with his brothers. He responds reasonably to training in other areas. We love him, this third little son of ours.

So what really was wrong with Judson? I think he had a physical abnormality in the first months of his life, causing him discomfort. His was a rocky babyhood. In retrospect, I see that spoiling him crept in unawares.

Somewhere in the transition between need and demand, I began to cater to his little self. It was sneakily gradual. Incredibly early on, he obviously realized that crying controlled me. I couldn’t see it. We couldn’t see it. We couldn’t see it until after we began to take back the parental control in his training. We still don’t know when it happened or how. But this we do know: God’s way works.

Prayer works. The rod of correction works. A wife standing behind her husband as he disciplines his child in love works. In a plan that defies human reasoning, let alone worldly teaching, the process of molding Judson’s will firmly bonded him to his father. This created security in his small world. Sterling is in charge. Judson is at rest and safe in this. It removed from him the burden of controlling his world. He is free to relate to either of us, free from the tyrannical demands of his small selfish nature. Something about the clarity of his daddy being the authority in his life has also established my authority over him.

Over two years have passed since Sterling began turning Judson’s heart and will towards his own. Today, Judson is a joyful, well-adjusted boy. He sits quietly in church and devotions; he enjoys fellowship meals and his friends; he eagerly spends time with either Daddy or Mommy. Stubbornness, anxiety, and mealtimes are three areas that require daily diligence in training him—more diligence than our previous two children needed, combined! But the good news is Judson responds well to discipline. Some days it feels like we aren’t getting anywhere until we look back at how far our son has truly come. We praise the Lord for His intervention in our lives by using a perceptive brother to speak into the situation. God’s Word, God’s way, has the keys for raising a happy child.
